Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that state prosecutors and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) have secured an arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro, accusing him of conspiring to murder four men in the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft operated by the anti-Castro group Brothers to the Rescue.According to the Attorney General's Office, Castro has been charged with one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with an incident in which Cuban military fighter jets shot down two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes over international waters.Authorities said three unarmed Cessna aircraft departed Opa-locka Airport in Miami-Dade County on Feb. After crossing the 24th parallel and flying outside Cuba's territorial waters, two of the planes were destroyed by air-to-air missiles fired by Cuban MiG fighter jets.According to the affidavit, the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba at the time and received no warning before being shot down.The warrant, obtained by the Office of Statewide Prosecution and FDLE, alleges Castro played a key role in authorizing the attack that killed four men with ties to Florida: Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr."Raúl Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy," Uthmeier said in a statement. According to a probable cause affidavit, Castro, who at the time served as Cuba's minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president, was among the final decision-makers who authorized the operation. Investigators allege Castro issued standing orders to military leaders to shoot down aircraft associated with Brothers to the Rescue if they appeared over the sea.State investigators also allege Cuban intelligence agents operating in South Florida infiltrated Brothers to the Rescue and provided flight information to the Cuban government as part of what was known as "Operation Scorpion."Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz called the warrant a "historic step toward accountability" for the four men killed in the attack, while FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein said the case demonstrates that "the passage of time does not diminish the pursuit of justice."The warrant charges Castro under Florida statutes governing conspiracy and first-degree murder. Prosecutors said the offense is a first-degree felony, and the court ordered that no bond be granted.State officials said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be filed.

Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Florida Panthers' fifth annual "Pink in the Rink" Night returned to Amerant Bank Arena on Saturday during a home game against the Seattle Kraken, honoring those who have battled breast and cervical cancer and the medical professionals working to treat the diseases and find a cure.Bill Zito, President of Hockey Operations and General Manager of the Florida Panthers, said the cause resonates with everyone.WATCH BELOW: Panthers host Pink in the Rink to honor breast and cervical cancer survivors"It's all of us, literally all of us." Zito said. "It has a personal touch for everybody. I don't know the situation, but as I'm describing this to you right now, you're thinking of someone. That's the thing everybody." Zito said.Zito said everyone has been impacted by cancer in one way or another — including his own family."My wife, Julie, is a breast cancer survivor and is very active in fundraising,” Zito said. “There will be a day when cancer doesn't exist. There's lots of really virtuous, smart people ready to work. They just need funding and that's where we come in." Zito said."Pink in the Rink" Night extends beyond fundraising, it also raise awareness for cancer research ans shares the resources available for families who are impacted by challenges a cancer diagnosis brings with it. Zito said.Before puck drop, Baptist Health Cancer Care offered their MammoVan, where people at the game could learn more from cancer care staff. They find programs for people who don't have insurance. Whatever it is you need, they'll find a way for you to get treatment to get healthy." Zito said.Fans at the game also received handheld fans — a functional and symbolic item for those going through cancer treatment. But it's also symbolic and it's a reminder of how impactful this night is and how important it is," Zito said. As game attendees wave and use there pink fans, Zito hopes it will serve as a reminder. "So every time you look at your little fan, you think someone's going through chemo, someone's going through treatment and they're using this. And so that connection It can bring every fan just a little bit of a reminder, a little bit of a reminder of why we're doing Pick at the Rink this evening." Zito said.Events like "Pink in the Rink" bring awareness and remind us just how important funding for cancer research is, a cause, like Zito says, that impacts everyone. WPTV is learning that potential road improvements are coming to a busy road in Port St. Lucie County staff are sharing designs and want to hear input from neighbors about a proposed project on Prima Vista Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Neighbors weigh in on Prima Vista Boulevard changesThey plan to improve a section of the roadway from Airoso Boulevard to U.S. Highway 1 by removing the center left turn lanesDan Zrallack, county engineer, said their plan is to replace the center left-turn lanes with a raised median."The center turn lane is often referred to as a suicide lane," Zrallack said. "The more turning movements you have, the more chances you have for accidents by restricting access and putting in the median turn lanes. We can kind of control where those turning movements are and protect the drivers as well as pedestrians walking along the roadway." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, there have been 578 crashes on that section of the Prima Vista Boulevard since 2020. Zrallack said the median will make the road safer. "Statistically, the safety improves by up to like 40 percent or more," Zrallack said. But not every neighbor is sold on the improvements. Kadaysha Wilkins lives on Prima Vista Boulevard and told WPTV the median will make traveling more complicated. "Adding medians or anything else is going to cause more chaos than good," Wilkins said. "Ten to 12 years of living here, I've never seen an issue with our turning lane." Wilkins said it'll make it more difficult to take her niece and nephew to school by using the median instead of driving across the street. "A five-minute ride has turned into a 15-minute travel," Wilkins said.Wilkins said trying to come home could also be an issue."Turning into my driveway, which could have taken two seconds, is that now going to take 15 minutes?” Wilkins said. Zrallack said he hears the concerns and hopes they can address them on Thursday night during their public meeting."We're hoping to get more of that by hearing from the community again and seeing what else we can do to refine the design," Zrallack said.A second in-person public meeting for the project was held Thursday at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center.

Having access to a gym is one thing. Actually using it is another.For Jennifer Frink, working out at home means avoiding some of the things she dislikes about going to a traditional gym.WATCH BELOW: Fitness at Your Door brings fitness trainers to your doorstep"I don't really like the gym, and I usually work out at home," Frink said. "You don't have to wait for machines or deal with people at the gym if you don't want to."It's one of the barriers Kashawn Fraser is trying to address through Fitness at Your Door, a South Florida wellness company that brings personal trainers directly to clients.Fraser said the company has grown to more than 250 certified personal trainers who undergo background checks, serving clients from Miami to Jupiter. The program is also expanding to the Treasure Coast."You can order Uber food to your door ... but to have someone show up for you where it matters the most, that's why this company was born," Fraser said.WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with Fraser to learn why he founded the organization.After playing professional football in the Canadian Football League and having multiple knee surgeries, he shifted his focus from his own fitness to helping others with theirs. "I had three reconstructive knee surgeries back to back," Fraser said. "I have been in your shoes. I've been hurt, I've been down, I've been out of shape, I've been in shape."For clients like Frink, having a trainer come to them can also take some of the anxiety out of going to a gym."You don't want to be on one of those YouTube videos where you are doing it wrong, and people are laughing at you," Frink said.The program also works with people living in 55-and-older communities. Fraser said staying active can be especially meaningful for people approaching retirement who want the energy to enjoy time with their families."You work so hard to get to retirement to enjoy your kids and grandkids and have the best energy you can," Fraser said.Across residential communities, gyms, fitness centers and clubhouses can go underused, even though residents have those amenities close to home. Fraser saw an opportunity to bring the workout into those spaces by having personal trainers meet clients where they already live.Click here to learn more about the program.

A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office.The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situationDeputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. We're always ready."Animal welfare advocates say cases like this highlight the importance of community support, foster homes and animal rescue resources throughout the Treasure Coast.Adoption expected in the coming weeksThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast expects Kali and Amara to be ready for adoption in approximately four to six weeks.Their foster family hopes the sisters will eventually find permanent homes with people who can provide the love and care they deserve."My hope is that they find somebody that needs them as much as they need their human," Jagdeo said.How the community can helpAs Kali and Amara continue their recovery, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says community support remains critical to helping animals in need.The organization is looking for additional foster families willing to temporarily care for animals while they await permanent homes. Protesters gathered in Palm Beach County as part of a nationwide "No Kings" day of action, with local organizers putting a focus on encouraging people to vote early ahead of the November midterm elections.The rally was organized locally by Speaking Up for America - Indivisible. Group leader Susan Foley said Saturday's demonstration marked the organization's eighth rally in two years and its fourth No Kings rally."Today is a special day, our fourth No Kings rally," Foley said. "This one is special because of its mission to vote early."WATCH: Palm Beach County ‘No Kings' rally urges early votingFoley said organizers are encouraging people to cast their ballots early rather than waiting until Election Day."If you vote early, your vote is locked in," Foley said.But for protesters who came out Saturday, the rally was also an opportunity to speak about issues they would like to see addressed both nationally and closer to home.WPTV's Christy Waite listened to protesters like Ann Hunter. She says she wants to see more attention paid to the financial challenges facing families."More consideration to the middle class and people that are in desperate circumstances struggling with their food, healthcare, everyday living expenses," Hunter said.For Cynthia Heller, a former educator, education funding is among the issues that brought her out."I was in education, so I would like to see more money go into education," Heller said.Protesters said events like Saturday's also give members of the community an opportunity to come together around issues that are important to them.One protester emphasized that regardless of political affiliation, participating in the election is what matters."I am happy to see people here, and no matter how they vote, they have to vote," the protester said.The Republican Party of Palm Beach County also responded to Saturday's demonstrations, pointing to Republican policies and the party's growing voter registration advantage in Florida.In a statement, the county GOP credited Gov. A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected when a bus rolls over, including whether wearing a seat belt could create an additional danger.WATCH: AN NTSB EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON SCHOOL BUS SEAT BELTSTwo weeks after the crash, investigative reporter Katie LaGrone put that question directly to Dr. Kristin Poland, a school bus safety expert with the National Transportation Safety Board.The crash killed 16-year-old Adinaluz Prieto Oyola during the morning commute on Oct. According to investigators, the school bus carrying 37 high school students was on its way to Winter Haven High School when another cut slammed into its rear, causing the bus to collide head-on with another vehicle and flip over.Following the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd was asked whether any of the dozens of students aboard were wearing seat belts at the time of impact. "Quite frankly, if you try to make everyone put a seat belt on, then we would have had 37 kids hanging from the roof by a seat belt," Judd said.His comments raise a key safety question: In a rollover crash, do seat belts protect students or potentially put them at greater risk?While Poland said the NTSB cannot yet discuss specifics of its investigation into the Polk County crash, she pointed to what the agency has learned from other school bus crashes."The real risk is when they’re violently thrown during the crash sequence about the inside of the bus, where they hit other occupants, or they could potentially hit hard points inside the school bus," Poland said.According to Poland, properly worn three-point restraints, which include both a lap and shoulder belt, provide the best protection even when a bus overturns."Those seat belts are designed so that students can still release the belts even if they're under tension, like if a student is hanging from the belt," she said.Poland acknowledged that the image of a child hanging by a seat belt after a rollover may sound frightening. But she said the greater danger comes during the crash itself, when an unrestrained student can be thrown around the bus.The NTSB has not determined whether a three-point seat belt could have changed the outcome of the Polk County crash. The school district confirmed the bus involved was only equipped with lap belts as are all the school buses in its fleet, according to a district spokesperson.A safety issue investigated for yearsFor reporter LaGrone, the questions surrounding school bus restraints aren't new. More than a decade ago, she investigated a St. Lucie County school bus crash that killed 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp, who was wearing a lap belt at the time.The NTSB investigated that crash and produced simulations demonstrating the difference between the protection provided by a lap belt and the protection provided when a shoulder belt is added.A few years later, the agency formally recommended that school districts in the U.S. upgrade school bus restraints to include both lap and shoulder belts. Florida was among the states called on to make three-point seat belts state law.What does Florida require?Currently, Florida only requires school buses to be equipped with lap belts, but students are not required to wear them.Nearly a decade after the NTSB's recommendation, Poland said some Florida school districts are moving toward three-point lap-and-shoulder belts. “We're seeing some progress with some of the school districts in Florida moving to the passenger lap shoulder belts,” she said.But our investigation found that the majority of public school buses in the state still have lap belts only.Cost is one hurdle. Still, Poland said installing the equipment is only part of improving student safety. "It's not enough just to have the lap shoulder belts on the bus, there also has to be an entire layered approach to ensure that the students are wearing the belts properly," she said. That approach also requires involvement and oversight from school districts and parents, Poland said.But Poland wants to emphasize that school buses remain the safest mode of transportation for students traveling to and from school, regardless of what kind of seat belts are on board. For Poland, seat belt use on school buses is a major step toward the agency's ultimate goal. "We think we can get to zero fatalities in school buses and that's what we're looking towards," Poland said.

Early voting begins Monday across Palm Beach County and parts of the Treasure Coast, giving voters an opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the Nov. The start of early voting comes after a weekend of No Kings protests across South Florida, where organizers encouraged voter participation and urged residents to make a plan to vote early. The demonstrations, held Saturday in communities including West Palm Beach and Palm Beach Gardens, were part of a nationwide movement protesting President Donald Trump and his administration. This weekend’s events placed an additional focus on voter turnout ahead of the 2026 general elections. When and where can you vote early? Early voting schedules vary by county, with some polling locations opening Monday and others later in the week. There are 28 early voting locations. An additional day of early voting is available Nov. to 4 p.m., with extended hours until 6 p.m. Eligible voters can cast their ballots at any designated early voting location within the county where they are registered. Voters should bring a valid photo ID with a signature. Those without acceptable identification may still cast a provisional ballot. In Palm Beach County, voters can check polling location wait times online and use an optional appointment program to schedule their check-in time. Important election deadlines: The deadline to register to vote in the general election was Oct. Voters planning to cast a ballot by mail have until Thursday, Oct. to request that a ballot be mailed to them. Completed vote-by-mail ballots must be received by election officials no later than 7 p.m. In Palm Beach County, ballots returned to a branch office or secure ballot intake station must arrive by 5 p.m. Election Day polling locations will be open from 7 a.m. Find your early voting location: Voters can find polling locations, county-specific hours and additional election information through their local supervisor of elections: Palm Beach County : VotePalmBeach.gov St. Lucie County: StLucieVotes.gov Martin County: MartinVotes.gov Indian River County: VoteIndianRiver.gov Okeechobee County: VoteOkeechobee.gov

More rain is expected this weekend across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, and WPTV is learning that Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing. Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates. Lucie prepares for rain, flooding concerns Samples added that water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and won't need to be lowered. Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. She said flooding has occurred there for years. WPTV was there when water levels rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she already sent messages to her customers for Saturday. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business." For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said. The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." The project may take years until completion, but Collins said she already thought about moving her business. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

For nearly 40 years, The Golden Girls have entertained audiences with humor, friendship and unforgettable characters. Now, those beloved ladies are coming to South Florida through the touring stage production "Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue."The show arrives at the Raymond F. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach on Oct. 25, bringing Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia back together in a new story that imagines the iconic friends still living under one roof decades after the original sitcom ended.Actor Vince Kelley, who portrays Blanche Devereaux, and Adam Graber, who plays Rose Nylund, say the comedy's enduring popularity comes from its ability to connect with people from all walks of life."It's a very multifaceted answer," Kelley said. "The generational appeal, the nostalgia and stuff like that."He said the sitcom remains a source of comfort for viewers who return to the familiar characters again and again."Women of a certain age who sometimes can feel forgotten or cast aside, this gives them a voice," Kelley said. "The LGBT community obviously has very strong ties. Everybody can kind of identify with one of the girls, so it's easy to see yourself in the show."Full Interview with CastAlthough the original sitcom was set in Miami, the cast believes its themes resonate throughout South Florida."The lifestyle is born from this area," Kelley said. "We're going to be in West Palm Beach. How many people in West Palm Beach are retirees of a certain age who are maybe living this life, living with friends? They have a timeshare; they're doing this."The actors said audiences across Florida often recognize elements of their own communities in the world created by the television series."It's all South Florida," Kelley said. "The alligators, the humidity, banana leaves."The performers also said Florida audiences have embraced the production since it first began touring in the state."We always look forward to coming to Florida because of how solid the fan base is," Kelley said.The production imagines a continuation of the television series rather than a simple tribute show.According to the cast, Sophia has been arrested for operating a drug ring at Shady Pines, while Blanche and Rose launch a dating app for seniors. Meanwhile, Dorothy is forced into the world of online dating and begins a relationship with the very attorney prosecuting Sophia.The result is a fast-paced comedy that blends modern humor with the personalities fans have loved for decades.The show also embraces some of the continuity quirks that longtime viewers know well.During the interview, the actors laughed about references in the original sitcom that seemingly placed Jupiter's Burt Reynolds Dinner Theatre just a short drive from Miami."None of it makes sense," Graber joked. "You just let it happen."For many fans, The Golden Girls represents more than comedy.The cast said audience members frequently share personal stories during meet-and-greet events, telling them how the show connected them with parents, grandparents and close friends.Others describe finding comfort in the sitcom during difficult periods of their lives.That emotional connection continues to help new generations discover Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia long after the series left the air.Whether viewers tune in for the one-liners, the friendships, or the nostalgia, the cast believes the secret is simple: everyone can find a little of themselves in one of the four friends.Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue comes to the Kravis Center on Sunday, Oct. 25, with performances at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.Organizers recommend buying tickets directly through Kravis.org to avoid scams and third-party resellers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. WEST PALM BEACH — Oxbridge Academy is unveiling its first-ever baseball field, built with a $1.8 million anonymous donation that transformed an empty space into a full ballpark right next to the school.WPTV News got an exclusive first look at the new facility, which features fresh-cut grass, new dirt, fencing, bases, a scoreboard and shady dugouts. The new facilities kick off a new era of baseball for the Thunderwolves.The field is a significant upgrade for a team that previously had to leave campus to practice. Senior Carlo Vasquez plays third base, first base and has also pitched for the team."I think it's gonna be good, because we have the field coming. We have a lot of freshmen coming in, so it's gonna be a young program, but for the future, it's gonna be good for them,” Vasquez said.Vasquez said the move will benefit the program for years to come."We used to go drive to Dyer Park and that was where we practiced at. So it was a lot harder, but we made it work. We used to practice on the soccer field,” Vasquez said.Now, instead of commuting, the Thunderwolves will take the field right next to their school."It's going to be great. It's going to be a lot easier. It's going to be easier to get the work in,” Vasquez said.Leading the program is head coach Juan Bustabad, who brings more than 30 years of professional baseball experience to Oxbridge.Bustabad was the school's first baseball coach until 2016; he returns this year excited to coach on the new field."We've been waiting for a long time, and it's finally here and these players are going to enjoy it the whole season,” Bustabad said.Under his leadership, Bustabad said he wants to bring fundamentals and a winning culture to the baseball program."Our goal is to be successful. First of all, you know, as a coach, you always want to win, but you also want to develop,” Bustabad said.The Thunderwolves went 8-8 last year, and Bustabad said this upcoming season the team will be young, with only two seniors on the roster."The most important thing is just relax, have fun, go out there and let's see how many wins can we put together this year,” Bustabad said.Vasquez said he expects the new bleachers to fill up on game days."Honestly, just your classmates coming to the games, having more people out here and just having a good time because you're by the football field. Everyone's just going to be coming. I think it's going to be great. It's going to be really fun,” Vasquez said.On Oct. 20, Oxbridge Academy will host a ribbon-cutting and dedication ceremony for its new baseball complex. The upgraded field is set to host its first games this spring.

Thirty-three years after his uncle was murdered, Brian Kunkel is still waiting for what he considers justice."There's a whole host of emotions with this," Kunkel said. "There's a tremendous amount of anger, and now as we speak, it kind of starts to build back up again."WATCH BELOW: 'It's time': Family seeks execution 33 years after loved one murderedHis uncle, Richard Kunkel, was a 32-year-old local florist remembered by his family as outgoing, generous and full of life."Richard was a fun-loving guy," Brian Kunkel said. Very outgoing — the type of person that literally would give you the shirt off his back."In 1993, Richard Kunkel went to Roosters nightclub in West Palm Beach.Court records show Ronald Knight and two other men went to the gay bar looking for a man to lure away, rob and beat."This was all premeditated," Brian Kunkel said. "He knew what he was doing."Court records show the men befriended Kunkel and convinced him to leave with them. Knight then drove him to a secluded area, where he shot and killed him.The men robbed Kunkel, stole his car and burglarized his home."Richard begged for his life," Brian Kunkel said. "He pleaded not to be shot. He was murdered in cold blood."Two years later, Knight was charged in another killing.In May 1995, 22-year-old Brendan Meehan was lured from Heartbreakers, then a gay nightclub on Olive Avenue in West Palm Beach, taken to a secluded area and killed.Knight was convicted of both murders and sentenced to death in 1998."These people had purposes in life, and it's gone," Kunkel said.More than three decades after Richard Kunkel's murder, Knight remains on death row.Now, Kunkel is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to sign his death warrant."It's been a long and arduous process," he said. "My grandparents are gone. They've passed without closure, and I know, at least in my grandmother's case, she died of really a broken heart.""This needs to be done. It needs to be finalized," Kunkel added. His request comes as Florida carries out executions at a pace rarely seen in the state.Florida executed a record 19 people in 2025. Seventeen people have been executed so far in 2026, with two more executions scheduled.That pace has drawn concern from death penalty opponents and defense attorneys, who warn increasingly compressed timelines could put additional strain on the appeals process."I can't imagine how they're keeping up with it in a way that ensures quality," capital defense attorney Carey Haughwout said.Death penalty opponents are also questioning how the state determines who is executed and when."We don't know how people are being chosen or why," said Grace Hanna with Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.But for Kunkel, the debate over whether Florida is moving too quickly stands in stark contrast to his family's experience.They have been waiting 33 years.Kunkel says his grandparents died without seeing Knight executed. His family has spent decades without Richard."Ron Knight, sitting in a jail, he can see daylight. He eats food, gets medical attention," Kunkel said. "Richard and Brendan, they don't enjoy any of that. They're in the ground, and they're lifeless. Thirty-three years is a long time."For Kunkel, the decades have not diminished the memory of the uncle behind the court records and death sentence."His smile was electric," he said. "He was a really good man."Kunkel said a representative from the Florida Attorney General's Office recently helped expedite a clemency hearing for Knight — a step that could clear the way for Gov. A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man’s possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said. Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home. According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside. During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Knowing an adult woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

More rain is expected this weekend across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, and WPTV is learning that Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing. Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates. Lucie prepares for rain, flooding concerns Samples added that water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and won't need to be lowered. Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. She said flooding has occurred there for years. WPTV was there when water levels rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she already sent messages to her customers for Saturday. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business." For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said. The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." The project may take years until completion, but Collins said she already thought about moving her business. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the police agency said in a news release. "We remain committed to thorough, evidence-based investigations and pursuing accountability when the evidence supports criminal charges." This remains an active criminal case. The Florida Panthers' fifth annual "Pink in the Rink" Night returned to Amerant Bank Arena on Saturday during a home game against the Seattle Kraken, honoring those who have battled breast and cervical cancer and the medical professionals working to treat the diseases and find a cure.Bill Zito, President of Hockey Operations and General Manager of the Florida Panthers, said the cause resonates with everyone."It's all of us, literally all of us." Zito said. "It has a personal touch for everybody. I don't know the situation, but as I'm describing this to you right now, you're thinking of someone. That's the thing everybody." Zito said.Zito said everyone has been impacted by cancer in one way or another — including his own family."My wife, Julie, is a breast cancer survivor and is very active in fundraising,” Zito said. “There will be a day when cancer doesn't exist. There's lots of really virtuous, smart people ready to work. They just need funding and that's where we come in." Zito said."Pink in the Rink" Night extends beyond fundraising, it also raise awareness for cancer research ans shares the resources available for families who are impacted by challenges a cancer diagnosis brings with it. "A wonderful celebration of not just fundraising, but of awareness, empathy, and spirit. Spirit for the fight." Zito said.Before puck drop, Baptist Health Cancer Care offered their MammoVan, where people at the game could learn more from cancer care staff. The Panthers also held a Rose Moment on the ice, honoring both survivors and those actively fighting cancer.Specialty "Pink in the Rink" jerseys were up for auction, with the proceeds going toward the Promise Fund."I mean, they do everything from, I mean, they organize Ubers to get people to hospice. They find programs for people who don't have insurance. Whatever it is you need, they'll find a way for you to get treatment to get healthy." Zito said.Fans at the game also received handheld fans — a functional and symbolic item for those going through cancer treatment. The idea came from one of the Panthers staff Juliana David."In the course of treatment, frequently patients will go through hot flashes or become very warm. So it was an interesting item to provide the fan. So it's not only functional for the patient, it's functional actually living in South Florida because it's so warm. But it's also symbolic and it's a reminder of how impactful this night is and how important it is," Zito said. As game attendees wave and use there pink fans, Zito hopes it will serve as a reminder. "So every time you look at your little fan, you think someone's going through chemo, someone's going through treatment and they're using this. And so that connection It can bring every fan just a little bit of a reminder, a little bit of a reminder of why we're doing Pick at the Rink this evening." Zito said.Events like "Pink in the Rink" bring awareness and remind us just how important funding for cancer research is, a cause, like Zito says, that impacts everyone. To learn more about funding and assistance visit the Promise Fund website.

Protesters gathered in Palm Beach County as part of a nationwide “No Kings” day of action, with local organizers putting a focus on encouraging people to vote early ahead of the November midterm elections.The rally was organized locally by Speaking Up for America - Indivisible. Group leader Susan Foley said Saturday’s demonstration marked the organization’s eighth rally in two years and its fourth No Kings rally.“Today is a special day, our fourth No Kings rally,” Foley said. “This one is special because of its mission to vote early.”WATCH: Palm Beach County ‘No Kings’ rally urges early votingFoley said organizers are encouraging people to cast their ballots early rather than waiting until Election Day.“If you vote early, your vote is locked in,” Foley said.But for protesters who came out Saturday, the rally was also an opportunity to speak about issues they would like to see addressed both nationally and closer to home.WPTV's Christy Waite listened to protesters like Ann Hunter. She says she wants to see more attention paid to the financial challenges facing families.“More consideration to the middle class and people that are in desperate circumstances struggling with their food, healthcare, everyday living expenses,” Hunter said.For Cynthia Heller, a former educator, education funding is among the issues that brought her out.“I was in education, so I would like to see more money go into education,” Heller said.Protesters said events like Saturday’s also give members of the community an opportunity to come together around issues that are important to them.One protester emphasized that regardless of political affiliation, participating in the election is what matters.“I am happy to see people here, and no matter how they vote, they have to vote,” the protester said.The Republican Party of Palm Beach County also responded to Saturday’s demonstrations, pointing to Republican policies and the party’s growing voter registration advantage in Florida.In a statement, the county GOP credited Gov. Ron DeSantis’ policies with Florida’s economic performance and highlighted Amendment 3, a proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot dealing with property taxes.The party also defended President Donald Trump’s approach to judicial appointments and said Republican voter registration and turnout show support for the party’s direction.“Florida has transitioned into a reliably red state, with the Republican Party of Florida maintaining an advantage of over 1.55 million registered voters over Democrats,” the statement said.State voter registration data as of Sept. 30 shows more than 5.67 million active registered Republicans compared with about 4.13 million Democrats, a difference of roughly 1.55 million voters.Amendment 3 would reduce the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5% and make other changes involving how counties and municipalities use property tax revenue.Similar demonstrations have taken place across the region, from Palm Beach County to Vero Beach, as protesters continue to make their voices heard ahead of the November elections.

A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills.The Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support.WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus"We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward," Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said.The Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause.Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti."We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar," AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said.AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys & Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy.For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection."I am a Haitian American. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow," Cesar said.The Boys & Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization.The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns.AmeriCorps members' work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys & Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service.The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments.The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers.Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs.With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys & Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program's previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday during a press conference.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff, chief deputy announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Hazellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, the chief deputy said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said.WATCH BELOW: Dashcam video of chase, bodycam video of arrest in Indian River CountyInvestigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation, the chief deputy said.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. He said the Flock system has aided in other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman.Wadlington was arrested on fleeing and eluding charges, deputies said, in addition to driving a stolen a vehicle. Both agencies said they are working very closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant for his arrest for the homicide very soon."This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Hundreds of residents across the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast gathered this weekend for "No Kings" protests, urging civic engagement and opposing President Donald Trump’s policies ahead of the midterm elections. Anita Smith, a protester, said, "I am really fed up with the way the institution our government is running." Just do a little research on what these people have done that want to get into the office, and what do you think they're going to do for you?" Lyle said. This weekend we're expected to see more heavy rain in our area. This may be exactly the kind of weekend forecast that many people in Port St. Lucie do not want to hear. Last week, parts of the city flooded when torrential rains hit Port St. According to our Stormtrac meteorologists, the city got about four inches of rain in a 48 hour period last week. Roads turned into lakes, water levels in canals rose quickly, and some drivers took their chances and drove through standing water deep enough to possibly leave them stalled with nowhere to go. One homeowner, who has a canal directly behind his house, says he was stunned to see the extent of the flooding. It was the worst he's seen in the two years he's lived in Port St. See also: Trump expected at Mar-a-Lago as Palm Beach road closures, No Kings rallies are planned "When I came out, I was like, Oh, my God! I've never seen it like this before!" said Peter Rodriguez, who lives at the intersection of SW Todd Avenue and SW Broadview Street in Port St. How concerned is he about the possibility of another flood this weekend? "I don't think it's gonna get that high. If it starts getting that high, then I'm gonna start to pray. Not another flood," he said. Luckily floodwater did not get into his house. But the water was deep enough he says, to prevent him from driving out of his driveway. One resident says he feels the city of Port St. Lucie could be doing more to prevent such flooding. "I really think they should do something, I mean really to take care of business, you know because we pay our taxes," said Frank Camarda, a Port St. Lucie resident on SW Leisure Lane. A city spokesman says they'll have Public Works employees on standby this weekend if heavy rain comes, if they need to clear storm drains or move pumps into position to lower water levels in certain areas such as near the intersection of Savona Boulevard and SW California Boulevard. A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

A West Palm Beach woman is facing a felony animal cruelty charge after investigators said her Yorkshire terrier was so severely malnourished that veterinarians gave the dog the lowest possible body condition score before it was euthanized.The investigation began Oct. 2 when Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control officers responded to Access Specialty Animal Hospital in Royal Palm Beach after staff reported a suspected animal cruelty case involving a 7-year-old Yorkshire terrier named King.Veterinary staff told investigators King arrived in critical condition suffering from severe emaciation, a heavy flea infestation and signs of prolonged neglect. According to the affidavit, veterinarians assigned King a 1 out of 9 body condition score on the Purina Body Condition Scale, the lowest possible rating, indicating extreme emaciation.The attending veterinarian told investigators the dog was non-responsive, severely hypothermic and in respiratory and cardiac distress when he arrived. According to the affidavit, the Yorkie was unable to breathe on his own. The veterinarian determined King's condition was the result of a chronic deterioration that developed over weeks or months rather than a sudden illness. Despite emergency lifesaving measures, including intubation and assisted ventilation, the dog's condition remained poor due to the severity of his condition. The veterinarian said the dog's emaciation as among the most severe she had encountered in her veterinary career and concluded King's suffering was most likely caused by prolonged neglect and a lack of adequate care.The affidavit states Marseille and another individual declined an advanced stabilization treatment recommended by the hospital because they could not afford the cost.Hospital staff identified Charlynn Marseille, 33, as the person who brought King to the veterinary hospital. Investigators later confirmed ownership through animal records and an interview at Marseille's West Palm Beach residence, where she acknowledged owning the dog.Investigators also referenced a 2023 complaint involving the same dog. According to the affidavit, a caller reported concerns that King had been left alone for days without food and was crying.Marseille was arrested Oct. 14 and charged with aggravated animal cruelty causing excessive pain or suffering. Lucie say students face dangerous conditions walking to school, including busy roads without sidewalks, speeding traffic and poor lighting . The concerns have drawn renewed attention after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School freshman was struck by an SUV while walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on Wednesday, Oct. Much of that stretch of the busy road has no sidewalks. On Southwest Paar Drive near Winslow Street, a sidewalk runs along one side of the road but not the other. Neighbors say children sometimes have to walk or wait for the bus just feet from passing traffic. The roads are over congested. The roads are not safe for the kids, Port St. Lucie resident Paul Virginia said. Neighbors also worry about speeding and limited lighting, particularly for students walking before sunrise. Irene Ange, who lives near Port St. Lucie Boulevard, said her granddaughter takes back roads to walk to school to avoid speeding cars and roadwork. I’m always afraid for them because there are a lot of cars that like to beat the bus, Ange said. She said the city and school district need to work together to better protect students. They deserve to be safe to walk to school, Ange said. "The city, the school district above all, needs to work with all this and have the children's safety and everything in mind." See also: Port St. Lucie residents weigh in on proposed Prima Vista Boulevard safety changes The city’s sidewalk master plan calls for sidewalks within two miles of schools and connections to major roadways. But residents point to sidewalks that end abruptly, including one on Cashmere Boulevard, and roads where sidewalks are available on only one side. "There needs to be more sidewalks for these kids," said Abby Virginia of Port St. Her husband Paul added, "On both sides of the road." The city has additional sidewalk projects scheduled through 2028. Neighbors say safety improvements are needed sooner. "The simple solution to solve the bus issue here is put a four-way stop," Paul Virginia said. An online petition is urging residents to attend the next City Council meeting on October 26 and call for immediate action to better protect students walking to school.

Lucie man was arrested Thursday night after leading St. Lucie County deputies on a high-speed chase that ended on South Hutchinson Island. The pursuit began in the 9600 block of South Ocean Boulevard when a Patrol Operations deputy attempted to stop the driver of a pickup truck for a traffic violation. Andrew Bolonka, the director of communications for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, said the driver fled instead of stopping, making a U-turn and spinning donuts in the roadway, forcing other motorists to take evasive action. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates After briefly stopping, the driver made another U-turn, cut across lanes of traffic, and accelerated toward the deputy's patrol vehicle. "The deputy tries to stop the vehicle; all of a sudden, the vehicle lunges, takes off, accelerates, does another U-turn, and then starts allegedly heading straight toward the deputy. Which you can see in the body-worn camera, where the deputy makes an evasive maneuver and says, 'Oh, he almost hit me,'" Bolonka said. Members of the department's Special Investigations Unit and deputies in the air assisted in the pursuit. The driver continued to flee even after stop sticks were deployed. Deputies eventually executed a PIT maneuver along Seaway Drive, bringing the vehicle to a stop. Despite repeated verbal commands to exit the truck, the driver refused, prompting deputies to deploy pepper balls into the vehicle. The driver then surrendered and was taken into custody without further incident. The suspect, identified as 37-year-old Joshua Gallagher of Port St. Lucie, faces several charges, including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription, and resisting arrest without violence. He remains in custody at the St. "When people make decisions like this, and they commit an act that puts not only the deputies and other law enforcement officers in peril, but they are also putting the general public in peril. If we can do so safely, we're going to put it to an end," Bolonka said. Authorities expressed relief that no one was injured during the incident. This weekend we're expected to see more heavy rain in our area. This may be exactly the kind of weekend forecast that many people in Port St. Lucie do not want to hear. Last week, parts of the city flooded when torrential rains hit Port St. According to our Stormtrac meteorologists, the city got about four inches of rain in a 48 hour period last week. Roads turned into lakes, water levels in canals rose quickly, and some drivers took their chances and drove through standing water deep enough to possibly leave them stalled with nowhere to go. One homeowner, who has a canal directly behind his house, says he was stunned to see the extent of the flooding. "I don't think it's gonna get that high. If it starts getting that high, then I'm gonna start to pray. Not another flood," he said. Luckily floodwater did not get into his house. Lucie say students face dangerous conditions walking to school, including busy roads without sidewalks, speeding traffic and poor lighting . The concerns have drawn renewed attention after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School freshman was struck by an SUV while walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on Wednesday, Oct. Much of that stretch of the busy road has no sidewalks. On Southwest Paar Drive near Winslow Street, a sidewalk runs along one side of the road but not the other. Neighbors say children sometimes have to walk or wait for the bus just feet from passing traffic. The roads are over congested. The roads are not safe for the kids, Port St. Lucie resident Paul Virginia said. Neighbors also worry about speeding and limited lighting, particularly for students walking before sunrise. Irene Ange, who lives near Port St. Lucie Boulevard, said her granddaughter takes back roads to walk to school to avoid speeding cars and roadwork. I’m always afraid for them because there are a lot of cars that like to beat the bus, Ange said. She said the city and school district need to work together to better protect students. They deserve to be safe to walk to school, Ange said. "The city, the school district above all, needs to work with all this and have the children's safety and everything in mind." See also: Port St. Lucie residents weigh in on proposed Prima Vista Boulevard safety changes The city’s sidewalk master plan calls for sidewalks within two miles of schools and connections to major roadways. But residents point to sidewalks that end abruptly, including one on Cashmere Boulevard, and roads where sidewalks are available on only one side. "There needs to be more sidewalks for these kids," said Abby Virginia of Port St. Her husband Paul added, "On both sides of the road." The city has additional sidewalk projects scheduled through 2028. Neighbors say safety improvements are needed sooner. "The simple solution to solve the bus issue here is put a four-way stop," Paul Virginia said. An online petition is urging residents to attend the next City Council meeting on October 26 and call for immediate action to better protect students walking to school.

A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after deputies responded to a reported domestic violence incident Saturday morning in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood. Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard, where they encountered a man in the front yard. The man went back inside after seeing law enforcement, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office . Deputies say they later contacted a man and woman at the front door. A deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop the weapon, but he shut the door and retreated inside, prompting a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still in the home. As Hunger Action Month comes to a close, Feeding South Florida is continuing to raise awareness about food insecurity affecting families and seniors across South Florida.WPTV's monthlong series visited four hunger-relief organizations throughout the region, wrapping up at Feeding Palm Beach County in Boynton Beach, where leaders highlighted the growing need for food assistance and the programs helping vulnerable residents."There are 1.7 million people all the way from Tequesta down to Key West struggling to put food on the table," said Paco Vélez, president and CEO of Feeding South Florida. “Now we find ourselves in a situation where prices are soaring, not just for fuel, but also for all the goods and services, especially for food.”Vélez said rising transportation and supply costs continue to increase demand at food distribution sites and partner agencies across South Florida."So many families are coming to us, so many families are coming to our partner agencies," Vélez said.At the organization’s Community Kitchen in Boynton Beach, Susan Taves, culinary director for Feeding South Florida, demonstrated how meals are prepared for seniors throughout the region."We make nutritionally balanced meals for mostly non-ambulatory seniors, and we deliver them frozen," Taves said.
