The proposed change would increase costs by about $11 per month, with service potentially starting in 2028 if the city moves forward. “This is something that is nonbinding, but it gives City Council an opportunity to get a sense of the will of the people and what they would prefer to see,” said Scott Samples, spokesperson for the city of Port St. The city emphasized that the poll is not a final decision. A "yes" vote would indicate support for the additional cost, while a "no" vote would signal opposition. However, the results will not automatically change the current trash pickup schedule. City Council controls the trash contract and service levels, meaning any changes would require council approval and an updated agreement with the current waste management provider, FCC Environmental Services. The city also noted that a second pickup would be an ongoing expense and could increase with inflation. “City Council would take this up. They would have to work with the vendor to understand what the logistics of that would be. And then, the City Council would then vote on whether or not to move forward with this,” Samples said. The poll aims to provide city leaders with insight into residents' preferences, but the final decision will rest with the City Council. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. They're excited to serve the town of Jupiter."By 5 a.m. Thursday, Jupiter Fire Rescue's firefighters and paramedics had already answered four calls while introducing the community to the people and equipment behind the new department.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 21-year-old man was fatally shot Wednesday night in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound, and authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. Martin County sheriff's deputies responded to the scene along Southeast Citrus Way, where they found Jarvis Preston with three gunshot wounds to the chest. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand your ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek explained that Preston and the shooter were friends. Witnesses reported that Preston had been drinking heavily throughout the day and began threatening the shooter and others while armed with a gun. "He's talking, I'm going to shoot you, I'm going to hurt you. The shooter walks towards him, now they're at the edge of the road, at which point the deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the shooter called 911 and attempted life-saving efforts before Preston was flown to St. Mary’s Hospital, where he died. Preston’s grandmother, Harriet Ford Gregg, said she heard the gunshots and later saw her grandson lying on the ground. "It was Jarvis laying on the ground out there, and the police officer was reviving him," Gregg said. She shared her grief over losing Preston, who lived with her, saying his empty bedroom is now too painful to face. I'm not going in there," Gregg said. A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said. "I think this is maybe our fourth tank, but yeah, definitely the first project that I've done that's kind of close to my hometown. And we're excited to be back and be a part of it. And it's really cool to be nominated. I hope that we have what it takes to be the winner, but we'll see." Stanley said it’s an honor to have their work recognized nationally, but he takes special pride in seeing it displayed in a place he still calls home: the Treasure Coast. "It's putting Fort Pierce Utilities Authority on the map in a really positive way," said Karyl Bertram, Environmental Laboratory Coordinator at Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. "We're very proud of our drinking water here. And yeah, it's just a really nice, warm feeling to know that we're being recognized for something as beautiful as this." According to Tnemec Company, Inc., one tank will be chosen by the public's vote, while 11 will be chosen by a committee of water tank enthusiasts. The people's choice voting closes on Friday, with the tank of the year expected to be announced next week.

Residents along Brooklyn Lane in Lake Worth say their only road in and out of the neighborhood is deteriorating, raising concerns about whether emergency vehicles will be able to reach their homes."You know it's one way in, one way out, so we're in trouble," resident Gerald Hruby said.WATCH: Lake Worth neighbors fear deteriorating private road could cut off emergency accessFor neighbor Doug Rua, a former EMT and police officer, the biggest concern is public safety."I'm concerned about fire trucks being able to maneuver around it or over it, along with ambulances," Rua said. Lucie community members had a chance to learn more about and comment on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard during a county information session at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center Thursday. The proposal focuses on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. It would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping designed to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down. A majority of the community members spoke out against the plan, saying they don't believe the changes would improve safety. County officials say the changes are intended to improve safety, reduce crashes, and help slow traffic along the corridor. "We understand it's not popular. That's why we have these," said St. Lucie County engineer Dan Zrallack. "We're taking away the ease of access for people who live along this corridor. There's a lot of driveways. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents." County staff estimate the project could cost about $6.1 million dollars, but don't know where that money would come from yet. See also: Jupiter woman sues DoorDash, alleges delivery driver sexually assaulted her County leaders said feedback from the meeting will help shape the project. The proposal is in the early stages. Lucie County still needs to design the roadway, and identify funding sources before any work can move forward. Residents who couldn’t attend the workshop can review plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

WPTV is learning that potential road improvements are coming to a busy road in Port St. Lucie County staff are sharing designs and want to hear input from neighbors about a proposed project on Prima Vista Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Neighbors weigh in on Prima Vista Boulevard changesThey plan to improve a section of the roadway from Airoso Boulevard to U.S. Highway 1 by removing the center left turn lanesDan Zrallack, county engineer, said their plan is to replace the center left-turn lanes with a raised median."The center turn lane is often referred to as a suicide lane," Zrallack said. "The more turning movements you have, the more chances you have for accidents by restricting access and putting in the median turn lanes. We can kind of control where those turning movements are and protect the drivers as well as pedestrians walking along the roadway." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, there have been 578 crashes on that section of the Prima Vista Boulevard since 2020. Zrallack said the median will make the road safer. "Statistically, the safety improves by up to like 40 percent or more," Zrallack said. But not every neighbor is sold on the improvements. Kadaysha Wilkins lives on Prima Vista Boulevard and told WPTV the median will make traveling more complicated. "Adding medians or anything else is going to cause more chaos than good," Wilkins said. "Ten to 12 years of living here, I've never seen an issue with our turning lane." Wilkins said it'll make it more difficult to take her niece and nephew to school by using the median instead of driving across the street. "A five-minute ride has turned into a 15-minute travel," Wilkins said.Wilkins said trying to come home could also be an issue."Turning into my driveway, which could have taken two seconds, is that now going to take 15 minutes?” Wilkins said. Zrallack said he hears the concerns and hopes they can address them on Thursday night during their public meeting."We're hoping to get more of that by hearing from the community again and seeing what else we can do to refine the design," Zrallack said.A second in-person public meeting for the project was held Thursday at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center.

After years of infertility, pregnancy loss and unanswered questions, one Jupiter mother is turning her personal journey into a source of hope for others.The inaugural Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park, bringing together families, wellness providers and community partners with a shared goal: ensuring that no one facing infertility or pregnancy loss feels alone.WATCH: Jupiter woman creates Hope Rising after infertility journeyFor founder Kimberly Malik, the event grew from her own experience navigating five miscarriages and four years of infertility."When you get told unexplained infertility, that's not really what you want to hear and that's not an answer I can accept," Malik said.She spent years researching, advocating for herself and searching for answers before ultimately learning she had a blood-clotting condition that contributed to her losses.Despite the heartbreak, Malik said the experience eventually led her to a larger purpose."Welcomed our rainbow baby on Nov. 8 of 2024, my husband's birthday, and I just felt this calling of don't let others walk alone," she said.That mission became the foundation of Hope Rising.Malik says one of the most difficult parts of infertility and pregnancy loss is the isolation many families experience.The Hope Rising event is designed to change that.Organizers are bringing together local businesses, wellness providers and community partners to create a Support Village where attendees can connect with resources and others who understand the journey firsthand."We can have those that unfortunately are on a fertility journey feel seen and supported," Malik said.Among those helping organize the event is Jenny Frattaruolo, owner of Jupiter Fit Club, who became part of Malik's support system during her fertility journey."Just having resources and having someone along the journey with you is everything," Malik said during an earlier interview.While the event centers around a 5K and fun walk, organizers say the focus extends far beyond race day.Participants will be able to leave messages of encouragement on wooden hearts, honor loved ones through remembrance activities and celebrate children born after pregnancy loss on a Rainbow Baby Wall.The event will also raise money for the Hope Rising Grant, which aims to help Florida families facing the financial challenges often associated with infertility treatment."Fitness is a great way to bring people together, so this race is going to bring a lot of women together and hopefully we can help them find resources," Frattaruolo said.Pregnancy loss remains a topic many families struggle to discuss openly, even though countless people are affected by it.Frattaruolo believes connection can make a meaningful difference."It's one of those, if you know, you know," she said. "I think we will all experience death and grief in our lifetime, but miscarriage is the only death you will experience inside your own body."For Malik, that understanding is exactly why Hope Rising exists.What began as a search for answers has evolved into a movement focused on support, community and hope.The Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park in Jupiter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. This weekend we're expected to see more heavy rain in our area. This may be exactly the kind of weekend forecast that many people in Port St. Lucie do not want to hear. Last week, parts of the city flooded when torrential rains hit Port St. According to our Stormtrac meteorologists, the city got about four inches of rain in a 48 hour period last week. Roads turned into lakes, water levels in canals rose quickly, and some drivers took their chances and drove through standing water deep enough to possibly leave them stalled with nowhere to go. The fastest-growing sport in the world just got more players. This week, the middle and high school students in Palm Beach County got to try pickleball for the first time.On Wednesday, the Palm Beach Royals, South Florida's Major League Pickleball team, brought the sport to Boys & Girls Clubs across the county.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach Royals bring pickleball to Boys & Girls Clubs"It's always fun to try new sports," 10th grader Lucas Phazekas said."I think it's pretty nice. I like it," eighth grader Quinton Lynum said.During the first practice, Palm Beach Royals ambassadors were on the court helping coach the students.Quinton jumped on the court for his introductory lesson."It's pretty complicated, but the more you do it, the easier it is," Lynum said.The ambassadors helped Lynum with technique and taught him the basics of the game."Well, they taught me how to hold a paddle, and when they taught me how to hold it, it kind of helped me. And when they taught me not to hit it so hard, it kind of helped me hit it more in bounds and get more points," Lynum said.Lucas Phazekas said pickleball is like a mix of sports."Tennis, but if it was like ping pong," Phazekas said.Phazekas said after one practice, he is starting to get the hang of it."I mean, I got it down somewhat at least," Phazekas said.New paddles were also donated to the Boys & Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County by Transworld Business Advisors."I hope the kids get to learn a new sport and get to be active and not be on their screens maybe for a few minutes and learning teamwork and learning new skills," Andy Cagnetta said. "We know the Boys and Girls Clubs are always worried about their budgets and where they're going to get equipment. And so we're happy as the business community to help that."Terrance Johnson with the Boys & Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County said the equipment will be put to good use, and any friendly activity to get students up and active is a huge benefit."It helps us save some money and keep some money in our pockets, and they can interact with the equipment for free. It's enough for multiple people to use at once," Terrance Johnson said.After just one hour of playing pickleball, Lynum said all kids should give it a try."I think if you have anything on your mind, this is the type of thing that will kind of get things off your mind and have a lot of fun," Lynum said.

As homeowners in Florida's Panhandle begin navigating insurance claims after Hurricane Isaias, policyholder advocates are sounding a warning."The storm after the storm is already on the way," says Doug Quinn of the American Policyholder Association. "An insurance system that charges more, covers less, and too often fails homeowners when they need it most."WATCH BELOW: 'Storm after the storm': Advocates warn homeowners about insurance claimsQuinn's organization, along with Rebuild: The National Disaster Survivors Association, says insurance companies may leave many homeowners with denied claims and reduced benefits."America is facing a home insurance affordability crisis, and Florida families are on the front line," said Quinn, who is currently in the Panhandle to assist homeowners.The insurance industry responded to the comments by strongly denying them."Bottom line is legitimate claims are not being denied," Mark Friedlander of the Insurance Information Institute said. "If a storm loss is covered by your wind storm coverage in your home insurance policy, those claims are covered."Leaders in Tallahassee and insurance executives insist the insurance landscape in Florida is improving with lower rates as more insurers enter the market after litigation reforms.A poll released by the University of North Florida in September revealed that 63% of Floridians are more concerned about insurance costs than property taxes.

Lucie man was arrested Thursday night after leading St. Lucie County deputies on a high-speed chase that ended on South Hutchinson Island. The pursuit began in the 9600 block of South Ocean Boulevard when a Patrol Operations deputy attempted to stop the driver of a pickup truck for a traffic violation. Andrew Bolonka, the director of communications for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, said the driver fled instead of stopping, making a U-turn and spinning donuts in the roadway, forcing other motorists to take evasive action. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates After briefly stopping, the driver made another U-turn, cut across lanes of traffic, and accelerated toward the deputy's patrol vehicle. "The deputy tries to stop the vehicle; all of a sudden, the vehicle lunges, takes off, accelerates, does another U-turn, and then starts allegedly heading straight toward the deputy. Which you can see in the body-worn camera, where the deputy makes an evasive maneuver and says, 'Oh, he almost hit me,'" Bolonka said. Members of the department's Special Investigations Unit and deputies in the air assisted in the pursuit. The driver continued to flee even after stop sticks were deployed. Deputies eventually executed a PIT maneuver along Seaway Drive, bringing the vehicle to a stop. Despite repeated verbal commands to exit the truck, the driver refused, prompting deputies to deploy pepper balls into the vehicle. The driver then surrendered and was taken into custody without further incident. The suspect, identified as 37-year-old Joshua Gallagher of Port St. Lucie, faces several charges, including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription, and resisting arrest without violence. He remains in custody at the St. "When people make decisions like this, and they commit an act that puts not only the deputies and other law enforcement officers in peril, but they are also putting the general public in peril. If we can do so safely, we're going to put it to an end," Bolonka said. Authorities expressed relief that no one was injured during the incident. Amendment 3 aims to change the property tax structure in Florida by saving money for homeowners and cutting revenue for cities and counties. It could have an impact on the Florida real estate market.A 2025 study by Realtor.com suggests home values in Florida could rise 7% to 9% if the referendum passes, and some real estate professionals say there will likely be an impact.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 could shake up Florida housing market"I don't see them going up to like the 7, 8, 9, 10 percent," says Jeff Lichtenstein of Echo Fine Properties in Palm Beach Gardens.However, he does see a possible rush of buyers entering the market."You better be prepared because if it happens, it will happen fast," Lichtenstein said. "I think there will be a mad rush to get in here, because if not, then you're waiting five years."That's because the referendum requires homeowners to be homesteaded in Florida by Dec 31 to receive the full tax savings right away.New home buyers entering the state would have a five-year waiting period to get the full homestead exemption.The Florida Realtors is publicly supporting Amendment 3 but isn't convinced about property values rising quickly."The cost of home is economically driven," Florida Realtors CEO Margy Grant. "It's a supply and demand conversation, and when inventory increases, prices stabilize and we've seen that in recent months."Amendment 3 needs 60% of the vote to pass on November 3.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. The family has set up a GoFundMe account for donations. Otto Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, has been sentenced to death for the 2021 murder of Richard Benson, a bike shop owner in Fort Pierce. Assistant State Attorney Brandon White, who prosecuted the case, called the sentence justice. "The jury got it right," White said. "This was probably one of the most heinous crimes in the history of our circuit. It was all caught on camera. It was well planned out." During the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed the jury security video from inside the bike shop. They said the video showed Lenke not just killing Benson but torturing him. "He tormented him and basically made Richard's life a living hell, those last two minutes of his life by pouring that accelerant on him and lighting him on fire," White said. White stated that jealousy was the motive behind the murder, as Benson had started dating a woman Lenke previously dated. White said because he was a former police officer, Lenke thought he knew how he could get away with murder. "The defendant used his 20-plus years of experience in law enforcement to plan this attack, to carry out this attack," White said. Benson's family, who appeared via Zoom from out of state, was not present in the courtroom as the judge sentenced Lenke to death. "I think this is something they wanted for Rich. This was justice," White said. The case is not yet concluded, as Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to review all death sentences. Lenke is also expected to appeal the decision. A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. An officer was flagged down by a citizen just after 9 a.m. who reported seeing a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said. Officers say they arrived and found a man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him out, but he was pronounced dead. Police identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are working to determine how the man entered the water and what he was doing before his death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified There were no apparent signs of trauma to the man's body, Santiago said, but he noted the body appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the area, speaking with potential witnesses and looking for surveillance footage that could help investigators determine how the man ended up in the lake, per FPPD. Santiago said investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have played a role in where the body was found. It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs were involved. Investigators are waiting for the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death. CBS12 News will provide updates as more information becomes available.

Having access to a gym is one thing. Actually using it is another.For Jennifer Fink, working out at home means avoiding some of the things she dislikes about going to a traditional gym.WATCH BELOW: Fitness at Your Door brings fitness trainers to your doorstep"I don't really like the gym, and I usually work out at home," Fink said. "You don't have to wait for machines or deal with people at the gym if you don't want to."It's one of the barriers Kashawn Fraser is trying to address through Fitness at Your Door, a South Florida wellness company that brings personal trainers directly to clients.Fraser said the company has grown to more than 250 certified personal trainers who undergo background checks, serving clients from Miami to Jupiter. The program is also expanding to the Treasure Coast."You can order Uber food to your door ... but to have someone show up for you where it matters the most, that's why this company was born," Fraser said.WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with Fraser to learn why he founded the organization.After playing professional football in the Canadian Football League and having multiple knee surgeries, he shifted his focus from his own fitness to helping others with theirs. "I had three reconstructive knee surgeries back to back," Fraser said. "I have been in your shoes. I've been hurt, I've been down, I've been out of shape, I've been in shape."For clients like Fink, having a trainer come to them can also take some of the anxiety out of going to a gym."You don't want to be on one of those YouTube videos where you are doing it wrong, and people are laughing at you," Fink said.The program also works with people living in 55-and-older communities. Fraser said staying active can be especially meaningful for people approaching retirement who want the energy to enjoy time with their families."You work so hard to get to retirement to enjoy your kids and grandkids and have the best energy you can," Fraser said.Across residential communities, gyms, fitness centers and clubhouses can go underused, even though residents have those amenities close to home. Fraser saw an opportunity to bring the workout into those spaces by having personal trainers meet clients where they already live.Click here to learn more about the program.

A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. An officer was flagged down by a citizen just after 9 a.m. who reported seeing a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said. Officers say they arrived and found a man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him out, but he was pronounced dead. Police identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are working to determine how the man entered the water and what he was doing before his death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified There were no apparent signs of trauma to the man's body, Santiago said, but he noted the body appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the area, speaking with potential witnesses and looking for surveillance footage that could help investigators determine how the man ended up in the lake, per FPPD. Santiago said investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have played a role in where the body was found. It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs were involved. Investigators are waiting for the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death. CBS12 News will provide updates as more information becomes available.

Investigators in Martin County are working to determine whether a fatal shooting in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound was a crime or if the shooter acted within Florida's stand-your-ground law. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said the shooter told them he and his friend were on Southeast Citrus Way on Wednesday night when an argument escalated. According to the shooter, his friend repeatedly threatened to shoot him and even showed him a gun. "The deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Sheriff John Budensiek said. Family members identified the deceased as Jarvis Preston. The sheriff’s office has not released the identity of the shooter. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand-your-ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Budensiek said. Dave Aronberg, the former Palm Beach County state attorney who is not involved in this case but has experience with stand-your-ground cases, said the shooter’s account suggests it could fall under the law. "The shooter must have reasonably believed that firing the weapon was immediately necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm," Aronberg said. However, Aronberg noted that if Preston did not pull a gun, never had a gun, or if the shooter was the aggressor, the stand your ground defense would not apply. "You can't start a fight, provoke the confrontation and then shoot your way out of it," Aronberg said. The sheriff said investigators are still working to locate and interview witnesses to the shooting. He added that the final decision on whether charges will be filed will be made in collaboration with the state attorney’s office. A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday during a press conference.WATCH BELOW: Sheriffs announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Hazellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, the chief deputy said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said.WATCH BELOW: Dashcam video of chase, bodycam video of arrest in Indian River CountyInvestigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation, the chief deputy said.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. He said the Flock system has aided in other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman.Wadlington was arrested on fleeing and eluding charges, deputies said, in addition to driving a stolen a vehicle. Both agencies said they are working very closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant for his arrest for the homicide very soon."This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The United Way of Martin County is calling on the community for support as transit services for residents face mounting challenges.The organization says the MARTY bus shutdown last week was just the tip of the iceberg. The United Way has been seeing an increased need for transit services following state budget cuts earlier this year.WATCH BELOW: United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requestsHenry Hayden relies on community transit services to get to and from work. As an adult on the autism spectrum, he and his mom, Leigh Hayden, say his job gives him purpose."It feels like I'm independent. I can do stuff on my own," Henry Hayden said. "I like working because I like to talk to people. I like to get some knowledge.""The gifts that come with having Henry employed — they're so huge," Leigh Hayden said.In August, state budget cuts reduced funding for Community Coach, a program that helps disabled people like Henry get around. The cuts meant any disabled riders under age 70 had to find a new means of transportation."I said I don't know what to do," Henry Hayden said."It was like having the bottom drop out. This is our lifeline, and until you know that, you really don't understand how important something like transportation is," Leigh Hayden said.Carol Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of the United Way of Martin County, says many turned to the organization's "Ride United" program following the Community Coach cuts. It is the same program that Martin County residents are now using amid the MARTY Bus shutdown."When that closed, everything fell on the United Way. It's just really put a strain on us financially," Houwaart-Diez said.Last year alone, "Ride United" provided over 7,600 trips. In the last three and a half months, the organization says it has already completed over 2,800 trips."We need help, we need people to really start looking at how we can get that funding restored because we shouldn't be the only solution," Houwaart-Diez said.Without services like "Ride United," people like Henry Hayden would lose their independence."I'm eternally grateful," Henry Hayden said."Transportation is the piece of the puzzle that hooks to self-esteem to groceries to purpose to his character," Leigh Hayden said.The United Way is calling on the community for help to support the increased need for community transit services.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie continues building sidewalks across the city, residents advocating for safer school bus stops and routes say more immediate measures are needed to protect children walking along busy roads. Lucie resident and grandmother, has been pushing city officials for safer bus stops, pedestrian stop signs and painted walkways, saying children should not have to risk their lives getting to and from school. Green said her concerns grew after watching her granddaughter and other children navigate traffic near their neighborhood off Southwest Paar Drive, where a sidewalk only exists on one side of the street. Green said once the bus drops the children off, the bus driver helps them cross the street to where the sidewalk is. However, the children who live on the opposite side of the street then have to cross back over without help. "Once the bus stopped and the kids were walking, cars were flying by. Literally, if you crossed your foot across that line, a child would have been run over or an adult. So that started my campaign to email our city officials, transportation officials, and we did get an opportunity to speak," she said. Green said she has continued communicating with city officials and transportation officials about potential safety improvements. She is calling for more sidewalks, pedestrian stop signs and marked walkways. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "Kids should be able to just walk along the street and make it home safely, walk to school safely," Green said. She mentioned the recent tragic incident in which a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school in Port St. "My heart goes out to the family. I, too, have lost a child before, so I understand that grief. When I met with city officials right there at the corner, I literally said, 'We don't need to lose another child,'" she told WPBF. Sidewalk projects underway across the city The city says sidewalks are currently being installed through its Capital Improvement Projects and Sidewalk Master Plan. Active projects include Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Alcantarra to Paar, Floresta Drive from Crosstown Parkway to Prima Vista, Kestor Drive, Volucia Drive and Lakehurst Drive. Recently completed projects include sidewalks on Abingdon Avenue, Import Drive, Brescia Street and Grand Drive, as well as Berkshire Boulevard Phase 1 and a Veterans Memorial Parkway connection to the Publix plaza and post office. Upcoming projects include California Boulevard from Crosstown Parkway to Prima Vista and the Peacock Trail at O.L. Park, from Dreyfuss Boulevard to Open View Drive. City officials say the public works department continues to evaluate existing priorities and identify additional locations for future improvements. An updated plan, including proposed future sidewalk locations, is expected to be presented to the City Council for approval in 2027. What about safety before sidewalks are built? The city says it has met with the St. Lucie County School Board as part of the master plan review to discuss school bus stops. City officials say the school board determines bus stop locations, which can change annually based on transportation needs and where children live. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The city also says crosswalks are evaluated as part of new projects. Under federal accessibility requirements, crosswalks must connect to compliant sidewalks and curb ramps at both ends, meaning they cannot be installed independently where accessible pedestrian infrastructure is absent. A push for more neighborhood input According to the city, the previous sidewalk master plan prioritized major roadways, particularly within 2 miles of schools, with the goal of connecting existing sidewalks rather than building isolated sections. The updated plan is expected to expand those connections into more neighborhoods, while continuing to prioritize heavily traveled areas and routes connecting schools, parks and recreational destinations. A call for action For Green, the issue goes beyond her own family. She said every resident has a connection to a child who could face similar dangers. She started a petition asking the city to implement several safety measures to protect children, including: Immediate transverse pedestrian crosswalks Immediate in-street pedestrian crossing signs Speed bumps to permanently slow down reckless drivers "Collectively, together, we’re stronger," Green said. The petition can be found here.

In life, they say it's not how you start; it's how you finish, and for Jayvon Dawson, his football start is one of a kind."Back in Little League, I first played as a quarterback trying to dab on everybody," said Dawson.WATCH BELOW: Jayvon Dawson went from QB to elite edge rusher at Santaluces, earning offer from MiamiDawson was a solid quarterback, but it wasn’t until he got to high school at Santaluces that he was humbled."My coaches were saying, 'You're not going D1 playing quarterback,'" said Dawson.Dawson is 6-foot-4 and more than 200 pounds, so coaches got creative in his first three years on where they'd pay him."He played receiver before we were able to get him on the defensive side of the ball," head coach Samuel Putmon said.That defensive side of the ball is where he shined.His junior year, he was a man amongst boys and had nearly every school you could think of calling."Miami, (the University of North Carolina), Georgia and many others," said Dawson.Dawson was a game-wrecker the last two seasons, getting to the quarterback at ease and stopping almost every run game the Chiefs faced.He was so good the University of Miami pulled out the big dogs during his recruitment."(Defensive coordinator Corey) Hetherman and (defensive line coach) Jason Taylor," said Dawson.Dawson wasn't born when Taylor was dominating the NFL for the Miami Dolphins, so he didn’t even know who was recruiting him until days later."I was looking up d-ends trying to work some moves on my game and get better at my game, and then he popped up playing for the Dolphins. Dawson committed to the school on the spot."I kept God first, always kept him first, I just kept going and being consistent and disciplined,” said Dawson.That positive mindset has him ready to become an early enrollee at The U this December, and before he steps on the campus, his head coach has glowing reviews for the U’s coaches and fans."He's a great kid, a humble kid, a hard worker who does what's asked of him. A suspected fentanyl trafficker is behind bars after investigators say he sold drugs to a person who later died of an overdose, then led law enforcement on a high-speed chase that reached 115 mph and ended in Martin County. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro identified the suspect as 43-year-old James Arthur Green, who he said is a 10-time convicted felon. According to the sheriff, the investigation began after a fatal fentanyl overdose on Oct. Detectives used the victim’s phone to contact Green, who allegedly returned to the victim’s home Tuesday to deliver more fentanyl. Investigators say Green even sent a picture to the victim’s phone showing where he had left the drugs, unaware that he had been communicating with law enforcement the entire time. "Obviously, he didn’t know that this person had passed away. We were communicating with them," Del Toro said. Later that day, investigators say Green attempted to sell more fentanyl during an undercover operation. When detectives moved in to arrest him, Green fled, striking an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office cruiser before leading law enforcement on a pursuit down Interstate 95. Authorities say the chase reached speeds of 115 mph and continued into Martin County. The pursuit eventually ended near Kanner Highway after Florida Highway Patrol troopers deployed stop sticks and performed a PIT maneuver to stop Green’s vehicle. Del Toro emphasized the dangers of fentanyl and the importance of removing suspected traffickers from the community. This is killing our citizens and our community and preying upon people that have substance abuse problems," Del Toro said. "So I’m very, very happy this person’s off the streets right now." Green now faces multiple drug-related charges, along with additional charges connected to the pursuit. He is being held on a $440,000 bond. Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said. "I think this is maybe our fourth tank, but yeah, definitely the first project that I've done that's kind of close to my hometown. And we're excited to be back and be a part of it. And it's really cool to be nominated. I hope that we have what it takes to be the winner, but we'll see." Stanley said it’s an honor to have their work recognized nationally, but he takes special pride in seeing it displayed in a place he still calls home: the Treasure Coast. "It's putting Fort Pierce Utilities Authority on the map in a really positive way," said Karyl Bertram, Environmental Laboratory Coordinator at Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. "We're very proud of our drinking water here. And yeah, it's just a really nice, warm feeling to know that we're being recognized for something as beautiful as this." According to Tnemec Company, Inc., one tank will be chosen by the public's vote, while 11 will be chosen by a committee of water tank enthusiasts. The people's choice voting closes on Friday, with the tank of the year expected to be announced next week.

A nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie is under investigation after allegedly stealing fentanyl from a critically ill patient’s IV bag on June 24 and 25, according to police. "They did an internal investigation where the Department of Health was then notified, in turn notifying PSLPD where we started our investigation in early August," said Officer Brittany McNally, public information officer for the Port St. Police said a family member of the patient reported seeing 54-year-old Leslie Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient’s fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket, and leave the room. "That’s not standard procedure, from what I understand at the hospital," McNally said. "But again, she’s not even assigned that patient. And there was no initial justification for her to even be in that room at the time." Investigators said Pope returned the following evening and approached the IV equipment again, but the family member intervened and stopped her. Hospital video reportedly showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, but investigators said she did not remove any fluid during the second incident. The investigation remains ongoing.

A Miami jury on Tuesday found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro — ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife.Hill, who has played for the NFL's Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery — one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025. The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages.The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence.The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and "treated me like I was, just, a man." Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called "false allegations" made by his estranged wife, while saying in one instance he shoved Vaccaro and “created a hole in the wall."Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself.It wasn't immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill's return to the NFL. He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated that he could be ready to play by November.

With less than 20 days until the midterm elections, new data from the Department of Labor shows the price of gasoline is contributing to rising inflation and higher prices.The numbers show the Consumer Price Index spiked over half a percentage point in just one month and is up 3.7% from a year ago. A 9.1% increase in the price of gas between August and September is driving those numbers as the ongoing war with Iran continues to put pressure on wallets.Despite the higher prices, the Social Security Administration on Wednesday projected a 3.6% cost of living increase in benefits for 2027, meaning roughly $75 a month more for the nearly 72 million Americans receiving Social Security. However, some seniors worry even that increase might not be enough to offset higher prices.RELATED STORY | Social Security checks are getting their biggest raise since 2023. Inflation may eat it anywayRepublicans and President Trump have been forced to defend the higher prices on the campaign trail. In Arizona Wednesday, Trump pledged a swift end to the war with Iran."The prices are all coming down, but when this war ends — it's going to end very soon by the way, very soon," Trump said. "But when the war ends, the prices are going to — they should be much lower."Despite a growing number of calls for the Trump Administration to end the war, it's not clear when the conflict will end, or how the president plans to bring it to a close. The war and higher costs are a major liability for Republicans in the final days of the midterm election campaign, with Democrats frequently invoking the issue of affordability — a top concern for voters — on the campaign trail.

The School District of Palm Beach County spent part of Tuesday night celebrating new academic recognition from the state. But as district leaders highlighted student achievement and school performance, teachers and employees used public comment to raise concerns about salary freezes, staffing cuts and growing pressures inside schools.The contrast unfolded during a school board meeting where Superintendent Mike Burke announced Palm Beach County had been named one of Florida's academically high-performing districts.WATCH BELOW: Teachers raise pay concerns amid academic honors"We are proud to say we are one of those academically high-performing districts," Burke told board members.According to Burke, Palm Beach County was one of just 18 of Florida's 67 school districts to receive the distinction. The designation is based on multiple factors, including district and school grades, compliance with class-size requirements and financial audit reviews."We hit all three criteria, and we are maintaining not just our A rating but this status as an academically high-performing school district," Burke said.The district also received another major recognition from the Florida State Board of Education. Burke announced that 45 Palm Beach County schools were named Schools of Excellence, including 23 elementary schools, 12 middle schools, seven high schools and three K-8 or combination schools.To qualify, schools must rank in the top 20% statewide in performance for at least two of the previous three years."So congratulations to our 45 schools of excellence," Burke said. "We put a lot on their plates as a school district. I want them to know how thankful we are and this board is in their commitment to their schools and their students."The accolades come as district leaders continue promoting Palm Beach County's educational offerings and encouraging families to explore the district's growing number of choice programs.But while school leaders celebrated the recognition, several educators who addressed the board argued that employees responsible for those achievements are facing significant challenges of their own."We see billboards proudly boasting Palm Beach County as the A-rated school district," Jaqueline Major, a teacher with the School District of Palm Beach County, said during public comment. "But please remember it's on the backs of the teachers not in the boardroom that that occurs."The comments come amid ongoing concern over district finances.Earlier this year, district officials warned that declining enrollment has significantly reduced state funding. The district has said enrollment losses resulted in roughly $60 million less in state funding and forced officials to make difficult budget decisions. The district has also eliminated 1,173 positions, although many affected employees were reassigned to other jobs.It has left some employees frustrated that discussions about potential salary freezes are happening at the same time the district is celebrating academic success."We did the heavy lifting, but how are we rewarded with a salary freeze and people forced to work second and third jobs to make ends meet," Major told the board, questioning district priorities."Protect your teachers, show your worth," Major said, adding: "Instead, we're left stranded on the island of financial disparity."The criticism extended beyond compensation. Some speakers raised concerns about staffing reductions, resource limitations and changes affecting school libraries.One longtime educator challenged school board members to spend time working inside schools to better understand what teachers face every day."If you want to run the district effectively, you need information based on reality, not PR," he said. Brewer III, partner at Brewer, Attorneys & Counselors—lead counsel to the coalition. “The West Palm Beach community should not have to fight to ensure its public servants follow the rules. The structure would rise 204 feet and include a pool deck and ballroom terrace facing south toward the historic neighborhood.The developer is Related Ross, controlled by billionaire Stephen M. Base rent begins at $1,117,000 per year with 3% annual increases, with the first nine months of rent deferred, the lawsuit states.The county's own consultant, BAE Urban Economics, valued the property-tax benefit that county ownership gives Related at approximately $2.5 million annually and approximately $1.3 billion over the potential lease term. The county also agreed to commit 590 spaces in the county's public Convention Center parking garage to the two hotels, releasing Related from a prior obligation to construct a parking garage on the hotel site.The complaint also notes that two independent appraisals valued the land at approximately $42.7 million and $43 million, while the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser places the market value of the parcel at $8.8 million. The county agreed to pay $26 million for the land and the completed hotel.The lawsuit further notes that, according to the county's own financial consultant, all projected payments to the county over 97 years carry a present value of approximately $275 million — roughly 3% of the headline figure of nearly $8.5 billion cited by officials.The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the Sept. 29 approval is void and a temporary and permanent injunction barring the county from executing, recording, or funding the transaction until the Board considers it at a properly noticed public meeting, with the full transaction documents made available to the public in advance."The residents of Grandview Heights and the others affected by this program deserve that much," the complaint states.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday during a press conference.WATCH BELOW: Sheriffs announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Hazellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, the chief deputy said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said.WATCH BELOW: Dashcam video of chase, bodycam video of arrest in Indian River CountyInvestigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation, the chief deputy said.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. He said the Flock system has aided in other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman.Wadlington was arrested on fleeing and eluding charges, deputies said, in addition to driving a stolen a vehicle. Both agencies said they are working very closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant for his arrest for the homicide very soon."This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
