Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is promising a broader crackdown on public corruption following the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct but acquitted him of bid tampering. The case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels in Fort Pierce and a nonprofit connected to Mimms’ niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position to benefit the nonprofit and later concealed his involvement. Mimms’ niece served on the nonprofit’s board. The organization received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization for a community center that was never built. Uthmeier pointed to the conviction as an example of the state’s efforts to hold public officials accountable. “We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take,” Uthmeier said. Uthmeier said the evidence showed that “shenanigans took place” to ensure the nonprofit received the award and that Mimms ultimately covered up his involvement. “He will be punished for abusing his office,” Uthmeier said. Uthmeier said his office’s Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway and described the Mimms case as the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to announce. Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. “No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable,” Keefe said. Uthmeier declined to comment on what sentence Mimms should receive. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Mimms is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. Avelo Airlines is adding a new nonstop route connecting West Palm Beach with the North Dallas area beginning in December.The airline announced Thursday that it will begin nonstop service between President Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT) and North Dallas/McKinney National Airport (DTX) on Dec. 17.Flights will operate twice a week, on Thursdays and Sundays. A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said. "I think this is maybe our fourth tank, but yeah, definitely the first project that I've done that's kind of close to my hometown. And we're excited to be back and be a part of it. And it's really cool to be nominated. I hope that we have what it takes to be the winner, but we'll see." Stanley said it’s an honor to have their work recognized nationally, but he takes special pride in seeing it displayed in a place he still calls home: the Treasure Coast. "It's putting Fort Pierce Utilities Authority on the map in a really positive way," said Karyl Bertram, Environmental Laboratory Coordinator at Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. "We're very proud of our drinking water here. And yeah, it's just a really nice, warm feeling to know that we're being recognized for something as beautiful as this." According to Tnemec Company, Inc., one tank will be chosen by the public's vote, while 11 will be chosen by a committee of water tank enthusiasts. The people's choice voting closes on Friday, with the tank of the year expected to be announced next week.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads.Sheriff Ric Bradshaw told WPTV's Michael Hoffman the exemption is connected to the agency’s role in protecting President Donald Trump when he is in Palm Beach County.WATCH: Why PBSO can keep license plate readers on state roadsThe cameras, often referred to as Flock-type cameras or automated license plate readers, capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to help locate vehicles and people.PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people.“The thing that I want people to understand is this: It’s a very good tool to find people that we’re looking for in a law enforcement capacity,” Bradshaw said. “Not just for the heck of it.”The technology has also played a role in several high-profile investigations.PBSO used license plate reader technology during the search for Ryan Routh after the apparent assassination attempt against Trump at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach.Most recently, the sheriff’s office said the cameras were used Tuesday while deputies tracked a robbery suspect. That incident ultimately ended in a deputy-involved shooting.But the continued presence of the cameras on state roads comes after Gov. Ron DeSantis directed the Florida Department of Transportation in August to take action to remove them from state roads.Bradshaw said Palm Beach County’s situation is different.“We filed a brief with the Department of Highway Safety up there in Tallahassee that, along with the Secret Service, and says, ‘Hey, this is why we can’t take them down,’ and they granted us that exemption,” Bradshaw said.That raised another question: If the exemption is connected to protecting the president, why can PBSO use those cameras for unrelated law enforcement investigations?WPTV’s Michael Hoffman put that question directly to Bradshaw.“There were some people who reached out to me and said, ‘Well, if they have an exemption to protect the president, why are they using it for other law enforcement activities?’ How would you respond to somebody with that concern?” Hoffman asked.“Well, because the law enforcement activities came first, the president came second,” Bradshaw responded. “We’ve been using them for six years, so he just became part of the system.”The cameras have also faced scrutiny over privacy and the potential for law enforcement misuse.Hoffman asked Bradshaw what safeguards PBSO has in place to prevent its system from being abused.“If you have the right guardrails, you have the right policies and procedures, you can stop that from happening,” Bradshaw said.“You can’t just put the information in there and say, ‘Gee, I’d like to see where my girlfriend was yesterday.’ This has to be a bona fide law enforcement investigation,” he added.Bradshaw said somebody audits the agency’s use of the system every week.The sheriff also pushed back against broader concerns that license plate readers amount to surveillance.“They call them surveillance. It’s not surveillance,” Bradshaw said. “Surveillance is when I think you committed a crime, and we’re going to follow you 24 hours a day, wherever you go. We’re going to be there watching you. This is just a snapshot of a particular point in time.”Bradshaw also argued there is no expectation of privacy when a person is traveling in public.Hoffman asked, "is there any scenario in which you you would take down these cameras?" "No," Sheriff Bradshaw said"Why is that?" Hoffman followed up. Because they're legal," he said. "They're a great investigative tool. We help the public with them, and it's a crime prevention tool that we use to solve cases."The sheriff said PBSO has license plate reader cameras on county roads in addition to those it has been allowed to keep on state roads.

A multi-vehicle crash on Florida's Turnpike in Delray Beach shut down all southbound lanes Thursday and left two people with serious injuries, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.Troopers responded to a seven-vehicle crash on the southbound lanes of State Road 91 (Florida's Turnpike) at Atlantic Avenue (SR 806).According to FHP, the vehicles were traveling southbound in multiple lanes when, for reasons still under investigation, one vehicle caused a chain-reaction crash involving seven vehicles. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue says the accident spanned across 300 yards of roadway (PBCFR).All southbound traffic was diverted off the Turnpike at the Atlantic Avenue exit, while crews worked at the scene. All lanes have since reopened.According to PBCFR, eight total drivers were taken to the hospital, and FHP says two drivers were classified as trauma alerts with serious injuries. The State Warning Point has been notified, according to FHP.No additional information has been released, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Two West Palm Beach neighborhood associations filed a lawsuit in Palm Beach County circuit court challenging the county's approval of a $26 million deal for a second convention center hotel, claiming commissioners violated Florida's open meetings law when they voted on the transaction with limited public notice.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach County approves second hotel next to convention centerThe Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association and the West Palm Beach Neighborhood Alliance filed the complaint October 14 in the 15th Judicial Circuit. The suit names Palm Beach County, Related Ross affiliates CityPlace South Tower II, LLC, CityPlace Hotel, LLC, The Related Companies, L.P., and CityPlace Retail, L.L.C., along with the CityPlace Community Development District, the City of West Palm Beach, and the City of West Palm Beach Community Redevelopment Agency as defendants.The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners approved the 34-part transaction on Sept. Commissioner Gregg Weiss, who represents the district where the hotel will stand, cast the only dissenting vote, the lawsuit states.Under the deal, the county will advance $26 million from its General Fund reserves to a Related Ross affiliate as construction deposits, acquire the completed hotel at 940 South Rosemary Avenue, West Palm Beach, and lease it back to Related Ross for up to 97 years. The project is an 18-story, 400-room hotel replacing a surface parking lot approximately 45 feet from neighboring townhomes.The lawsuit claims the county gave the public no reasonable notice before voting on the deal. County officials placed the proposed transaction on an "add-on" agenda item just six days before the Sept. 29 vote, invoking a procedure the Board's own rules reserve for emergency circumstances. The complaint says no emergency existed.The full 715-page transaction file was not made available to the public until 8 a.m. 29, ninety minutes before the meeting began. Commissioners themselves received approximately 600 pages of the agreements just five days before the vote.Margaret Frazzini, president of both plaintiff organizations, spoke at the Sept. 29 meeting."Not enough time for us to assemble the people who had something to say," Frazzini said.She also told the Board the process left residents feeling "unheard and invisible."WATCH BELOW: Residents question Related Ross ties on Downtown Development Authority boardAt least one Grandview Heights resident who had participated in previous city hearings on the hotel said he could not rearrange his work schedule on six days' notice to attend the county vote.The county administrator, Joseph Abruzzo, later acknowledged the county had "verbally agreed" with Related to bring the transaction to a vote in September, and that the timing was set in part to accommodate Related's goal to break ground by the end of that month, the lawsuit states.At the meeting, the county attorney told the Board that "the law only requires us to provide a minimum of 24 hours" and that five days' notice was "consistent with our agenda processes."The lawsuit argues that six days' notice — and 90 minutes to read 715 pages of documents — does not constitute reasonable notice of a $26 million, 97-year commitment of public funds and public land. The complaint argues action taken without reasonable notice is "void ab initio," meaning invalid from its inception.The plaintiffs' members live in and around the Grandview Heights Historic District, a neighborhood listed on the National Register of Historic Places on July 8, 1999. The neighborhood's one- and two-story homes, built between 1910 and 1948, sit one block south of the hotel site, across L Street.The hotel is planned for an approximately 1.8-acre parcel at 940 South Rosemary Avenue. The nearest townhomes are approximately 45 feet from the hotel's planned pool deck. The structure would rise 204 feet and include a pool deck and ballroom terrace facing south toward the historic neighborhood.The developer is Related Ross, controlled by billionaire Stephen M. A Related Ross executive told an audience of real estate professionals in 2026 that the company's pipeline in Palm Beach County exceeds $10 billion. Ross sat in the front row of the Commission Chambers during the Sept. 29 vote, according to the complaint.WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach residents push for transparency on downtown redevelopmentResidents said they have raised concerns about the project for years, according to the complaint. 18, 2025 meeting with Related, Grandview Heights residents objected to valet safety hazards and to noise, lighting, and privacy impacts from the planned pool deck and ballroom terrace. The Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association submitted a 14-page written objection to the City's Development Services Director on June 14, 2026.At a City Planning Board hearing on June 16, 2026, plaintiffs' members opposed the hotel, citing traffic congestion, pedestrian safety, and noise and light pollution from the planned pool deck and ballroom terrace. A pedestrian counter installed at the intersection of L Street and South Rosemary Avenue in May 2026 recorded more than 600 pedestrians per day during the low season. The association estimated the count will exceed 1,000 per day "in season."On Aug. 31, 2026, the West Palm Beach City Commission authorized the 18-story, 400-room hotel by adopting Ordinance No. 5179-26 and related resolutions. The approved hotel received three development waivers, including one that reduced required ground-level frontage along L Street from 20% to 9.5%.The county will lease the completed hotel back to Related for an initial 33-year term, with renewal options totaling a potential 97-year lease. Base rent begins at $1,117,000 per year with 3% annual increases, with the first nine months of rent deferred, the lawsuit states.The county's own consultant, BAE Urban Economics, valued the property-tax benefit that county ownership gives Related at approximately $2.5 million annually and approximately $1.3 billion over the potential lease term. The county also agreed to commit 590 spaces in the county's public Convention Center parking garage to the two hotels, releasing Related from a prior obligation to construct a parking garage on the hotel site.The complaint also notes that two independent appraisals valued the land at approximately $42.7 million and $43 million, while the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser places the market value of the parcel at $8.8 million. The county agreed to pay $26 million for the land and the completed hotel.The lawsuit further notes that, according to the county's own financial consultant, all projected payments to the county over 97 years carry a present value of approximately $275 million — roughly 3% of the headline figure of nearly $8.5 billion cited by officials.The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the Sept. 29 approval is void and a temporary and permanent injunction barring the county from executing, recording, or funding the transaction until the Board considers it at a properly noticed public meeting, with the full transaction documents made available to the public in advance."The residents of Grandview Heights and the others affected by this program deserve that much," the complaint states.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Corporations given lucrative government contracts to carry out President Trump’s immigration agenda have contributed millions of dollars in campaign donations to Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterm election.A Scripps News review of Federal Election Commission records shows The GEO Group, the nation’s largest owner of immigration detention centers, is also one of the biggest corporate donors supporting Republicans this midterm election.A GEO subsidiary, GEO Reentry Services LLC, has contributed $4.4 million dollars to MAGA Inc. a super PAC supporting President Trump.RELATED STORY | AI interest groups pour tens of millions of dollars into 2026 election Companies will sometimes make campaign contributions through a subsidiary that is itself not a federal contractor to avoid violating an FEC rule that bars contractors from giving to candidates and political committees, said Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigations at the Campaign Legal Center.“We think that's a really big problematic loophole in the law,” Fischer said. “The reason that federal contractors are prohibited from making political contributions is to prevent pay to play in the contracting process.”The GEO Group donated through its subsidiary as the company reports record revenue tied to President Trump’s administration reopening profit-detention immigration centers closed during President Biden’s term.“Last year was the most successful period for new business wins in our company’s history,” GEO Group Chairman and CEO George Zoley told investors during a public quarterly financial update in August.The GEO subsidiary has also given $1.3 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC focused on keeping the GOP’s majority in Congress.GEO Group did not respond to questions about its 2026 campaign spending.FEC records show political action committees for both GEO Group and CoreCivic, the second largest operator of ICE detention centers, are also contributing directly to dozens of Republicans on the ballot.Several recipients are incumbent lawmakers who sit on committees that set DHS spending levels or have immigration oversight power.Both GEO Group and CoreCivic PACs have given the maximum allowed $10,000 contribution to Rep. Andrew Garbarino, R-New York, who is the chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premiumThe PACs have also donated to Maine Sen. Susan Collins, the top Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Ashley Moody, a Florida Republican who sits on both the judiciary and homeland security committees.The PACs are also giving to the Republican National committee and two main congressional committees working to elect GOP members. GEO Group's PAC has already donated three times as much money to those three committees compared to the 2024 election, the Scripps News analysis of FEC records showed.A CoreCivic spokesperson responded to questions with a statement that said the company supports candidates and elected officials who understand the “limited but important solutions” the company can provide to address national challenges.“Our political engagement is focused on educating policymakers about those solutions and the services we provide,” the statement said.While major corporations often donated to both Democrats and Republicans, GEO Group and CoreCivic’s support overwhelmingly is going to Republicans.CoreCivic’s spokesperson pointed to Democrats refusing to accept donations from certain businesses. Democrats have called for shuttering immigration detention centers.“Political contributions from the private prison industry have become politically toxic for Democrats,” Fischer said. “I think it's very likely just a pure business decision that they see Republicans as being more beneficial to their financial interests. With many federal contractors, they don't see red and blue, they see green.”

Whether your idea of Halloween involves collecting candy with the kids or screaming your way through a haunted house, the South Florida Fairgrounds has an event designed for you.This October, the fairgrounds once again become home to two popular seasonal attractions: Spookyville, a family-friendly Halloween celebration at Yesteryear Village, and Fright Nights, a nighttime attraction featuring haunted houses, scare zones, rides, and entertainment.Spookyville transforms historic Yesteryear Village into a Halloween destination geared toward children and families.Guests can enjoy safe trick-or-treating throughout the village, costume parades, live entertainment, food vendors, and plenty of opportunities for festive family photos. The attraction's historic buildings are decorated with pumpkins, spider webs, fall decorations, and Halloween displays.Visitors can also enjoy rides, a petting zoo, balloon artists, and special performances. Among this year's entertainers is Wizard Aloysius, who brings magic tricks and family-friendly entertainment to the event on select dates.Spookyville runs October 17-18, 23-25, and 30-31.When the sun goes down, the atmosphere changes dramatically.Fright Nights returns to the South Florida Fairgrounds with four haunted attractions, roaming scare actors, carnival rides, live entertainment, food vendors, and a midway designed to test visitors' courage.The event has become a Halloween tradition for thrill-seekers across South Florida and offers an alternative to traveling to larger attractions outside the area.During a behind-the-scenes visit, WPTV's T.A. Walker got a firsthand look at what it takes to become one of the monsters responsible for scaring guests. After receiving scare training, costume, and makeup, he attempted life as a Fright Nights scare actor under the pirate persona "Captain Arby's."The results were mixed.While a few guests played along, many walked by unfazed, proving that creating a memorable scare is much harder than it looks.Fright Nights runs October 15-17, 22-24, and 29-30.The South Florida Fairgrounds offers Halloween fans two distinctly different experiences throughout October. Families looking for safe seasonal fun can enjoy Spookyville during the day and evening, while older guests seeking thrills can test their nerves at Fright Nights after dark.Whether you're searching for treats or tricks, there's a Halloween adventure waiting at the South Florida Fairgrounds.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? A suspected drug trafficker linked to a deadly fentanyl overdose investigation is behind bars after investigators say he fled from detectives, hit a law enforcement vehicle and led authorities on a high-speed chase on I-95 in St. Lucie and Martin counties.Investigators said the arrest of James Arthur Green, 43, came after a weeks-long narcotics investigation that also uncovered a suspected connection to a fatal fentanyl overdose.According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division conducted multiple undercover purchases of drugs, gathering evidence during those operations that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died from an overdose.On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone during another controlled narcotics operation and placed an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs.Later that day, detectives conducted a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly participated in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine.When detectives attempted to arrest him, Green fled, allegedly hitting a sheriff's office vehicle and fleeing onto southbound I-95.Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of approximately 115 mph. During the chase, detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone out of his vehicle.The Florida Highway Patrol and Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it entered Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks before performing a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end.Investigators recovered the one pound of methamphetamine and two ounces of fentanyl associated with the controlled purchase, along with an additional 22 grams of methamphetamine, two grams of crack cocaine and one gram of fentanyl.As part of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigation, Green faces charges including trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of cocaine, four counts of trafficking methamphetamine, sale of cocaine and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.The Florida Highway Patrol also charged Green with two counts of aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer, trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of methamphetamine, two counts of fleeing and eluding, tampering with evidence, reckless driving, dangerous excessive speeding and resisting an officer without violence.According to the sheriff's office, Green was already out on bond in an unrelated Miami-Dade County case at the time of his arrest. Lucie County Jail without bond.The fatal overdose investigation remains active.

WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights.But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport."We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience."Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard."They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."But the lodging is more than just for passengers.Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond."The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

Police are searching for a hit-and-run cargo van driver accused of fatally striking a 44-year-old man riding a gas scooter before he crashed into a nearby business and ran away in Fort Pierce. On Tuesday, the victim was identified as Andy Ramon Martinez-Pantoja. Police officers received multiple 911 calls just before 9 p.m. Sunday about a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, which later was identified as a gas scooter, close to the intersection of Okeechobee Road and 25th Street, near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. A white cargo van was behind the scooter, traveling east on Okeechobee Road, Maj. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier at a briefing Monday afternoon. The van driver fled the scene and made a U-turn to drive in the wrong direction across the median on Okeechobee Road, but he crashed into the side of a building, the Kings Queens Unisex Salon. The man then ran from the scene. Salon owner Sheila Hampton showed the damage, and is thankful no one was inside at the time. Hampton said she feels for the victim and his family. "His family told me he was just leaving from one of his friend's houses and just going home," she said. A second vehicle, a Toyota pickup truck, was also struck, but no one was injured. Lucie County Sheriff's Office K-9 Unit and Aviation Unit assisted Fort Pierce police and the K-9 Unit in efforts to locate the driver. They are in possession of the van. Police described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark-colored top with light-colored pants or shorts. "So, that in itself proves intent that that person knew exactly what they were doing at the time and was just trying to simply get away," Santiago said. Anyone with information should call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Just days after MARTY public bus services abruptly shut down in Martin County, county commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to allow the county administrator to negotiate a new contract with a company that could restore service. The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was among the drivers impacted when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously operating MARTY, abruptly stopped services last Thursday. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials say they are hopeful negotiations with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, potentially allowing buses to begin operating again next week. President Donald Trump used a Western campaign swing on Wednesday to pitch Republicans as vigilant supporters of gun rights and to defend his acceptance of a luxury jet from Qatar to use as Air Force One.At an evening rally in Montana, Trump hewed close to the kind of attack lines that his party wants to hear as the president travels the country, and he warned that the Second Amendment would be “under siege" if Democrats win in November’s midterm elections.But his message was more off script earlier in the day as he visited an economically struggling corner of rural Arizona. Trump opened his remarks there by describing how the new jet parked behind him was a gift from the Qatari royal family.RELATED STORY | Trump in Arizona to support GOP candidates in close midterm races“When you’re given gifts, you take ’em, right?” Trump told the crowd in Bullhead City. “When they give you a 747, you say two words: ‘Thank you.’”Trump’s comments came during the second and final day of a Western swing, part of a midterm roadshow designed to rally the Republican Party ahead of Nov. 3 elections that will determine control of Congress. His first stop was Alaska on Tuesday, where he announced Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project there and pardoned two Alaskans who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations.The president continued to bestow favors in Montana, where he announced a new military testing range that had been sought by the state's Republicans."Montana will help ensure the American military always reigns supreme,” he said.As Americans grapple with persistent concerns about the cost of living, Trump often reverts to some of his personal priorities, including renovation projects in Washington or trappings of the presidency, including the luxury jet.Trump accepted the new plane last year despite strong criticism, including from some of his staunchest Republican supporters.Trump zeroes in on guns while campaigning in MontanaTrump's visit to Western Montana’s 1st District was aimed at boosting House candidate Aaron Flint, a former aide to retiring Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, who was Interior secretary in Trump’s first-term Cabinet.Flint’s opponent is Sam Forstag, a Democratic labor union leader and Forest Service smokejumper, a specialized firefighter who gets to fires by aircraft and parachute.Forstag has said he supports expanding voluntary safe storage of firearms for people in a mental health crisis, but he describes himself as a gun rights champion and he says firearms are relied upon in Montana for hunting and staying safe.Trump, speaking to a crowd of his supporters in a horse show arena in Kalispell, near Glacier National Park, called Forstag “extreme” and said Democrats “will take your guns away if we don’t keep it going.”He noted that Republican candidates Kurt Alme, running for the Senate, and Aaron Flint, running for the House, have earned top ratings from the National Rifle Association.Meanwhile, Democratic Senate candidate Alani Bankhead has earned an F, and Forstag was given a question mark by the NRA because he “refused to fill out a form,” Trump said.He did not mention Seth Bodnar, the independent in the Montana Senate race who is backed by top Democrats in the state.Luxury Air Force One serves as backdrop and speech fodderIn Arizona, soaring music played as the former Qatari jet flew low over the local airport where supporters awaited Trump in the heat. The president, wearing his signature red baseball cap, emerged with a wave and a fist bump and slowly descended the stairs as speakers blasted Lee Greenwood's “God Bless the USA," the song that marks Trump's entrance at campaign events.Air Force One, now wearing Trump's new red, white, blue and gold paint scheme, and mountains filled the background as he started speaking about how he learned that the Qataris had “the best of all the 747s.” He described to the crowd, which was standing in the sun at a rural desert airport to hear him speak, how he called Qatar’s emir and asked to borrow the aircraft before the leader instead offered it as a gift.RELATED STORY | Trump is heading all the way to Alaska in a sign of just how close its Senate race may beMohave County, where Bullhead City is located, has higher poverty and unemployment rates than the state and nation, with a lower per-capita income, according to Census and state unemployment data.Trump also spoke extensively about his aesthetic flourishes around Washington: the White House ballroom that is under construction and a just-completed helipad on the South Lawn, along with a triumphal arch he has planned for the capital city."The fake news media doesn't talk about how well we're doing" as a country, Trump said. Journalists ask him instead about “affordability," he said, pronouncing the word in a dismissive tone.Trump traveled to Arizona to rally support for Rep. Andy Biggs, who is seeking to defeat Democratic Gov. Republicans running in the state's two competitive U.S. House districts, Jay Feely and Rep. Juan Ciscomani, did not attend the event.GOP strategy is shifting as Election Day nearsWith under three weeks left in the campaign, the Western swing comes as Trump’s party has begun retreating from a handful of battleground U.S. House races and Democrats aim to raise money for candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year.The shifting money in the final weeks of midterm campaigns reflects an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on Trump’s low public approval.Trump has kept up a brisk pace of hour-plus-long rallies — new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia called it a “midterm blitz” — in his effort to stem expected Republican losses and fight a historical trend in which the president’s party typically loses seats in elections halfway through their term in the White House.Trump twice won Arizona, in 2016 and 2024, but lost the state in 2020. Montana’s 1st District is slightly less Republican overall than the state, which voted for Trump by double digits in each of his three presidential campaigns.Arizona is the lone swing state in recent stopsHis other visits so far in October have taken him into traditionally solid Republican territory — Alabama, Nebraska, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas — as he weathers low approval ratings, rising costs and the Iran war.Arizona stands out as the lone swing state among the president’s recent stops, though the airport rally was in a county Trump won with 78% of the vote in 2024.Biggs has been a stalwart ally of the president and assisted Trump's attempt to block certification by the House of Trump's 2020 election defeat. A one-time head of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, he's represented a safe GOP seat since winning election in 2016.He faces Hobbs, who narrowly defeated Republican Kari Lake in the governor's race four years ago. Arizona was long a GOP stronghold, and registered Republicans still outnumber Democrats and independents by a comfortable margin, but voters have repeatedly rejected Trump allies and handed the state's top offices to Democrats.Trump said Biggs “will always stand with law enforcement” and took aim at Hobbs, who he said “does the bidding of the cartels” on the U.S.-Mexico border. Hobbs counters that she has strengthened the border by sending National Guard troops there and has boosted local law enforcement funding.

A fire that spread through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon left a father injured and displaced a family, while neighbors and church members rallied to help them begin the cleanup process. The fire happened on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood near St. According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. Lucie County Fire District responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. Crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage. When firefighters extinguished the flames, significant damage was left behind, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot. Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out. He suffered burns to his legs and was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this." By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

More than 100 people gathered Wednesday evening to weigh in on development rules covering 12 acres along South Flagler Drive, where residents say high-rise construction is increasing traffic and encroaching on historic neighborhoods.The city of West Palm Beach held the public workshop at St. Catherine Greek Orthodox Church to collect feedback on zoning regulations within the South Flagler Overlay District. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache attended the workshop and spoke with residents about their concerns.City staff focused the discussion on parking, building density and height. Residents, however, used the meeting to voice broader concerns about what they described as excessive development along the waterfront.“The traffic has increased exponentially,” one attendee said.Residents question neighborhood impactWest Palm Beach has undergone a major transformation, with new construction reshaping its downtown and waterfront.Several residents said they do not oppose development but want city leaders to consider its cumulative effects on traffic, infrastructure and surrounding neighborhoods.“I’m not against developing and making better and bringing value to our neighborhood, but can we take into consideration the overall impact?” one resident asked.WPTV identified at least six new or planned developments along Flagler Drive. Longtime residents said the projects are changing the character of the waterfront and could place increasingly tall buildings next to historic homes.“If we want high-rises, they have a place, downtown or near downtown,” resident Amy Triggs said. “It’s not appropriate to build a high-rise near a 1920s neighborhood.”Resident Jeff Eagle said he opposes a building approaching 200 feet in height near a historic neighborhood.“I don’t want a 190-some-odd-foot-tall building in a historic neighborhood,” Eagle said.City reviewing waterfront zoningIn July, the West Palm Beach City Commission paused waterfront redevelopment approvals for six months while the city reviews its zoning regulations.City officials said property owners have development rights, but the review is intended to keep residents informed and give the community an opportunity to comment before projects move forward.The city is expected to review feedback collected through its community survey on Nov. 4.“The majority of the people all want the same thing,” Eagle said. “And we’ll see who our elected officials are listening to.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. For Mary Nava, building a beauty business in Palm Beach Gardens has meant more than creating a career. After leaving Venezuela and starting over in South Florida, the Latina entrepreneur says she is now able to create opportunities for other women while building the future she wanted for her family through her business, Lashes Brows and Beauty by Mary.Nava told WPTV she came to South Florida about a decade ago with a clear goal, even though she did not yet know what her path would look like.WATCH: Palm Beach Gardens entrepreneur opens doors for Latinas"I need to build a future for my family, for my kids, for me," Nava said.Today, Nava works alongside a team of Latina beauty professionals, an accomplishment she once did not imagine for herself.Building that future required Nava to leave behind the life she knew in Venezuela."I left behind my country. I left behind my family, my profession," she said.After becoming certified in Lake Worth, Nava decided to establish herself in Palm Beach Gardens.The transition presented new challenges. Nava said she had to adapt to a different culture, learn a new language and earn the trust of clients in a community where English was predominantly spoken."One of the biggest challenges I had was build a client from scratch," Nava said. "I needed people trusting in me and my services."But Nava said quitting was never an option."I don't know how, but the only thing I need to know is I couldn't give up," she said.As Nava's business grew, so did her ability to help other women pursue their own careers."Now I can open the door for other women to grow with me together," Nava said.For Nava, that opportunity represents a full-circle moment."This country gave me opportunities, and now I can bring opportunities to someone else," she said.Her story also reflects a deeply personal definition of success. Rather than measuring it only by her own achievements, Nava said she values the opportunities she can create for others and the example she can set for the next generation.That example is already having an impact at home.Nava's daughter, Maiah Rodriguez, said she hopes to follow the work ethic she sees in her mother."When I grow up, I want to be like her and do hard work, just like her," Rodriguez said.For Nava, a journey that began with leaving her country and starting over has grown into something larger: a chance to build a future for her family while helping other women build futures of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads.Sheriff Ric Bradshaw told WPTV's Michael Hoffman the exemption is connected to the agency’s role in protecting President Donald Trump when he is in Palm Beach County.WATCH: Why PBSO can keep license plate readers on state roadsThe cameras, often referred to as Flock-type cameras or automated license plate readers, capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to help locate vehicles and people.PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people.“The thing that I want people to understand is this: It’s a very good tool to find people that we’re looking for in a law enforcement capacity,” Bradshaw said. “Not just for the heck of it.”The technology has also played a role in several high-profile investigations.PBSO used license plate reader technology during the search for Ryan Routh after the apparent assassination attempt against Trump at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach.Most recently, the sheriff’s office said the cameras were used Tuesday while deputies tracked a robbery suspect. That incident ultimately ended in a deputy-involved shooting.But the continued presence of the cameras on state roads comes after Gov. Ron DeSantis directed the Florida Department of Transportation in August to take action to remove them from state roads.Bradshaw said Palm Beach County’s situation is different.“We filed a brief with the Department of Highway Safety up there in Tallahassee that, along with the Secret Service, and says, ‘Hey, this is why we can’t take them down,’ and they granted us that exemption,” Bradshaw said.That raised another question: If the exemption is connected to protecting the president, why can PBSO use those cameras for unrelated law enforcement investigations?WPTV’s Michael Hoffman put that question directly to Bradshaw.“There were some people who reached out to me and said, ‘Well, if they have an exemption to protect the president, why are they using it for other law enforcement activities?’ How would you respond to somebody with that concern?” Hoffman asked.“Well, because the law enforcement activities came first, the president came second,” Bradshaw responded. “We’ve been using them for six years, so he just became part of the system.”The cameras have also faced scrutiny over privacy and the potential for law enforcement misuse.Hoffman asked Bradshaw what safeguards PBSO has in place to prevent its system from being abused.“If you have the right guardrails, you have the right policies and procedures, you can stop that from happening,” Bradshaw said.“You can’t just put the information in there and say, ‘Gee, I’d like to see where my girlfriend was yesterday.’ This has to be a bona fide law enforcement investigation,” he added.Bradshaw said somebody audits the agency’s use of the system every week.The sheriff also pushed back against broader concerns that license plate readers amount to surveillance.“They call them surveillance. It’s not surveillance,” Bradshaw said. “Surveillance is when I think you committed a crime, and we’re going to follow you 24 hours a day, wherever you go. We’re going to be there watching you. This is just a snapshot of a particular point in time.”Bradshaw also argued there is no expectation of privacy when a person is traveling in public.Hoffman asked, "is there any scenario in which you you would take down these cameras?" "No," Sheriff Bradshaw said"Why is that?" Hoffman followed up. Because they're legal," he said. "They're a great investigative tool. We help the public with them, and it's a crime prevention tool that we use to solve cases."The sheriff said PBSO has license plate reader cameras on county roads in addition to those it has been allowed to keep on state roads.

The United Way of Martin County is calling on the community for support as transit services for residents face mounting challenges.The organization says the MARTY bus shutdown last week was just the tip of the iceberg. The United Way has been seeing an increased need for transit services following state budget cuts earlier this year.WATCH BELOW: United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requestsHenry Hayden relies on community transit services to get to and from work. As an adult on the autism spectrum, he and his mom, Leigh Hayden, say his job gives him purpose."It feels like I'm independent. I can do stuff on my own," Henry Hayden said. "I like working because I like to talk to people. I like to get some knowledge.""The gifts that come with having Henry employed — they're so huge," Leigh Hayden said.In August, state budget cuts reduced funding for Community Coach, a program that helps disabled people like Henry get around. The cuts meant any disabled riders under age 70 had to find a new means of transportation."I said I don't know what to do," Henry Hayden said."It was like having the bottom drop out. This is our lifeline, and until you know that, you really don't understand how important something like transportation is," Leigh Hayden said.Carol Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of the United Way of Martin County, says many turned to the organization's "Ride United" program following the Community Coach cuts. It is the same program that Martin County residents are now using amid the MARTY Bus shutdown."When that closed, everything fell on the United Way. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. WPTV is celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month, and we're sharing stories of the people and families helping shape our community.At the Guaranty Building in downtown West Palm Beach, history isn't just preserved inside the walls.WATCH BELOW: HISPANIC HERITAGE: Cuban immigrant family builds lasting legacyIt's part of the family story behind one of South Florida's architecture firms dedicated to preserving history.For nearly four decades, REG Architects has helped design, restore and preserve landmarks across the region whose work can be seen throughout Palm Beach County.But for co-founder Rick Gonzalez, the firm's story began with something much smaller."My father and I, in 1988, with zero money and two drafting tables, rented a very small office space, and we started," Gonzalez said.The company was founded by Rick Gonzalez and his late father, Ricardo Gonzalez, two Cuban immigrants who came to the United States with one suitcase.Together they built a business rooted in architecture, planning and historic preservation."One of the strongest influences was my father," Rick said. "I'd go to construction sites with him, and it was really cool to watch that."Rick remembers following his father to construction sites as a child, watching projects come together and developing a passion for the profession.What started as a small father-son business has grown into an award-winning architecture firm behind some of Palm Beach County's most recognizable projects. Over the years, REG Architects has worked on the restoration of the historic 1916 Palm Beach County Courthouse, which they helped uncover from the building that was constructed around it. They've also worked on projects at Mar-a-Lago, Trump International Golf Club, the Sandhill Crane Golf Clubhouse in Palm Beach Gardens and Havana Restaurant in West Palm Beach, where they got inspiration from a single postcard. Today, the firm is also working on renovations at St. Ann Catholic Church and School in West Palm Beach, expansion projects on the campus, and Spanish-influenced affordable housing developments for the West Palm Beach Housing Authority.Rick said his Cuban heritage continues to influence his work today."Oh my goodness, tremendously. I always loved Cuba and Havana in particular, the study of history and of the historic buildings in Havana," said Rick. "We use historical context when we design buildings. We want to make sure that we tie future building uses to the past."REG architecture prides itself on its diversity, giving credit for the success not just to the company's leadership but to the team working alongside them."We're very diverse, like America. So we have, we have an architect lady from Africa, we have several from Colombia, Cuban Americans, we have North Americans, we have people from everywhere, and that camaraderie, the working together, that's what makes an architectural firm great," said Rick.Today, that mission is being carried forward by the next generation.Rick's son, Ricardo Gonzalez, named after his grandfather, joined the company nearly five years ago and now helps lead the firm's business development and marketing efforts."It's such a legacy and an eagerness inside of me to preserve that," said Ricardo.Ricardo said the influence of his grandfather can still be seen in both the buildings his family designed and the values passed down through generations."He brought it from Cuba. He said, 'Here's our stamp, here's our footprint,' and it's there today," said Ricardo.For Ricardo, preserving history extends far beyond architecture."Continue on the legacies of your elders, your grandparents," said Ricardo. "Continue to tell those family stories."The family's story, which began with a small office, two drafting tables and a dream, now serves as a blueprint for future generations.Ricardo said Hispanic Heritage Month is an opportunity to celebrate culture while honoring the sacrifices and traditions that came before.For young Latinos looking to build their own future, Rick offers simple advice."I would tell young Latinos in general to follow your dream, and if you have an accent, don't worry about it," said Rick.He said success doesn't come from where someone started, but from the work they're willing to put in along the way."Your personality, the hardworking way that you are, is what's gonna get you ahead in this beautiful country," Rick said.For the Gonzalez family, preserving history means more than restoring buildings. It means ensuring the values, traditions and lessons passed down from one generation to the next continue to stand the test of time.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.California mails ballots to all registered voters.The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen votersA separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary.Unclear how many names DOJ flaggedLos Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan confirmed in a statement that his office received the letter and a thumb drive, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls.He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn't yet accessed any files. The letter, which Logan made public, does not specify the number of individuals flagged by the federal government.Logan said his office is working with the secretary of state and attorney general's offices to decide how to proceed. Neither of those two offices immediately responded to an emailed request for comment.“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established,” Logan wrote. “And any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”Nationwide search for alleged noncitizen votersThe Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midtermsAs part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.Election official calls 48-hour deadline “unreasonable”Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state's detailed voter information.Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son , who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later. Now, the family’s decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory. Organ donation advocates say the family’s choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists. The teen’s family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families. “It’s a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it’s the right thing,” said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft. Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector’s office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors. For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family’s decision carries special meaning. “Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place,” Gray told WPTV. Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed. “I know for a fact that I wouldn’t be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair,” he said. Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match. “That’s five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow,” he said. Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States. Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation. “One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives,” Gray said. Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said. “Let’s all be heroes and save lives,” Gray added. Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life’s most difficult moments. “I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others,” Craft said. “If you can help somebody else, it’s an amazing thing.” For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities. In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family’s decision could now help save lives and ensure their son’s legacy continues through the people he may help. Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast. Travelers tell WFLX that limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans. At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WFLX reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go. “In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around,” said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options. A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways’ route between the New York area and Vero Beach has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning. A New York City physician told WFLX the change has affected his work schedule. “I’m a physician working in New York City, and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients’ schedules two days in a row,” he said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO) has identified the robbery suspect involved in a deadly deputy-involved shooting incident that shut down a major Boynton Beach roadway for several hours Tuesday.PBSO identified the suspect as Gregory Dobkins, 51, of West Palm Beach.WATCH WPTV REPORTER MICHAEL HOFFMAN'S REPORT BELOW:The incident unfolded Tuesday afternoon near Woolbright Road, where a large law enforcement presence prompted the closure of the roadway in both directions. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.A PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said.
