Martin County commissioners are moving forward with a proposed one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers, giving the county more time to study their potential impact before allowing new projects to move forward. The Board of County Commissioners unanimously approved the proposal on its first reading Tuesday, Oct. A second public hearing is scheduled for Oct. 27 before the moratorium can receive final approval. The proposed ordinance would temporarily stop the county from accepting new applications for large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas of Martin County. It would not apply to municipalities. Under the proposal, large-scale data centers are defined as facilities with an anticipated peak electrical demand of 50 megawatts or more. County officials say the pause would give them time to study concerns surrounding data centers, including noise, water usage, electricity consumption, wastewater disposal and potential environmental impacts. During Tuesday's meeting, officials also revealed that the county received an application for a data center on Monday, just one day before the hearing. See also: Florida drug trafficking bust leads to 19 arrests, 6 more suspects sought Applications deemed complete before the moratorium takes effect would be allowed to move forward under existing regulations. Commissioner Sarah Heard questioned whether 365 days would be enough time for the county to complete the necessary research. She also asked whether the moratorium could apply to smaller facilities using 20 megawatts or more of electricity. County staff explained that the 50-megawatt threshold comes from state law defining large-scale data centers. Commissioner Edward Campi said the county needs to hear from experts on both sides of the issue before making long-term decisions. Campi referenced a recent visit to Virginia, where he toured an area with approximately 120 data centers and observed their appearance and noise levels. He said the proposed moratorium would provide an opportunity for supporters and opponents to share their perspectives. Blake Capps also supported the proposal, saying the county needs to carefully consider where data centers could be located, including areas within its urban services boundaries. Commissioner Heatherington was absent from Tuesday's meeting. The county first directed its attorney to draft the moratorium in August as concerns grew over the potential impact of large-scale data centers. The proposal will return to commissioners for a second public hearing on Tuesday, Oct. If approved, the moratorium would give Martin County up to a year to review its regulations before accepting new applications for large-scale data centers.

There have been moments during the first five games of the season when Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis has shown the arm talent and athleticism that made new GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and coach Jeff Hafley bring him over from Green Bay to usher in a new era in Miami.There have also been challenges — such as issues with accuracy and decision-making that were evident in Sunday's 31-24 loss to Cincinnati. Willis began the game 0-for-4 and didn’t complete a pass until the second quarter, finishing 15 of 27 for 137 yards and a touchdown passing and rushing. He threw two interceptions. And he lost a fumble for the third game in a row.Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said he's not considering any quarterback changes, but stressed the need for improvement from Willis and the Dolphins' passing game.Hafley also cautioned against placing the sole blame on Willis, who started just the 11th game of his career and is leading a young offense with mostly inexperienced receivers who are still developing chemistry."We need to be better. Malik needs to be better, OK?" Hafley said. The headline is we all need to be better, and I mean that."Willis has completed just 56.2% of his passes this season and has more interceptions (four) than passing touchdowns (two). He appeared unsettled to begin Sunday's game, missing open receivers on a couple of instances and throwing picks to Bengals safety Jordan Battle on back-to-back drives in the second quarter.Still, Willis has shown his ability to elevate Miami's rushing attack with his legs. His 74 yards rushing on Sunday were the most ever by a Dolphins quarterback in a single game. He had a 39-yard run in the fourth that was the longest rush by a quarterback this season, and the longest by a Dolphins QB since Ryan Tannehill had a 40-yard scamper during a game in 2014."So there’s times it’s great,” Hafley said. "And then there’s times when it needs to be better. It needs to be better from him, we need to get the right route run at the right depth. It needs to be better for sure, but there are signs of it. There was flashes yesterday in that game."Willis said he was encouraged by Miami's ability to pull within a touchdown late but added at some point, the young Dolphins will need the results to match their effort."It is too much and too hard to keep saying, ‘We’re just young’ or ‘We’re trying to build this and build that,’” Willis said. "At the same time, we've got to hold each other accountable because we can’t keep doing this to ourselves. If we’re going to be in games versus good teams, we've got to be able to take advantage of it and go and win those games, because there’s no point to be in the game if you can’t go and win it."The Dolphins have stuck with their run-first identity despite losing star running back De'Von Achane for the season a couple of weeks ago. Third-year running back Ollie Gordon has led a solid rushing attack the past two games, and Miami's run blocking has improved.The Dolphins' pass rush was not able to replicate the success it had when it had four sacks against Kyler Murray in Week 4. Miami didn't generate much pressure against Joe Burrow, failing to get a sack in a game for the fourth time this season.Gordon. One week after rushing for a career-high 100 yards against Minnesota, he had 18 carries for 88 yards against Cincinnati, including a 22-yard rush and a 1-yard rushing touchdown. He has three TDs in his past three games, matching his total from last season.Special teams. Chris Tabor's unit has had a rough start to the season and began Sunday's game by giving up an 81-yard kickoff return. Jaylen Wright also fumbled a kick return — before recovering it — and kicker Riley Patterson missed an extra point and had a kickoff fall short of the landing zone.RG Jonah Savaiinaea injured his ankle in the second quarter Sunday, and cornerback JuJu Brents left with a stinger.68.4% — Willis' passer rating through the first five games, which is the worst among the 20 quarterbacks who have started all five of their teams' games this season.The Dolphins have a bye during Week 6, which Hafley said the team will use to get healthy and evaluate the performance of both players and coaches.

October marks National Disability Employment Awareness Month, an annual observance recognizing the contributions people with disabilities make to workplaces across the country.The observance dates back to 1945, when it began as a weeklong national recognition of the contributions of people with physical disabilities. WATCH BELOW: Jupiter Goodwill employee celebrates 19 years on the jobIn 1988, Congress expanded the commemoration to a month, and it evolved to recognize the importance of increasing employment opportunities for people with disabilities, including those with mental health conditions and other nonobvious disabilities. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy, created in 2001, now leads the annual observance. At a Goodwill store in Jupiter, that message can be seen through an employee who has spent nearly two decades putting his own talents to work.WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with Jeffrey McFadden Jr., who has worked at the Jupiter Goodwill for 19 years, but for him, going to work is about much more than earning a paycheck."I like to smile at others, uplift people and make other people smile," McFadden said.Staying with the same employer for nearly two decades is something he and his family take pride in."My dad said that is a big achievement, to be in a job for so long, and it's a blessing to be a part of this atmosphere and get to meet really nice people," McFadden said.He said his path into the workforce included attending Goodwill's transition school, where he received job training."I went to the Goodwill transition school where we get job training, and it helped us get jobs," McFadden said.Abra Joseph, the director of donated goods, said Goodwill's programs are aimed at helping people who face barriers to employment find and maintain jobs."Sixty percent of our team members self-identify as having some type of barrier to employment," Joseph said.She said the goal is to "create an environment where our team members feel valued, respected, and supported."But McFadden's talents extend far beyond his job.At 6 feet, 5 inches tall, Jeffrey has also made his mark on the basketball court as a Special Olympics athlete. He played center, has won multiple gold medals and earned Athlete of the Year honors in 2013."I got my awards and gave a Hall of Fame speech. I still remember that day," Jeffrey said.Perhaps that's the message at the heart of National Disability Employment Awareness Month: with the right opportunity, what's possible can be limitless.

Many Americans say they’ve been confused or even fooled by political ads using artificial intelligence this campaign season, and want more rules governing how the technology is used, according to a new Scripps News/Talker Research poll.More than four-in-ten registered voters say they’ve seen something they thought was real in a political ad, only to later find it was AI-generated. Another 30% said they saw something they weren’t sure was real or AI.Some of the most talked about ads of the campaign have featured AI-generated candidates like Sen. Jon Ossoff in a beauty salon, James Talarico reciting old quotes out of context, and Sherrod Brown overstaying his welcome at a birthday party.More than half of survey respondents (56%) said they have seen Republicans using AI ads, compared with 49% saying they have seen ads for Democrats.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsAnd more than three-quarters of voters say there should be rules around how the technology is used in politics.In the absence of federal regulation, states have passed their own laws aimed at curbing the influence of AI or deepfakes in campaign advertising. Some states require disclosures or bar deepfake videos from being published in the weeks leading up to Election Day. But many of the regulations fail to keep up with the evolving use of what can be a cheap and effective new tool.An analysis from the Wesleyan Media Project from early September found AI tools had been used in at least 164 ads, 69% of which did not disclose AI was used. Eighty percent were from Republicans or Republican-leaning groups.Still, a similar amount of voters in both parties say there should be rules around how the technology is used, according to the Scripps News/Talker Research poll, including 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans.Concerns about how AI could impact areas outside politics also cut across party lines. Large swaths of the country worry about the impact AI could have on their jobs (61%), government institutions (83%), financial institutions (81%), and their physical safety (57%).Nearly 80% say they see content they believe was generated by AI at least once per day.This random double-opt-in online survey of 1,000 U.S. registered voters was commissioned by Scripps News and conducted by market research company Talker Research, in accordance with the Market Research Society’s code of conduct. Data was collected from Sept. The margin of error is +/- 2.2 points with 95% confidence

It’s a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called “one of the best and most respected senators in D.C.” Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put “Alaska first” and emphasizing cost-of-living issues.During Tuesday's rally, Trump announced that Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project that he has been highlighting amid Sullivan's campaign and that it would invest more than $4 billion. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. The White House did not immediately provide further details.Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. And he announced pardons for two men who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations for tampering with federally mandated monitoring devices on certain vehicles.Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedlyDemocrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn’t elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn’t vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide 1964 reelection.Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump’s approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets.Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally. That means the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him.“The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen.The Trump administration has prioritized expanding oil and gas drilling in the state. Vice President JD Vance last week campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan and Republican Rep. Nick Begich.Sullivan recently joined Trump in the Oval Office, where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into the proposed Alaska gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized.Versions of a gas project have been proposed in Alaska for decades.Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan’s home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support for the incumbent.Trump last campaigned in Alaska to try to defeat a fellow RepublicanAlaska is home to around 740,000 people, making it slightly less populous than Denver. It ranks 48th out of 50 states in population, smaller than all but Vermont and Wyoming.Trump nonetheless headlined a 2022 rally in Anchorage opposing Republican Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski after she voted to convict him on a charge of incitement of insurrection during his second impeachment trial, following the attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, who challenged Murkowski that year, but that didn't stop incumbent Murkowski from winning reelection.In Wasilla, Max Christensen was waiting in line for the rally and said he hoped to hear more specifics from Trump about the natural gas project, and said he was “really curious just to see how he’s going to handle things like inflation and gas prices and things like that.”Christensen, 22, said he thinks Trump has been a great president “despite all his flaws and stuff," adding, “I think he really does genuinely care about the people of the United States of America.”This year, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballotTrump has complained about Alaska’s unique elections system. The state has open primaries, in which the four top vote-getters — regardless of party affiliation — advance to the general election, which uses ranked choice voting.RELATED STORY | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premiumThat's led to a scenario where there also will be another Dan Sullivan on the November ballot: retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whom Trump and other allies of Sen. Sullivan have called a sham candidate. Sullivan has denied this, but Trump continued to hammer the other Sullivan at his rally.“They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get things a little confused,” Trump said, as he repeatedly urged his supporters to vote for “the real Dan Sullivan.”Trump also touted Begich, who is facing a competitive challenge from Bill Hill, an independent.Alaska has a history of rewarding candidates with an independent streak — something Vance acknowledged during his trip to Fairbanks last week."In very deep red years, Alaska is competitive. In very deep blue years, Alaska is still competitive,” Vance said. “I think it’s just a reality of the politics of the state.”Independence has been hard to find in the Republican Party, where Trump for years has had total control. Some Republicans facing tough elections have begun tiptoeing away from the president on key issues such as Iran and tariffs, but not Sullivan, who has been vocal in supporting both.Trump also questioned why three Republicans were running against a Democrat for governor and endorsed Bernadette Wilson, who finished third in the August primary but was the top vote-getting Republican. This came at the same time state GOP leaders — including outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy — are urging voters to rank Republicans on the ballot.Many Republicans — despite reservations with ranked voting — have seen a ranking strategy in that race as crucial for Republicans trying to win the seat.Trump's trade war with Canada may also be a factorTrump has also triggered a trade war with Canada, which shares a 1,500-plus-mile border with Alaska and is among the state's most important trading partners.The U.S. banned nearly $1 billion worth of imports from its neighbor — including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles — after previously imposing 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian products. Canada has responded with reciprocal bans and its own import levies, and the back-and-forth could raise prices for Alaska consumers.RELATED STORY | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsMaking Canada an enemy of sorts is "discomforting" for many Alaskans, said pollster Moore.“We associate, I think, probably more closely with the Canadians — more than a lot of the Lower 48," he said.

Lucie family is seeking justice after their German shepherd, Titus, was struck and killed by a truck in a hit-and-run incident last Tuesday on Goodman Avenue. "I want justice served because you didn’t stop; you killed my dog after you hit him," Michelle Baker, Titus' owner, said. Michelle and Dillon Baker, parents of two young children, are struggling to explain the loss to their 11-year-old son and 2-year-old daughter. The incident occurred around noon when the family’s dogs hopped the fence and ran down the road. Despite efforts to track them using GPS collars, the Bakers were unable to locate the dogs in time. "He knew he hit something because he stopped, then he kept going," Dillon Baker said. Surveillance footage shows a silver truck hitting Titus, stopping briefly, and then continuing to drag the dog down the road before running him over. "My dog did not deserve to go out like that," Michelle Baker said. The driver did not return to the scene, and animal control is investigating the incident as a hit-and-run. The family believes the act constitutes animal cruelty. "That’s a crime, that’s a full-on crime, it’s murder," Michelle Baker said. Back at the Baker home, Gypsy, who witnessed the incident, has not been the same since Titus’ death. The family has a message for the driver. "Pay attention, pay attention and care about what’s on the road in front of you," Michelle Baker said. WPBF contacted animal control for further comment on the incident; as of Monday night, they have not responded. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier highlighted the recent conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms at a press conference Wednesday, calling it the first major outcome from the state's newly created public corruption unit and warning that more investigations are underway across Florida.Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier said public officials who abuse their positions for personal gain will face increased scrutiny from his office and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE)."Public officials are held to an even higher standard," Uthmeier said. "If you work in a city hall, serve on a commission, if you hold public office or work for a state agency, you have a duty to serve the public and not use your job to enrich yourself."Last week, a St. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, but acquitted him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024, Mimms used his position to benefit a nonprofit organization on whose board his niece served by helping secure the land deal and later concealing his involvement. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mimms failed to disclose his familial relationship and took steps to influence and cover up the transaction.Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate."The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up," Uthmeier said.According to Uthmeier, the nonprofit later received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for planned development on the property, though he said the infrastructure project never materialized."We'll keep digging," Uthmeier said. "I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going."Uthmeier said since the public corruption unit was launched, investigators have opened more than 25 active public corruption investigations or cases statewide."This is the first big announcement," he said. "You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust."FDLE Larry Keefe said the agency is making public corruption investigations a top priority."When the people of Florida lose their sense of trust in their institutions, it's death by a thousand cuts," Keefe said. Sentencing for Mimms is expected at a later date."This will be the first of many, sadly," Uthmeier said. "I hope we don't have to do too many, but we'll do as many as necessary to ensure the public knows that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers, and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take."

Many Americans say they’ve been confused or even fooled by political ads using artificial intelligence this campaign season, and want more rules governing how the technology is used, according to a new Scripps News/Talker Research poll.More than four-in-ten registered voters say they’ve seen something they thought was real in a political ad, only to later find it was AI-generated. Another 30% said they saw something they weren’t sure was real or AI.Some of the most talked about ads of the campaign have featured AI-generated candidates like Sen. Jon Ossoff in a beauty salon, James Talarico reciting old quotes out of context, and Sherrod Brown overstaying his welcome at a birthday party.More than half of survey respondents (56%) said they have seen Republicans using AI ads, compared with 49% saying they have seen ads for Democrats.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsAnd more than three-quarters of voters say there should be rules around how the technology is used in politics.In the absence of federal regulation, states have passed their own laws aimed at curbing the influence of AI or deepfakes in campaign advertising. Some states require disclosures or bar deepfake videos from being published in the weeks leading up to Election Day. But many of the regulations fail to keep up with the evolving use of what can be a cheap and effective new tool.An analysis from the Wesleyan Media Project from early September found AI tools had been used in at least 164 ads, 69% of which did not disclose AI was used. Eighty percent were from Republicans or Republican-leaning groups.Still, a similar amount of voters in both parties say there should be rules around how the technology is used, according to the Scripps News/Talker Research poll, including 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans.Concerns about how AI could impact areas outside politics also cut across party lines. Large swaths of the country worry about the impact AI could have on their jobs (61%), government institutions (83%), financial institutions (81%), and their physical safety (57%).Nearly 80% say they see content they believe was generated by AI at least once per day.This random double-opt-in online survey of 1,000 U.S. registered voters was commissioned by Scripps News and conducted by market research company Talker Research, in accordance with the Market Research Society’s code of conduct. Data was collected from Sept. The margin of error is +/- 2.2 points with 95% confidence

A major stretch of South Ocean Boulevard in Palm Beach is scheduled to close Friday morning until further notice, prompting traffic changes for residents and commuters in the area. According to the Town of Palm Beach's website, South Ocean Boulevard (State Road A1A) will close between South County Road and Southern Boulevard beginning at 5 a.m. The closure will remain in effect until further notice.Town officials said information about traffic checkpoints, modified bridge-opening schedules and temporary marine security zones is available on the town's Planned Traffic Impacts webpage.The closure announcement comes as federal aviation officials issued a Temporary Flight Restriction, or TFR, for VIP movement in the West Palm Beach area. The notice is scheduled to take effect Saturday, Oct. 17, and remain in place through Sunday, Oct. 18.Similar road and airspace restrictions have been implemented in the past during visits by President Donald Trump to his Mar-a-Lago residence.At this time, neither the Town of Palm Beach nor federal authorities have publicly confirmed whether Trump is expected to be in Palm Beach this weekend.Motorists are encouraged to plan ahead and expect delays in the area surrounding the closure.

Republicans are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising in battleground Senate races as they scramble to defend increasingly competitive GOP seats in the final stretch of the midterms.But when it comes to how far they can stretch a dollar, they’re effectively paying premium prices at Whole Foods while Democrats are shopping deals at Costco.RELATED STORY | Trump is heading all the way to Alaska in a sign of just how close its Senate race may beAcross nine of the most competitive Senate races last month, Republicans cumulatively outspent Democrats on broadcast TV ads by nearly 100% more, $233 million to $121 million, according to AdImpact data, but only saw about 40% more rating points.The disparity comes down to a difference in strategy. Republicans are relying heavily on outside groups, like super PACs, that pay elevated rates for ads and are making big buys late in the campaign, when inventory is stretched.By contrast, Democrats are taking advantage of discounted rates for candidates and earlier, less expensive reservations.At this stage in the game, Republicans are spending more to get less, which means the “shock and awe” of their massive dollar advantage isn’t necessarily translating to an actual impact on the ground, according to veteran Republican strategist John Thomas.A better metric, he said, is to consider the gross rating points, or GRPs, a unit advertisers use to measure the reach and frequency of an ad campaign, independent of how much was paid for it.In those nine races – where outside groups accounted for about 9 in 10 Republican ad dollars, compared to about half for Democrats – Democrats paid $201 per GRP, while Republicans paid about $274.In some races in September, Democrats actually outpaced Republicans in GRPs, completely overcoming their spending edge.In North Carolina, for example, Republicans outspent Democrats by about $17 million to $14 million on TV ads in September, as former Gov. Roy Cooper poses a major threat to former RNC Chair Michael Whatley and the GOP chances of holding Sen. But Democrats got more than 71,000 GRPs from their spend while Republicans got about 58,000. And at the beginning of October – recognizing the costly, difficult road ahead for Whatley – Republicans actually began cutting their remaining ad bookings by about $15 million.Democrats were also outspent last month by Republicans in Maine by about 32%, another premier battleground race where former state Sen. Troy Jackson is looking to unseat veteran GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who has received major backing from national Republicans. But here, again, despite being outspent, Democrats got 6% more GRPs for their money.Even in Texas – where Democrats were blasted by Republican ad money in September, outspent more than 4 times over – the GRP gap was proportionally much smaller. Republicans got only 2.6 times more GRPs.A GOP super PAC had to spend more than $22 million to air its top ad, touting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s record as a prosecutor, about 15,500 times in September. Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico’s campaign spent a little under $4 million to air its most aired ad, casting Paxton as “the most corrupt politician in Texas,” about 8,000 times. That amounts to less than one-fifth the spending for about half the airtime.Lauren French, communications director for Senate Majority PAC, a leading Democratic super PAC, also emphasized that buying TV late in the cycle becomes exorbitantly expensive. “The nitty-gritty of campaigning is that not all ad space costs the same,” she said.“If you are buying something in February, it’s going to be a lot cheaper, and you’re going to get a lot more bang for your buck than, say, if you’re buying it in September. So that’s why you’re seeing this huge disconnect between what Republicans are paying and what Democrats are paying on average in some of these races,” French said.In seven of the top nine Senate races by total TV and radio ad spending in September, Democrats paid less per GRP than Republicans.The two exceptions were New Hampshire and Alaska. Confident in their nominees, Republicans were able to secure comparable or better rates in both states’ key markets. In New Hampshire, this was reinforced by Republicans allocating relatively more to cheaper secondary markets.“Broadly speaking, Republicans are using their money pretty ineffectively, and public polling is saying that people are not seeing their ads as much as one would expect. So, by that definition alone, some of their money is being set on fire. We are being outspent in a lot of these states, which means we have to make more strategic decisions,” French said.Thomas said that Texas, in particular, was emblematic of this effect, with GOP outside groups mounting an urgent rescue effort for Paxton and pouring money into the state. He noted that Paxton allies had taken to buying ad time on national NFL broadcasts because local markets had grown so crowded. That’s why people across the country are seeing Texas Senate ads in games that don’t include the Dallas Cowboys or Houston Texans.RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election Day“In some cases, because the commercial rate is so high in a local, like a Houston spot, it actually sometimes can be cheaper to buy a national spot,” he said.Democrats’ efficiency advantage might have been much greater, given their candidates have consistently raised more money their Republican opponents on a campaign-to-campaign basis, allowing them to spend more directly on their own ads at cheap rates.But thanks to a recent Supreme Court ruling, for the first time this year, national party committees can take advantage of candidate ad rates through coordinated buys.This means well-funded national committees like the National Republican Congressional Committee or National Republican Senate Committee can team up with candidates – like Mike Rogers in Michigan or Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio – and foot the bill for pricey ad campaigns while getting candidate discounts.The expansion of coordinated buying has allowed Republicans to blunt the Democratic candidate fundraising advantage. Democrats can do the same, but the GOP has taken to it far more aggressively: In September, GOP advertisers spent more than $30 million on coordinated ad buys, compared to about $5 million from Democrats.Outside groups like super PACs still play a dominant role, however, due to their unique ability to accept unlimited donations and make unlimited expenditures.“The money is actually very, very inefficient, but the benefit, even with the inefficiency of a super PAC, is one or two people can cut checks and fund the whole thing,” Thomas said.

Lucie Boulevard say more needs to be done to protect pedestrians as construction continues on the busy road. Their concerns come after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died from injuries he suffered when he was hit by an SUV while walking to school. Police say the freshman was walking along the edge of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on the morning of Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He was pronounced clinically deceased two days later. His family chose to donate his organs . Much of the roadway remains under construction, and there are no sidewalks along large sections of the corridor. Recent heavy rain also left portions of the shoulder flooded, further limiting space for pedestrians. "He was just going to school," said neighbor Irene Ange. "He was just starting his high school year. He had the right to be safe." Irene Ange, who has lived near the boulevard for more than two decades, says students often walk or bike close to traffic, sometimes before sunrise. The stretch of road is dangerous, Ange said. It’s very dark, and drivers are not following the speed limits. Ange said she saw first responders rushing to the crash site and was heartbroken for the student and his family. See also: Suspect booked into Martin County Jail after undercover drug sting, sheriff says The teen’s mother told CBS12 by phone that her son was a people person who made friends easily. She said the family does not want this to happen to another child. The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four and adding sidewalks on both sides of the road. FDOT says the sidewalks will be eight to 10 feet wide. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2028, with an estimated cost of about $25.6 million. CBS 12 saw crews building sidewalks several blocks from where the crash happened. FDOT did not respond to questions about what pedestrian safety measures are in place while construction continues. "No accountability with that response because now there's another death," Ange said. Ange says more needs to be done now to keep children safe on their way to school. "This did not have to happen to this family," Ange said. The family now have to mourn him." The driver initially told officers he believed he had struck a construction barrel and has been cooperating with investigators. It remains unclear whether any charges will be filed.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives announced Friday it will no longer enforce National Firearms Act registration and approval requirements for suppressors, short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns.The move eliminates what was often a months-long process that required buyers to obtain federal approval, register the items with the government and pay a tax stamp before taking possession. Federal background checks are still required.For firearm retailers in West Palm Beach, the change is already having an impact.At We Kick Brass, owner Mike Perez said customers previously had to navigate a lengthy approval process to legally purchase suppressors and certain firearms regulated under the National Firearms Act."People were legally able to own these firearms," Perez said. "They just had to wait a longer process. It had to get ATF approval."For decades, suppressors and short-barreled rifles and shotguns were subject to National Firearms Act requirements that included registration, federal approval and a tax stamp.The ATF announced Friday it will no longer enforce those requirements for those items.The move follows a federal court ruling in Texas involving National Firearms Act registration requirements and comes after Congress reduced the tax stamp fee from $200 to zero.Perez said the biggest change is the amount of paperwork buyers no longer have to complete."The biggest change is less paperwork," Perez said. "It's a lot easier for someone to come in here and purchase a firearm and feel safe about it and secure about it."He said some customers who once faced waits stretching nine months, 14 months or longer may now be able to take possession much sooner."They no longer have to wait 14 months, or nine months, or even more than a day if they have a concealed weapon firearm permit," Perez said. "They can leave with that same day and start training immediately and empower themselves and be able to protect themselves or their family."Perez said interest surged almost immediately after the federal announcement.When WPTV's Michael Hoffman visited We Kick Brass, several customers were at the shop picking up suppressors.Perez believes the changes will make firearms and accessories that were already legal to own more accessible to law-abiding buyers.Perez also has personal experience with short-barreled rifles. In 2018, he was involved in a self-defense shooting in which he used one."I used a short-barreled rifle to save my mother's life," Perez said. "They are just simply put the best and most effective tools."Asked what could happen if a future administration attempted to reverse the policy, Perez said he believes current owners would likely be protected."I imagine that they would be grandfathered in," Perez said. "You can't make millions of Americans felons overnight by the flick of a pen. It just makes no sense."The ATF's policy change does not eliminate all National Firearms Act regulations.Machine guns and destructive devices, including bombs, rockets and grenades, remain subject to federal requirements.Customers purchasing firearms must also continue to undergo background checks and comply with all applicable federal and state laws.For those concerned about expanded access to suppressors and short-barreled firearms, Perez said the changes affect law-abiding citizens."We are just allowing people, law-abiding citizens, the ability to protect themselves with the right firearm to do so," Perez said.Florida gun owners should also be aware that state law prohibits short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns unless they are lawfully owned under federal law. The ATF has said it cannot provide guidance on whether an unregistered firearm would satisfy that requirement under Florida law.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseA PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation. the road is back open.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.

Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city. One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store. “This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. “This is getting closer to the finish line,” Samples said. The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home. McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow. “They see all the development that’s occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. “It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here.” City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail. “This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. “It’s kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there’s more to come.” The other plan is space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital, featuring inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a more than 55,000-square-foot building. “A growing area needs services, and that’s just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access,” McCurry said. McCurry said the plans for retail, healthcare and entertainment are fulfilling the city’s master plan for what Southern Grove was destined to become. “The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen,” McCurry said. Samples said Costco still must close on the land, move on to construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday unanimously to move forward with a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities.Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi explained it's "an opportunity to say, 'pause,' let's hear from people, let’s have the opportunity for experts to come and speak to us on both sides.”Watch report from Cassandra Garcia:Commissioners explained they would consider extending the moratorium later if they need more time.“If it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, whatever it takes, whatever it takes, we should be doing this,” said Martin County Commissioner Eileen Vargas.Tuesday's vote marked the first of two hearings scheduled this month on the proposed moratorium.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Martin County eyes pause on data center developmentCommissioners are expected to revisit the issue on Oct. 27, when another vote will be required.Residents are now hoping the county will use the time to consider their concerns.“For me it’s wildlife so these areas are in largely rural or large plots of land and so you take that area and develop it and these facilities are massive—millions and millions of square feet, no animals can live there anymore, or the hum is going to affect the animals,” said Sergei Kelley, who spoke at the meeting.Martin County resident Scott Butler added, "The fear of the use of all this water we have [...] and understanding what these data center[s] are going to use.”The discussion comes as Martin County has already received an application for a data center. The county received the application Monday, one day before commissioners considered the moratorium. It’s the first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. The application is considered a hyper-scale data center, at over 950-thousand square feet proposed on a lot off Kanner Highway west of I-95. Because the application was submitted before the proposed moratorium, it would not be affected by the measure.The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development in Martin County.One resident at the meeting told commissioners, "Once land is converted into industrial use, the consequences can remain long after."Ann Vandersteel, another resident, added, "We need to have serious studies completed in order to go forward with something of this consideration."WPTV continues to hear from residents about those concerns as commissioners consider what restrictions, if any, to place on future data center development.

"They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." When investigative reporter Kate Hussey asked whether he believed that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes."I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. One showed firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees.Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation.The three have maintained the activity was consensual and "all in good fun.""It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson previously told WPTV."We're all still friends," Boudrias said.Their terminations sparked pushback from firefighters and members of the community, which eventually led to the union's no-confidence vote."The amount that voted no confidence really sends a message that we have, in their opinion, a lack of confidence in their leadership," union representative Ryan Sapp said.Sapp is representing the three firefighters in their fight for reinstatement. With previous settlement offers now off the table, Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote."His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said.The vote comes as the district is already undergoing changes in leadership.Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December. Meanwhile, a reassignment notice obtained by WPTV Investigates shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief.Clasby questioned the decision, particularly given the no-confidence vote against Gonzalez."I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," Clasby said.The district told WPTV that Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and said the move had been under discussion "for some time prior to recent events."In a statement, the district said it "recognizes" the results of the no-confidence vote and the importance of listening to its personnel.The district said it remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking "appropriate action" to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters.Sapp said rebuilding that trust could prove difficult."I think it's hard whenever you see those staggering numbers, that lack confidence in leadership, to rebound it back," he said.The Fire Board is also weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled.That work is expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.Sapp said their last settlement offer, an offer to reinstate the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension, was not accepted. "I do want to say, this is a great department," Sapp added. We have great men and women that work here. In light of all this bad publicity we've had, I promise you these members, these employees that I have, they genuinely enjoy serving this community and do the absolute best they can do." The District's full statement reads below:

A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseA PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation. the road is back open.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Man in Seaway Bridge Indecent Exposure Cases
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police arrested Kyle Kennedy, 27, Friday after investigating multiple reports of indecent exposure involving women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge. Investigators reviewed earlier reports, identified patterns linking the incidents, interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups. Two victims positively identified Kennedy as the suspect during those lineups, leading to his arrest, police said.

Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation.

Fort Pierce resident Leidi Cruz said she regularly walks the bridge and has never had any issues. "It's just crazy to know that there's something like that going on," Cruz said.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has information about the incidents to call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-467-6800. Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: Martin County Woman Gets Fire Department's First Heroic Heart Award for Pool Rescue
hero.body:
Martin County fire officials have presented 20-year-old Madison Isler with the department's first-ever Heroic Heart Award after she pulled 3-year-old Luna Hernandez from the bottom of an apartment pool on Aug. 23 and performed CPR that saved the girl's life. Isler will also be recognized at an upcoming Martin County Commission meeting.

Isler said she noticed Luna motionless at the bottom of the pool while walking to retrieve a hair clip she had left on the opposite side. "I had to go get my hair clip that I left on, like, the opposite side of the pool. And as I was walking, I saw a shadow, and it kind of looked like a smudge on your sunglasses," Isler said. She jumped into the water and pulled Luna out. Finding the child blue, unresponsive, and not breathing, Isler began CPR while shouting for someone to call 911. A pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and rushed over to help.

Isler said at least 10 adults were at the pool when Luna went under, and that drownings often happen silently and quickly. She has nicknamed Luna the "unicorn baby." "Because this doesn't happen. Drownings don't end like this. When they're babies 3 years old like this, they just go under, slip right under really quick. And she's a unicorn," Isler said. "There were at least 10 adults at the swimming pool when she went down. So, it just happens right in front of you and silently quick, so for me to walk by and see it was a pretty slim chance. I call her the unicorn baby," she said.

Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented Isler with the award. "Because of the actions of one young woman who happened to be at the right place at the right time, Luna was given another chance. A chance to go home, a chance to grow up, a chance to make memories with her family. A chance to live a life that she was waiting for," Cianciulli said. "Madison is an incredible young woman." Isler's father, who works for Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, and her mother, who is retired from the department, attended the presentation. Luna's mother, Kristine Hernandez, was out of town when the incident happened. She shared photos of her daughter's smile and credited the timing of Isler's actions. "Stopping on the way to the pool to get a hair clip. There're just minor little details in the story that it's God's work that he put her when we needed her, like at the right place, at the right time," Hernandez said. "I'm just thankful for the life that Luna gets to live now," she said, adding that such accidents can happen to anyone. During a recent meeting between the two, Luna, described as shy around cameras, clung to Isler, whom she has come to see as her new best friend.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue Honors Woman Who Saved Drowning 3-Year-Old With CPR
hero.body:
A 20-year-old Martin County woman has been honored by Martin County Fire Rescue for using CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, the department presented Madison Isler with its inaugural Heroic Heart Award.

The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. "It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl." The girl was 3-year-old Luna, who was motionless at the bottom of the pool. "I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said. She called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, relying on skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. "You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."

A family friend who works as a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue. "Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital. Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help. "It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.

Nearly two months later, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters, this time to celebrate the outcome of the rescue. The department presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award in recognition of her actions, making her the first person to receive it. "Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition. For Isler, the honor took a back seat to seeing Luna alive and thriving. "What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said, adding that she affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby." Hernandez said she remains overwhelmed with gratitude toward Isler and her family. "I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Fourth Extension, Sets Dec. 8 Deadline
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement on financing and lease terms or risk the city reconsidering the deal entirely.

The Three Corners project is planned for the site of the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge, with proposals calling for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths. Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said he has worked on the project since 2019 and wants the city to secure favorable terms for residents. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens," Cotugno said.

Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial side of the developer's proposal, but he made clear that the council will walk away if ClearBlue's plans do not match the city's goals. "We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." To help close the gap, the council is appointing a liaison to work directly with the developers and bring them in for in-person discussions on the project.

Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue had been requesting a liaison for months and welcomed the move. "It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said. "We're glad we finally have one on the books now." Salera said ClearBlue has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project and remains committed to finishing it. "We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." Cotugno said he shares that hope as long as both sides keep moving toward a resolution. "I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," he said.

hero.headline: More Than 100 Cats Rescued From Port St. Lucie Hoarding House
hero.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens are now receiving medical care and nourishment after being pulled from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the Humane Society of St. Lucie shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie, said many of the cats arrived in poor health. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. Wees said staff are still sorting out which cats belong to which litters. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was called in quickly after Wees reached out. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. Nickelsen said the extra support is already paying off, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," she said.

St. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine whether any criminal charges will be filed. The Humane Society of St. Lucie is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as they continue treatment and work toward foster placement and adoption.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Dec. 8 Deadline
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for the developers of the Three Corners project, giving ClearBlue until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement with the city or face the possibility of restarting negotiations from scratch. The extension gives both sides more time to work out financing and lease terms for the long-stalled waterfront development planned at the old Vero Beach Power Plant site at the base of the 17th Street Bridge.

"I've been on this thing since 2019," Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens." The Three Corners plans call for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths on the property. Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial aspects of the developer's proposal, but he made clear the city is not committed to seeing the deal through if terms cannot be reached.

"We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." The council is appointing a liaison to help with negotiations and to work directly with the developers as talks continue. Cotugno said he is willing to keep negotiating as long as progress continues to be made.

ClearBlue spokesperson Bob Salera said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue has been requesting an in-person meeting for months and is glad one is now scheduled. Salera said the company has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project.

"We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." The Dec. 8 deadline marks the fourth time the city council has extended the negotiating window for ClearBlue, and Cotugno has indicated the city wants to see tangible movement toward a final agreement before granting any further delays.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Man Sentenced to Time Served in Hotel 'Exorcism' Attack
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman and throwing water on her at a Vero Beach hotel has been sentenced to nine months in jail, with credit for time already served. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. He had been held in St. Lucie County Jail since his arrest and was credited with 297 days of time served.

The case began December 23, 2025, when deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office responded to the Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. A second witness told investigators she heard a woman yelling "Stop," "Rape" and "Help Me" before seeing a man appear to drag the woman back into the room. When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, identified as Coppeto, who was visibly wet and shaken.

Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him.

Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. He was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery following the incident. With his plea and sentencing now complete, the case is closed.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Man in Seaway Bridge Indecent Exposure Cases
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police have arrested a man accused of exposing himself to women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge in multiple incidents. Kyle Kennedy, 27, was arrested Friday after investigators reviewed previous reports and identified patterns linking the cases. Detectives interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups, and two victims positively identified Kennedy as the suspect, police said.

Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity on the bridge or has information about the incidents to call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-467-6800. Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.
