cards.headline: Man Dies in Lakewood Park After Domestic Call Turns Into Barricade Standoff
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County deputies evacuated a woman and children through a side window before finding a man dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound during a Fort Pierce barricade situation. The sheriff's office says there is no ongoing threat to the community.
cards.body:
A man died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after a domestic violence call in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood turned into a barricaded-subject standoff Saturday morning, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard and encountered a man in the front yard, who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.

Deputies later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. A deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, but the man shut the door and retreated inside, setting off a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still in the home. Deputies said the man came outside several times during the standoff and indicated he would surrender after making a phone call, but each time he went back inside.

During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Fearing for the safety of an adult woman and children still inside, deputies entered the home without alerting the occupants and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff's office said. Deputies then found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The sheriff's office said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives with the agency's Criminal Investigations Division, along with crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office, remained at the scene to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident. Anyone struggling with thoughts of suicide can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7, or chat online at 988lifeline.org.

hero.headline: Sheriff Eric Flowers to Witness Execution of Deputy's Killer Tuesday
hero.body:
William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection Tuesday at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed Gov. Ron DeSantis to sign the death warrant, plans to attend the execution in Raiford and says it will bring the agency closure nearly a year after losing Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. A pending appeal before the U.S. Supreme Court could still delay the execution.

According to court records, Cpl. Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. on Sept. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts during the encounter and the two struggled over it. Records show Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back while Raczkoski was running away, and that the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, Reaves admitted to the shooting, saying, "I've never met a finer officer in my life." He told detectives he feared returning to prison as a convicted felon and said, "I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked."

Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 after finding that one of the prosecutors had previously represented him in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week. His attorneys, along with a group of military veterans, asked DeSantis for clemency, citing Reaves' service as a ground combat soldier in Vietnam starting in 1969 and his 100% disability rating from the Department of Veterans Affairs for post-traumatic stress disorder. They argued the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service and that he was shut out of a fair clemency process after the attorney assigned to him met with him only about five minutes before his clemency interview. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding, and DeSantis denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant.

In a filing last month, Reaves' attorneys also accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s and alleged one of them helped shape testimony from a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected that claim on Oct. 2, finding it was not backed by any sworn statement and was speculative. Reaves did not raise the claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Flowers said Raczkoski's brother will join him at the execution; Raczkoski's parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, "Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed." Flowers said his goal is for the last thing Reaves sees to be an Indian River County Sheriff's Office uniform, "knowing that justice finally came." hero.headline: Florida Secures Arrest Warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 Jet Shootdown
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that state prosecutors and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement have secured an arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro, accusing him of conspiring to murder four men in the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft operated by the anti-Castro group Brothers to the Rescue. Castro has been charged with one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with the attack, in which Cuban military fighter jets destroyed two unarmed planes over international waters.

Authorities said three unarmed Cessna aircraft departed Opa-locka Airport in Miami-Dade County on a February flight in 1996. After crossing the 24th parallel and flying outside Cuba's territorial waters, two of the planes were destroyed by air-to-air missiles fired from Cuban MiG fighter jets. According to a probable cause affidavit, the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba at the time and received no warning before being shot down. The attack killed four men with ties to Florida: Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr.

The warrant, obtained by the Office of Statewide Prosecution and FDLE, alleges that Castro played a key role in authorizing the attack. The affidavit states that Castro, who at the time served as Cuba's minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president, was among the final decision-makers who approved the operation. Investigators allege he issued standing orders to military leaders to shoot down aircraft associated with Brothers to the Rescue if the planes appeared over the sea. State investigators also allege that Cuban intelligence agents operating in South Florida infiltrated Brothers to the Rescue and fed flight information to the Cuban government as part of an operation known as "Operation Scorpion."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Tests Water Sensors, Clears Drains Ahead of Weekend Rain
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Public Works crews spent the past week clearing debris from storm drains and grates as more rain is expected across the Treasure Coast this weekend. The city is also testing new pilot water-level sensors designed to send alerts to select staff when water levels rise at specific locations, according to Scott Samples, communications manager for the City of Port St. Lucie.

"It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. He added that water levels in the city's retention ponds and canals are currently adequate and will not need to be lowered ahead of the rain.

The preparations come as chronic flooding continues to plague the intersection of California and Savona boulevards, where water levels rose last week. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming near that intersection, said flooding has been a recurring problem there for years. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins said she already warned customers that Saturday grooming appointments may need to be rescheduled. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," she said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."

The city is working on a larger drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood that would include raising portions of the roadway near the flood-prone intersection. Samples said the project would resolve the recurring flooding once finished, but the effort remains in the data collection phase and has not yet moved into design. That means a permanent fix could still be years away. Collins said the ongoing flooding has disrupted her business operations. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," she said. "That's just not OK." She said she has considered relocating Pets Play Grooming altogether, though that option comes with its own challenges. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. She said flooding has occurred there for years. WPTV was there when water levels rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she already sent messages to her customers for Saturday. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business." For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said. The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." The project may take years until completion, but Collins said she already thought about moving her business. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Drug Bust: Gang Member, Two Others Charged in Fentanyl Case
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie Police Department narcotics investigation into a reputed gang member's fentanyl and cocaine distribution has led to three arrests and the seizure of drugs, firearms and gang-related items, police said. Detectives identified Albert Johnson, 36, as an identified gang member involved in distributing fentanyl and cocaine. After building evidence linking Johnson to cocaine sales, detectives arrested him without incident and then executed a search warrant at his home on Southwest Burlington Terrace.

The search of Johnson's home led to the arrest of a juvenile, who was charged with tampering with physical evidence and cannabis-related offenses. A 19-year-old identified as Fleur was also arrested and charged with cannabis possession and possession of drug paraphernalia.

Police said the investigation resulted in the seizure of 69.5 grams of cocaine, 12 grams of fentanyl, 10 ounces of cannabis and 1 gram of MDMA. Officers also recovered three firearms, narcotics packaging equipment and gang-related items from the search.

The case underscores the scope of gang-connected drug distribution authorities say they are working to disrupt in Port St. Lucie. The seizure of fentanyl alongside cocaine, cannabis and MDMA, combined with the recovery of multiple firearms and gang-related items, reflects the breadth of narcotics activity investigators linked to Johnson before his arrest.

hero.headline: Turnpike Reopens in Martin County After Semi Jackknifes Near SE Bridge Road
hero.body:
All northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in Martin County reopened Friday afternoon after a jackknifed semi-truck shut down traffic and sent one person to the hospital. The crash happened shortly before noon near mile marker 125, underneath the SE Bridge Road overpass, causing heavy delays for drivers.

The Florida Highway Patrol said the truck driver lost control, causing the crash. Paramedics took one patient with minor injuries to the hospital by ground, according to Martin County Fire Rescue spokeswoman Jillian Kay.

Lanes began reopening to traffic just after 1 p.m. Friday, easing the backup that had built up along the busy corridor during the midday hours.

Kay said the Martin County Sheriff's Office and the Florida Highway Patrol also responded to the scene and will investigate the cause of the crash.

hero.headline: Man Dies in Apparent Suicide After Fort Pierce Barricade Standoff
hero.body:
A man died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricaded-subject standoff with deputies in the Lakewood Park neighborhood of Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies evacuated a woman and children from the home before finding the man dead, and the sheriff's office says there is no ongoing threat to the community.

Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident at a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. They found a man in the front yard, but he went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Deputies later made contact with a man and woman at the front door, and a deputy spotted what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession. The deputy ordered him to drop the weapon, but he shut the door and retreated into the home, triggering a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still inside.

Over the course of the standoff, the man came outside several times and told deputies he would surrender after making a phone call, but he repeatedly went back into the house, according to the sheriff's office. During his final retreat inside, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Concerned for the safety of an adult woman and children still in the home, deputies entered without alerting the occupants and evacuated them through a side window. They later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The sheriff's office said there is no ongoing threat to the community following the discovery. Detectives with the agency's Criminal Investigations Division, along with crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office, remained at the scene to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident. Anyone struggling with thoughts of suicide can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7, or chat online at 988lifeline.org.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound Man Killed by Friend Was Trying to Rob Him, Sheriff Says
cards.teaser: Jarvis Preston, 21, died after his friend shot him with an AR15 during an alleged robbery attempt in Hobe Sound. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says no arrest has been made while investigators weigh whether the shooting was self-defense.
cards.body:
Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound died Thursday after being shot by a close friend two days earlier, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. New details released by Sheriff John Budensiek show the shooting followed an alleged attempted robbery, and investigators are now working with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooter acted in self-defense. No arrest has been made.

The shooting happened Wednesday night on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood. Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Sheriff Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob the friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Budensiek said.

According to the sheriff, the friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend during the encounter. The second time, he and Preston, who was carrying a handgun with a 30-round magazine, got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Budensiek said. The handgun was recovered at the scene. Preston was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where he died Thursday. Budensiek said the man who shot Preston tried to render aid and stayed at the scene afterward.

Preston's mother, Ebony Preston, said her son was not married and was the father of a small child. She said she does not know what led to the shooting and struggled to understand how it happened between two close friends. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" she said. Preston's stepfather, Rodney Clemon, said he also could not make sense of it. "That's what I don't understand how it come about, 'cause they best friends," he said. Ebony Preston said the family is left with more questions than answers. "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?" she said. The Sheriff's Office says it continues to work with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooting was legally justified under Florida's stand your ground law or whether charges will be filed.

Police seized 69.5 grams of cocaine, 12 grams of fentanyl, 10 ounces of cannabis, 1 gram of MDMA, three firearms, narcotics packaging equipment and gang-related items during the investigation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Tests New Water Sensors as Weekend Rain Threatens Flooding
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Public Works crews are preparing for more rain expected this weekend across the Treasure Coast, with staff clearing debris from drains and grates throughout the week. Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and will not need to be lowered ahead of the storm.

The city is also testing new pilot water sensors designed to alert select staff when water levels rise in specific locations. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said.

The preparations come as chronic flooding continues to threaten businesses at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming near the intersection, said flooding has occurred there for years and that water levels rose at the intersection again last week. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins said she has already messaged customers about possibly rescheduling Saturday appointments. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," she said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."

The city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood that includes raising portions of the roadway near the troubled intersection. Samples said the project would resolve the flooding once finished. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," he said. The project is still in the data collection phase before it moves into design, meaning a fix could be years away. Collins said the ongoing flooding has disrupted her ability to operate. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," she said. "That's just not OK." She said she has considered relocating her business but is hesitant given the difficulty of such a move. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Preps Pumps and Crews as More Heavy Rain Threatens Weekend
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie officials are staging Public Works crews and pumps ahead of forecasted heavy rain this weekend, a week after a four-inch deluge turned city roads into lakes and left residents anxious about a repeat. Stormtrac meteorologists say the city received about four inches of rain over 48 hours last week, causing canal water levels to rise quickly and roads to flood so deeply that some drivers risked getting stalled in standing water.

Peter Rodriguez, who lives at the intersection of SW Todd Avenue and SW Broadview Street, has a canal directly behind his house and said he had never seen flooding like it in the two years he has lived in Port St. Lucie. "When I came out, I was like, Oh, my God! I've never seen it like this before!" he said. Floodwater did not enter his home, but it was deep enough to block him from driving out of his driveway. Asked how worried he is about another flood this weekend, Rodriguez said, "I don't think it's gonna get that high. If it starts getting that high, then I'm gonna start to pray. Not another flood."

Not every resident is convinced the city is doing enough. Frank Camarda, who lives on SW Leisure Lane, said he believes officials need to take stronger action. "I really think they should do something, I mean really to take care of business, you know because we pay our taxes," he said. A city spokesman said Public Works employees will be on standby this weekend if heavy rain arrives, ready to clear storm drains or move pumps into position to lower water levels in flood-prone spots such as the intersection of Savona Boulevard and SW California Boulevard.

Scott Samples, the city's Strategic Communications Manager and Public Information Officer, said crews have been monitoring canals and retention ponds and have not needed to lower water levels this week, which he called a good sign. "They've been monitoring the canals and the retention ponds. And again, they haven't had to lower them this week which is a good sign. They're where they think they need to be. So, we're as prepared as we can be. You never know what Mother Nature is going to throw at you, but this team is doing everything it can to try to to mitigate the risks as much as possible,

cards.headline: Former Officer Otto Lenke Sentenced to Death in Fort Pierce Bike Shop Murder
cards.teaser: A jury's death sentence against Otto Lenke for the 2021 torture-murder of bike shop owner Richard Benson now heads to automatic review by the Florida Supreme Court.
cards.body:
Otto Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, has been sentenced to death for the 2021 murder of Richard Benson, a bike shop owner in Fort Pierce. Assistant State Attorney Brandon White, who prosecuted the case, called the sentence justice following the hearing.

"The jury got it right," White said. "This was probably one of the most heinous crimes in the history of our circuit. It was all caught on camera. It was well planned out." During the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed the jury security video from inside the bike shop that they said captured Lenke not just killing Benson but torturing him. "He tormented him and basically made Richard's life a living hell, those last two minutes of his life by pouring that accelerant on him and lighting him on fire," White said.

White said jealousy drove the killing, since Benson had started dating a woman Lenke had previously dated. White said Lenke, drawing on more than two decades in law enforcement, believed his background would help him get away with the crime. "The defendant used his 20-plus years of experience in law enforcement to plan this attack, to carry out this attack," White said.

Benson's family watched the sentencing remotely via Zoom from out of state and was not present in the courtroom when the judge handed down the death sentence. "I think this is something they wanted for Rich. This was justice," White said. The case is not yet final. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to automatically review all death sentences, and Lenke is also expected to appeal the decision.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound Shooting Victim Identified as Sheriff Details Confrontation, No Arrest Yet
hero.body:
The man shot and killed Wednesday night in Hobe Sound has died, the Martin County Sheriff's Office confirmed, and investigators are now weighing whether the shooting was an act of self-defense. The victim's mother identified him as Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound, who was shot by his best friend. No arrest has been made.

The shooting happened on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood. Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Wednesday. Sheriff John Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob his friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Budensiek said.

According to the sheriff, the friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend. The second time, he and Preston, who was armed with a handgun carrying a 30-round magazine, got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Budensiek said. The handgun was recovered at the scene. Preston was taken to a hospital in West Palm Beach, where he died. Budensiek said the shooter tried to render aid to Preston and stayed at the scene afterward.

Budensiek said investigators have not yet determined whether the shooting was self-defense or a crime, and the sheriff's office is working with the State Attorney's Office to decide whether charges will be filed or whether Florida's stand your ground law applies. Preston's mother, Ebony Preston, said she does not know what led to the shooting and struggled to understand how it happened between two close friends. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" she said. She said Preston was not married and was the father of a small child. "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?" she said. Preston's stepfather, Rodney Clemon, also said he could not make sense of what happened. "That's what I don't understand how it come about, 'cause they best friends," Clemon said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Man Accused of Trying to Ram Deputy During Hutchinson Island Chase
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie man is facing an aggravated assault charge after deputies say he tried to ram a patrol vehicle during a high-speed chase that ended with a PIT maneuver on South Hutchinson Island. Joshua Gallagher, 37, was arrested Thursday night following the pursuit, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

The chase began in the 9600 block of South Ocean Boulevard when a Patrol Operations deputy tried to stop Gallagher's pickup truck for a traffic violation. Andrew Bolonka, director of communications for the Sheriff's Office, said Gallagher fled instead of stopping, making a U-turn and spinning donuts in the roadway, forcing other motorists to take evasive action. After briefly stopping, Gallagher made another U-turn, cut across lanes of traffic and accelerated toward the deputy's patrol vehicle.

"The deputy tries to stop the vehicle; all of a sudden, the vehicle lunges, takes off, accelerates, does another U-turn, and then starts allegedly heading straight toward the deputy. Which you can see in the body-worn camera, where the deputy makes an evasive maneuver and says, 'Oh, he almost hit me,'" Bolonka said. Members of the Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Unit and deputies in the air assisted in the pursuit. Gallagher kept fleeing even after deputies deployed stop sticks. Deputies eventually executed a PIT maneuver along Seaway Drive, bringing the truck to a stop. Gallagher ignored repeated verbal commands to exit the vehicle, prompting deputies to deploy pepper balls into the truck before he surrendered and was taken into custody without further incident.

Gallagher faces several charges, including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and resisting arrest without violence. He remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail. Bolonka said the incident put more than just law enforcement at risk. "When people make decisions like this, and they commit an act that puts not only the deputies and other law enforcement officers in peril, but they are also putting the general public in peril. If we can do so safely, we're going to put it to an end," he said. Authorities said they were relieved no one was injured during the chase.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Pilots Water Sensors Ahead of Weekend Rain
cards.teaser: Public Works crews cleared drains and are testing new water-level sensors as rain threatens flood-prone spots like California and Savona boulevards.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing for more rain expected this weekend across the Treasure Coast, clearing drains and testing new technology meant to catch flooding before it spreads. Scott Samples, communications manager for the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates throughout the city.

Samples said water levels in retention ponds and canals are currently at an adequate level and will not need to be lowered ahead of the storm. The city is also piloting new water sensors that send alerts to select staff when water levels begin to rise in specific locations. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said.

The intersection of California and Savona boulevards remains one of the city's known trouble spots. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming near the intersection, said her business floods there regularly and that her staff is bracing for this weekend's storm. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Water rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she has already warned customers that Saturday grooming appointments, one of her busiest days, may need to be rescheduled. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."

The city is working on a larger drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood that would include raising portions of the roadway near the intersection. Samples said the project would resolve the chronic flooding once finished, but the work is still in the data collection phase before design can begin, meaning completion could take years. Collins said the delays are frustrating, especially since flooding closes her business. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." She said she has considered relocating her business altogether. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Braces for More Flooding After Last Week's Deluge
cards.teaser: Heavy rain expected this weekend has Port St. Lucie on alert after four inches of rain in 48 hours last week turned city roads into standing lakes. Public works crews will be on standby to clear storm drains and reposition pumps if needed.
cards.body:
Heavy rain forecast for this weekend has Port St. Lucie residents and city officials watching closely after last week's storms flooded roads across the city. Stormtrac meteorologists reported the city received about four inches of rain in a 48 hour period last week, overwhelming drainage and sending canal water levels rising quickly.

Roads turned into what residents described as lakes, and some drivers attempted to push through standing water deep enough to stall their vehicles. Peter Rodriguez, who lives at the intersection of SW Todd Avenue and SW Broadview Street and has a canal directly behind his house, said the flooding was unlike anything he had seen in his two years living in Port St. Lucie. "When I came out, I was like, Oh, my God. I've never seen it like this before!" Rodriguez said.

Asked how worried he is about another round of flooding this weekend, Rodriguez said he does not expect water levels to reach the same heights as last week. "I don't think it's gonna get that high. If it starts getting that high, then I'm gonna start to pray. Not another flood," he said.

A city spokesman said public works employees will be on standby this weekend in case heavy rain returns. Crews are prepared to clear storm drains and move pumps into position to lower water levels in flood-prone spots, including near the intersection of Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard.

hero.headline: Amendment 3 vote looms, real estate agents warn of rush before homestead deadline
hero.teaser: Florida voters decide Nov. 3 on a property tax measure that could push buyers to close before Dec. 31 to lock in full homestead savings right away.
hero.body:
Florida voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to approve Amendment 3, a measure that would change the state's property tax structure by saving money for homeowners while cutting tax revenue for cities and counties. The referendum needs 60% approval to pass, and real estate professionals say it could trigger a rush of homebuyers before the end of the year.

The amendment requires homeowners to be homesteaded in Florida by Dec. 31 to receive the full tax savings immediately. New buyers who move into the state after that date would face a five-year waiting period before qualifying for the full homestead exemption. Jeff Lichtenstein of Echo Fine Properties in Palm Beach Gardens said that timeline could push buyers to act quickly if the amendment passes.

"You better be prepared because if it happens, it will happen fast," Lichtenstein said. "I think there will be a mad rush to get in here, because if not, then you're waiting five years."

A 2025 study by Realtor.com suggested home values in Florida could rise 7% to 9% if the referendum passes. Lichtenstein said he does not expect increases that steep. "I don't see them going up to like the 7, 8, 9, 10 percent," he said, though he does anticipate a surge of buyers entering the market ahead of the deadline.

Florida Realtors, the state's trade association for real estate agents, is publicly supporting Amendment 3 but is less certain that it would drive a quick jump in property values. Florida Realtors CEO Margy Grant said home prices are shaped primarily by broader economic forces rather than the tax change alone. "The cost of home is economically driven," Grant said. "It's a supply and demand conversation, and when inventory increases, prices stabilize and we've seen that in recent months." Florida voters will have the final say on Amendment 3 when they go to the polls Nov. 3.

Staff have also been testing new pilot water sensors that will send alerts to select city employees if water levels start to rise in certain areas. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said.

The preparations come as flooding continues to threaten businesses near the intersection of California and Savona boulevards, an area that has flooded for years. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming near the intersection, said her staff is bracing for the weekend storm. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Water levels rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she has already warned customers that Saturday grooming appointments may need to be rescheduled. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."

The city is working on a long-term fix for the area through a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway near the intersection. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said. The project is still in the data collection phase before it moves into design, meaning it could take years to complete. Collins said the ongoing flooding has disrupted her business operations. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." She said she has considered relocating the business but is hesitant given the difficulty of such a move. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

hero.headline: Hobe Sound Man Shot by Best Friend Dies, No Arrest Yet in Banner Lake Case
hero.body:
A 21-year-old Hobe Sound man shot by his best friend during a confrontation on Southeast Citrus Way has died, the Martin County Sheriff's Office confirmed. Jarvis Preston died Thursday, a day after the shooting in the Banner Lake neighborhood off Florida Avenue. No arrest has been made.

Sheriff John Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob his friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend. During the second encounter, Preston and the friend got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Budensiek said. Preston was armed with a handgun fitted with a 30-round magazine, which investigators recovered at the scene. He was shot from about 10 feet away. Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Wednesday. Preston was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where he did not survive.

Budensiek said the shooter attempted to render aid to Preston and stayed at the scene afterward. The sheriff said investigators have not determined whether the shooting was self-defense or a case warranting criminal charges, and that his office is working with the State Attorney's Office to decide whether stand your ground applies or if charges will be filed.

Preston's mother, Ebony Preston, said her son was not married and was the father of a small child. She said she does not know what led to the shooting and struggled to understand how it happened between two close friends. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" she said. She added, "It's a lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?"

Preston's stepfather, Rodney Clemon, also said he could not make sense of what happened. "That's what I don't understand, how it come about, 'cause they're best friends," he said. The Sheriff's Office investigation remains active, and no charges have been filed as authorities continue reviewing the circumstances of the shooting.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Man Faces Charges After Chase Ends on South Hutchinson Island
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie man is facing aggravated assault and drug charges after deputies say he tried to ram a patrol vehicle and led them on a high-speed chase that ended with a PIT maneuver on South Hutchinson Island. Joshua Gallagher, 37, was arrested Thursday night and remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail.

The pursuit began in the 9600 block of South Ocean Boulevard when a St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations deputy tried to stop the driver of a pickup truck for a traffic violation. According to Andrew Bolonka, director of communications for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the driver fled instead of stopping, made a U-turn and spun donuts in the roadway, forcing other motorists to take evasive action. After briefly stopping, the driver made another U-turn, cut across lanes of traffic, and accelerated toward the deputy's patrol vehicle.

"The deputy tries to stop the vehicle; all of a sudden, the vehicle lunges, takes off, accelerates, does another U-turn, and then starts allegedly heading straight toward the deputy. Which you can see in the body-worn camera, where the deputy makes an evasive maneuver and says, 'Oh, he almost hit me,'" Bolonka said. Members of the Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Unit and deputies in the air assisted in the pursuit. The driver kept fleeing even after deputies deployed stop sticks, and deputies eventually executed a PIT maneuver along Seaway Drive to bring the truck to a stop. When the driver refused repeated verbal commands to get out, deputies deployed pepper balls into the vehicle, and the driver then surrendered and was taken into custody without further incident.

Gallagher faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription, and resisting arrest without violence. "When people make decisions like this, and they commit an act that puts not only the deputies and other law enforcement officers in peril, but they are also putting the general public in peril. If we can do so safely, we're going to put it to an end," Bolonka said. Authorities said they were relieved no one was injured during the incident.

hero.headline: Former Officer Otto Lenke Gets Death Sentence in Fort Pierce Bike Shop Murder
hero.body:
A judge has sentenced former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter Otto Lenke to death for the 2021 murder of Richard Benson, a bike shop owner in Fort Pierce. The sentencing closes out a case prosecutors say shocked the circuit, with the conviction built largely on security video from inside Benson's shop.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White, who prosecuted the case, said the jury reached the right verdict. "The jury got it right," White said. "This was probably one of the most heinous crimes in the history of our circuit. It was all caught on camera. It was well planned out." During the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed jurors the security footage, which they said captured Lenke not only killing Benson but torturing him beforehand.

"He tormented him and basically made Richard's life a living hell, those last two minutes of his life by pouring that accelerant on him and lighting him on fire," White said. White told jurors the attack was driven by jealousy, since Benson had started dating a woman Lenke had previously dated. White said Lenke believed his more than 20 years of law enforcement experience would help him get away with the killing. "The defendant used his 20-plus years of experience in law enforcement to plan this attack, to carry out this attack," White said.

Benson's family watched the sentencing remotely via Zoom from out of state and were not in the courtroom when the judge handed down the death sentence. White said he believed the outcome was what Benson's relatives had hoped for. "I think this is something they wanted for Rich. This was justice," White said. The case is not yet final. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to automatically review all death sentences, and Lenke is expected to appeal his conviction and sentence.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Watches for More Flooding as Weekend Rain Approaches
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie officials are preparing for the possibility of more flooding this weekend as heavy rain is expected to return to the area, just days after torrential storms swamped parts of the city. Meteorologists say Port St. Lucie received about four inches of rain in a 48-hour period last week, turning roads into standing lakes and causing canal water levels to rise quickly. Some drivers attempted to push through deep standing water, risking getting stalled with nowhere to go.

The flooding hit hard in neighborhoods near canals, including around the intersection of SW Todd Avenue and SW Broadview Street. Peter Rodriguez, who lives there and has a canal directly behind his house, said he had never seen flooding like it in the two years he has lived in Port St. Lucie. "When I came out, I was like, Oh, my God. I've never seen it like this before!" he said.

Asked how worried he is about another round of flooding this weekend, Rodriguez said he does not expect water levels to reach the same extreme. "I don't think it's gonna get that high. If it starts getting that high, then I'm gonna start to pray. Not another flood," he said.

A city spokesman said public works crews will be on standby this weekend if heavy rain develops. Workers are prepared to clear storm drains and move pumps into position to lower water levels in trouble spots, including near the intersection of Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard. City officials are urging residents in flood-prone areas to stay alert as the new storm system moves into the region.

cards.teaser: All northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike are back open after a jackknifed semi near mile marker 125 shut down traffic for over an hour. One person was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.
cards.body:
All northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in Martin County reopened Friday afternoon after a semi-truck jackknifed, causing heavy delays. The crash happened shortly before noon near mile marker 125, underneath the SE Bridge Road overpass.

According to the Florida Highway Patrol, the truck driver lost control, causing the crash. Martin County Fire Rescue spokeswoman Jillian Kay said paramedics took one patient with minor injuries to the hospital by ground.

Lanes began reopening to traffic just after 1 p.m. Kay said the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol also responded to the wreck and will investigate.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Polls Residents on Paying $11 More a Month for Extra Trash Pickup
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie is asking residents in a nonbinding straw poll whether they would support paying roughly $11 more per month, about $131 more a year, for a second weekly trash pickup. Residents currently get one garbage pickup per week, and the additional service could start in 2028 if the City Council decides to move forward.

Scott Samples, spokesperson for the city of Port St. Lucie, said the poll is meant to gauge public opinion rather than set policy. "This is something that is nonbinding, but it gives City Council an opportunity to get a sense of the will of the people and what they would prefer to see," Samples said. A "yes" vote would show support for the added cost, while a "no" vote would signal opposition, but the results will not automatically change the current pickup schedule.

Any change to trash service still has to go through the City Council, which controls the city's solid-waste contract and service levels. That means council members would need to approve any new schedule and reach an updated agreement with the city's current waste provider, FCC Environmental Services. The city also noted that adding a second weekly pickup would become an ongoing expense that could rise over time with inflation.

"City Council would take this up. They would have to work with the vendor to understand what the logistics of that would be. And then, the City Council would then vote on whether or not to move forward with this," Samples said. City officials say the poll is designed to give council members insight into what residents want before any formal proposal comes up for a vote, but the final call on whether Port St. Lucie households pay more for twice-weekly trash pickup rests with the council.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Drug Bust Nets Fentanyl, Cocaine, Guns, Three Arrests
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie Police Department narcotics investigation led to three arrests and the seizure of fentanyl, cocaine, firearms and gang-related items.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie Police Department narcotics investigation has led to three arrests after detectives seized fentanyl, cocaine, cannabis, MDMA, three firearms and gang-related items. Detectives received information that Albert Johnson, 36, an identified gang member, was involved in fentanyl and cocaine distribution. After gathering evidence linking Johnson to cocaine sales, detectives arrested him without incident before executing a search warrant at his home on Southwest Burlington Terrace.

The search led to the arrest of a juvenile, who was charged with tampering with physical evidence and cannabis-related offenses. A 19-year-old identified as Fleur was also arrested and charged with cannabis possession and possession of drug paraphernalia.

Police seized 69.5 grams of cocaine, 12 grams of fentanyl, 10 ounces of cannabis, 1 gram of MDMA, three firearms, narcotics packaging equipment and gang-related items during the investigation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Push Back on $6.1 Million Prima Vista Boulevard Plan
hero.body:
St. Lucie County held its first public workshop on a proposed $6.1 million redesign of Prima Vista Boulevard Thursday at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center, and most residents who attended said they doubted it would make the road safer. The plan would replace the center turn lane on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. 1 with a raised median and add landscaping meant to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down.

County officials said the goal is to improve safety, reduce crashes, and slow traffic along the corridor. St. Lucie County engineer Dan Zrallack acknowledged the resistance from residents during the meeting. "We understand it's not popular. That's why we have these," Zrallack said. "We're taking away the ease of access for people who live along this corridor. There's a lot of driveways. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents."

Many of the community members who spoke at the workshop said they were not convinced the changes would actually reduce crashes or improve conditions on the corridor. County staff estimate the project would cost about $6.

County leaders said the feedback gathered at Thursday's session will help shape the project going forward. The proposal remains in its early stages, and the county still needs to design the roadway and secure funding before any construction can begin. Residents who missed the workshop can review the plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound Shooting Victim Dies; Sheriff Weighs Self-Defense vs. Homicide Charges
hero.body:
The man shot by his best friend during a confrontation in Hobe Sound has died, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound, was shot Wednesday night on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood, and he died Thursday. No arrest has been made, and the Sheriff's Office is now working with the State Attorney's Office to decide whether the shooting was a case of self-defense under Florida's Stand Your Ground law or a chargeable homicide.

Sheriff John Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob his friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice along with his girlfriend. During the second encounter, the friend and Preston, who was carrying a handgun with a 30-round magazine, got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he drops right there," Budensiek said. Preston's handgun was recovered at the scene. He was taken to a medical center in West Palm Beach, where he did not survive. Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Wednesday.

Budensiek said the shooter attempted to render aid to Preston and stayed at the scene after the shooting. The sheriff said investigators have not yet determined whether the shooting was self-defense or a homicide, and the shooter's name has not been released while the investigation continues.

Preston's mother, Ebony Preston, said her son was shot by his best friend and that she does not know what led to the confrontation. She said Preston was not married and was the father of a small child. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" she said. She added, "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?" Preston's stepfather, Rodney Clemon, also said he was struggling to understand what happened between the two friends. "That's what I don't understand how it come about, 'cause they best friends," Clemon said.

cards.headline: Rescued Hobe Sound Kittens Buried Alive Recovering in Foster Care
cards.teaser: Kali and Amara, the two kittens pulled alive from a backyard burial site in Hobe Sound, are gaining strength with a foster family and could be ready for adoption within weeks.
cards.body:
Two kittens rescued last week after being buried alive in Hobe Sound are recovering steadily in foster care and could be ready for adoption in four to six weeks, according to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies pulled the kittens, now named Kali and Amara, from the ground after 36-year-old Alba Chavez allegedly buried multiple kittens alive because she believed they were demons. Two other kittens were found dead at the scene, and a fifth remains missing. Chavez faces criminal charges in the case and is being held on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement hold, according to the sheriff's office.

Body camera video released by the Martin County Sheriff's Office shows deputies digging to reach the kittens, with one deputy expressing surprise that the animals were still alive during the rescue. The roughly 4-week-old kittens were initially lethargic after being pulled from the ground but have since become increasingly active.

When the Humane Society needed a foster home for the survivors, local nurse Jennifer Jagdeo and her family stepped in right away. "As an animal lover, I think we're all shocked by it," Jagdeo said. "For me, my focus has been them and healing them." She said the kittens have made steady progress under around-the-clock care. "They're walking around now, they wrestle with each other and play," Jagdeo said. "They drink the bottle like it's nobody's business. They're just little joys." Her son, Ryland Vick, said he was saddened by what happened to the kittens. "Why would they do this when they're just so cute?" he said.

Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said the organization continues to respond to difficult animal welfare cases across the region, including large-scale rescue and hoarding investigations. "We hope that there's an end to it, and it just doesn't seem like there's an end to it," Fisher said. "But we're always here for the animals. We're always ready." The Humane Society is seeking additional foster families willing to temporarily care for animals awaiting permanent homes, and the organization is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund, which helps cover veterinary care for animals rescued from cruelty and neglect. Jagdeo said she hopes Kali and Amara eventually find permanent homes together. "My hope is that they find somebody that needs them as much as they need their human," she said.

cards._canonical_context_headline: Sheriff: Deputies Heard Kittens Crying Underground in Hobe Sound Burial Case
cards._canonical_context_body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek on Friday gave new details on the arrest of a Hobe Sound woman accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive, revealing that deputies heard the animals crying from beneath the ground during a backyard search. Alba Chavez, 36, faces four felony counts of animal torture after deputies said she buried kittens up to 3 feet underground at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park, with two kittens rescued alive and two found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property.

Deputies responded to the mobile home park Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had killed two kittens on Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, fearing for three remaining kittens, had locked them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. When they returned, they found the bedroom door forced open and the kittens gone, prompting the call to law enforcement. Deputies found Chavez standing in the roadway, and she reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens, telling deputies she believed the animals had demons, calling them ugly and saying she did not want black or brown cats in the home.

Chavez then led deputies to the backyard where the kittens had been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. As deputies dug through the rain-soaked ground, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were pulled out alive and rushed to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries from lack of oxygen while the animals were buried, and he said the kittens could still die from their injuries despite being rescued. The two kittens killed Monday were found dead at the burial site.

cards.headline: Stuart's Atlantic Diving Team trains young divers toward scholarships and Olympic goals
cards.teaser: Young divers with Stuart's Atlantic Diving Team are training under coach Pito Alberty with hopes of college scholarships, international competition and the Olympics.
cards.body:
A group of young divers in Stuart is training with hopes that their sport will carry them to college scholarships, international competition and even the Olympics. The athletes train with the Atlantic Diving Team under coach Osvaldo "Pito" Alberty, who teaches divers of all ages, backgrounds and experience levels the Olympic sport of diving.

Grace Erickson, a local diver now in eighth grade, said diving has been her passion since early childhood. "On my preschool poster I wrote what I wanted to be when I got older was a diver," Erickson said. She said the sport keeps surprising her. "It's been really exciting; it's new things every twist and turn, both in your head and diving off the board," Erickson said. Erickson said she has come to love platform diving in particular, along with the friendships she has built with teammates over the years. She hopes to take her diving to the college level.

Alberty, who has coached Erickson for years, said he wants to see her and her teammates push the sport to new heights. "We are like a family here. We treat each other with respect and courtesy, and we push each other to do better than everyone else," Alberty said. He said starting divers young opens doors down the road. "The younger we get them, the better it is because over time they can get scholarships. If they want to do international diving, they can qualify for international competitions or even the Olympics," Alberty said.

Among the team's newer members is 14-year-old Carissa Smith, who switched from gymnastics to diving about two months ago. Smith said her gymnastics background has helped her adjust to the new sport, though she has not yet competed because she wants to master the basics first. "I was recently a gymnast and just about two months ago I started diving," Smith said. She said the sport has already won her over. "It feels like you're flying; it's exhilarating just being able to get better at my diving," Smith said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Push Back on Prima Vista Boulevard Safety Plan
hero.body:
Most residents who attended a St. Lucie County information session Thursday on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard said they oppose the plan, arguing it would not make the road safer. The session, held at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center, focused on a proposal to redesign the stretch of Prima Vista Boulevard between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. 1. The plan would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping intended to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down.

County officials said the changes are meant to improve safety, reduce crashes, and slow traffic along the corridor. During the meeting, however, a majority of the community members who spoke said they did not believe the proposed redesign would achieve that goal. County leaders said the feedback collected at the session will help shape how the project moves forward.

The proposal remains in its early stages. St. Lucie County still needs to design the roadway, estimate project costs, and identify funding sources before any construction work can begin. No funding has been secured for the project at this point.

Residents who were unable to attend Thursday's workshop can still review the plans and submit comments by emailing Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

hero.headline: Flock Cameras Help Indian River Deputies Catch Suspect in Grandfather's Death
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 35-year-old man early Thursday after a cross-county chase ended in a Walmart parking lot, following the discovery of his grandfather's body in Okeechobee County. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief announced the arrest of Earl Douglas Wadlington III during a Thursday press conference, tying it to the homicide of 88-year-old veteran Paul Eugene Baker.

The case began when Baker's daughter-in-law requested a welfare check after not hearing from him for several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators called highly unusual. "She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said. Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property and found Baker dead. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide. Baker's vehicle and other property were also missing. Investigators learned Wadlington had recently been living with his grandfather after no other family member would take him in. Hazellief said Wadlington has more than 800 felonies in his criminal background. "The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.

Because the daughter-in-law held power of attorney for Baker, deputies entered the missing vehicle into the ALPR license plate reader system shared with partner agencies across the Treasure Coast, flagging it as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but withheld a public alert. "We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said. The agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and certain permitted locations under a Florida Department of Transportation order, but cameras at other qualifying locations remained active. "To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said. Senior detective Ashley Rojas led the investigation, according to Hazellief.

Indian River County's Flock camera system detected the stolen vehicle Thursday morning, leading deputies to Wadlington's location. Flowers described the roughly 4 a.m. pursuit, which was captured on video, as Wadlington fled through a Walmart parking lot. "One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said. The Sebastian Police Department assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the chase. "Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.

Flowers defended the county's continued use of Flock cameras despite public criticism of the system. "For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said. He noted the cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation and have aided other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman. Wadlington was arrested on charges of fleeing and eluding, and driving a stolen vehicle. Both agencies said they are working closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant charging him with homicide. "This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Proposes Raised Median for Prima Vista Boulevard After 578 Crashes
hero.body:
St. Lucie County is proposing to remove the center left-turn lanes on Prima Vista Boulevard between Airoso Boulevard and U.S. Highway 1 and replace them with a raised median. County staff are presenting the designs and seeking input from neighbors on the project.

County engineer Dan Zrallack said the center turn lane is often called a "suicide lane" because more turning movements create more chances for accidents. He said the raised median will let the county control where turning movements happen, protecting both drivers and pedestrians along the roadway.

According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, that stretch of Prima Vista Boulevard has had 578 crashes since 2020. Zrallack said the median is intended to make the road safer.

"The more turning movements you have, the more chances you have for accidents by restricting access and putting in the median turn lanes. We can kind of control where those turning movements are and protect the drivers as well as pedestrians walking along the roadway." hero.headline: Witnesses: Hobe Sound Man Was Armed, Drunk Before Friend Shot Him
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek is reviewing whether Florida's Stand Your Ground law applies in the fatal shooting of 21-year-old Jarvis Preston, who was killed Wednesday night by a lifelong friend during a confrontation in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound. New details released by the sheriff show witnesses said Preston had been drinking heavily throughout the day and began threatening the shooter and others while armed with a handgun before he was shot.

Martin County sheriff's deputies responding to Southeast Citrus Way found Preston with three gunshot wounds to the chest. Budensiek said Preston and the shooter were friends and described how the confrontation escalated. "He's talking, I'm going to shoot you, I'm going to hurt you. The shooter walks towards him, now they're at the edge of the road, at which point the deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Budensiek said.

The sheriff said the shooter called 911 and attempted life-saving efforts on Preston before he was flown to St. Mary's Hospital, where he died. Budensiek said investigators have not yet determined whether the shooting will be classified as self-defense. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand your ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Budensiek said. No arrest has been made as the sheriff's office continues to evaluate the circumstances of the shooting.

Preston's grandmother, Harriet Ford Gregg, said she heard the gunshots and went outside to find her grandson on the ground. "It was Jarvis laying on the ground out there, and the police officer was reviving him," Gregg said. Preston lived with his grandmother, and she said she has been unable to bring herself to enter his bedroom since his death. "I'm not going in there," Gregg said.

cards.headline: Banner Lake Neighbors Mourn as Deputies Weigh Charges in Fatal Shooting
cards.teaser: Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage and witness accounts to determine whether a Hobe Sound man's fatal shooting of his lifelong friend qualifies as self-defense under Florida's Stand Your Ground law.
cards.body:
A 21-year-old Hobe Sound man died after being shot by a man the Martin County Sheriff's Office describes as his friend, and neighbors in the tight-knit Banner Lake community are now grieving the loss while investigators determine whether the shooting qualifies as self-defense under Florida's Stand Your Ground law. The shooting happened on SE Citrus Way in Banner Lake, and the victim has been identified as Jarvis Preston. The Martin County Sheriff is still weighing whether the facts support a homicide charge or a Stand Your Ground defense, and the man who fired the shots has been detained for questioning but has not been publicly identified.

According to the sheriff's office, Preston and the man had been drinking together Wednesday afternoon. Detectives believe Preston kept drinking into the evening, then tried to rob his friend. The friend got away, but investigators say Preston followed him home and threatened him there. "The deceased starts to pull out a handgun. Shooter pulls his AR-15, acts a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," said John Budensiek of the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Investigators say that after the shooting, the shooter dropped his weapon, took the handgun away from Preston, and began rendering aid until deputies arrived.

Detectives are now searching for surveillance video and interviewing witnesses as they work to determine whether Stand Your Ground applies. "We're really not ready to make that determination. But I want to make sure we do it the right way to send the right messages to the right people, so this doesn't happen again," Budensiek said.

The shooting has shaken Banner Lake, where neighbor Stephanie Rose said she knew both men. "It's just sad, really sad," Rose said. "They were good kids, I mean they got a long perfect, I mean they were friends. I don't know what happened." As Preston's family and neighbors come to terms with his death, Rose said she had been planning to pay her respects in person. "Unbelievable and it's just sad. I was just on my way to give them my condolences," she said.

During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. hero.headline: Grandson Arrested After Chase in Vero Beach in Okeechobee Veteran's Death
hero.body:
A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led investigators to a homicide and ended with the arrest of the victim's grandson following a pre-dawn police chase through Vero Beach, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers and Okeechobee County Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday. Paul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident, was found dead on his property. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody around 4 a.m. after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot and deployed stop sticks to disable the stolen truck he was driving. Hazellief called it "a tragedy and a family tragedy" that began as a simple welfare check.

The case started when Baker's daughter-in-law, who had not heard from him in several days, went to check on his residence and found the house in disarray. "She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said. Deputies obtained and executed a search warrant, finding Baker dead on the property in a manner investigators said made clear right away that it was a homicide. His only vehicle and other property were missing from the home. Investigators learned Wadlington had recently been living with Baker after no other relative would take him in, given his lengthy criminal history of more than 800 felonies. "The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.

Because the daughter-in-law held power of attorney for Baker, investigators were able to enter his missing vehicle into the ALPR license plate reader network shared among Treasure Coast agencies, flagging it as connected to a homicide suspect. Deputies tracked the vehicle but withheld a public alert to avoid tipping off the driver. "We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said. Though the agency recently had to remove Flock cameras from state roads under a Department of Transportation order, cameras at other qualifying locations remained active, which Hazellief said was key to advancing the case. Senior detective Ashley Rojas led the investigation.

Indian River County's Flock system detected the stolen vehicle, leading deputies to Wadlington early Thursday. Flowers said the truck was rigged to stop running, which is why Wadlington eventually got out and fled on foot through the Walmart lot before being caught. Sebastian Police assisted during the chase. Wadlington faces charges of fleeing and eluding and driving a stolen vehicle, and both agencies said they are working with the state attorney's office to secure a warrant charging him with homicide. "This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.

hero.headline: After Fatal Crash, Neighbors Press FDOT for Lighting on Port St. Lucie Boulevard
hero.body:
Neighbors along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for better lighting after a fatal crash last week, saying the ongoing road-widening project has left the corridor dangerous for pedestrians and drivers, especially at night. The Florida Department of Transportation has not said whether it will add any interim safety measures in response.

Howard Shapiro, who lives near the construction zone, said the roadway has no lighting outside at night, which worries him because children walk along it to reach nearby schools. "I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there," Shapiro said. He said a new sidewalk being installed as part of the project will help, but added that street lights need to follow.

FDOT is overseeing construction along a stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Alcantara Boulevard and Parr Drive. The project began in 2025 and involves widening the road from two lanes to four, along with adding new sidewalks and lighting, according to FDOT's website.

Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said the completed project will improve both safety and traffic flow on the roadway. "We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway," Samples said. When asked whether city staff could provide any temporary safety measures while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can.
