hero.headline: AmeriCorps Literacy Mentors Return to Martin County Boys & Girls Clubs
hero.teaser: After a funding-driven hiatus, AmeriCorps volunteers are back at four Martin County Boys & Girls Clubs with a goal of reaching 575 K-5 students and boosting literacy skills by 65%.
hero.body:
AmeriCorps literacy mentors are returning to the Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County after a funding-driven pause, with new goals for reaching young readers across the county. The federal mentorship program places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support, and organizers aim to serve 575 kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys & Girls Club locations.

The Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County first brought AmeriCorps to the area in 2019. For six years, volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said the program's absence was keenly felt. "We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward," Maine said.

AmeriCorps Program Director for the Martin County Boys & Girls Club, Russell Lamberti, said the program has set a specific target for its return. "We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar," Lamberti said. AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar said the mission carries personal meaning for him as well. "I am a Haitian American. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow," Cesar said.

The Boys & Girls Clubs says the program delivered strong results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4, and about the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. Students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. Beyond the classroom, AmeriCorps members completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service.

The program's return comes as literacy remains a countywide priority. The organization also runs programs including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs.

cards.headline: Martin County Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service With $3M Contract
cards.teaser: County commissioners unanimously authorized emergency talks with MTM Transit to bring back MARTY bus service, with hopes buses could run again next week.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new one-year contract worth approximately $3 million with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's public bus system. The vote comes days after MARTY public bus service abruptly shut down last Thursday, leaving riders without service and drivers without jobs.

Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been operating MARTY, stopped service suddenly, citing rising operating costs including fuel and maintenance. Bill Lawrence, a former MARTY bus driver who lost his job in the shutdown, said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the days following the shutdown searching for a way to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. After reviewing several proposals, the county identified MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the new agreement would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers laid off last week is a priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating the county's previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume running as soon as next week.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Boulevard Neighbors Push for Lighting After Fatal Crash
hero.body:
Neighbors along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for better lighting after a fatal crash last week on the stretch of road now under construction. Howard Shapiro, who lives in the area, said the roadway lacks lighting, especially in the early morning and at night, creating danger for pedestrians and drivers alike.

"I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime," Shapiro said. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there." Shapiro said a new sidewalk under construction will help, but added that street lights need to be part of the project too.

The Florida Department of Transportation is overseeing the work along Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Alcantara Boulevard to Parr Drive. Construction began in 2025, and FDOT's website says crews are widening the road from two to four lanes while adding new sidewalks and lighting. Scott Samples, with the City of Port St. Lucie, said the finished project will bring a significant improvement in safety and traffic flow. Asked whether the city could put in any temporary safety measures while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can."

Questions remain about whether FDOT will add any interim safety measures to the corridor following last week's fatal crash.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Voters to Decide Sales Tax Renewal, Mosquito Control Expansion
cards.teaser: November's ballot asks St. Lucie County voters to renew a half-cent infrastructure sales tax for another decade and to expand mosquito control service into Tradition and the southwest county.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County voters will decide two ballot questions in November tied to the county's growing population and its strain on infrastructure and services. The first question asks voters to renew the existing half-cent sales tax, originally approved in 2018 and set to expire in two years, for another decade. The measure is not a new tax and would keep the total sales tax rate at 7%, with the half-cent portion continuing to fund infrastructure projects such as road improvements, sidewalks and stormwater drainage, along with larger projects like widening St. Lucie County roadways.

"Now we're seeing that impact, you know, the delayed maintenance and the increased growth we've seen picked up, we're starting to have to play catch-up with those infrastructure projects and the needs are still there," said Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County.

The second ballot question asks voters whether to expand the county's mosquito control district to include the Tradition area and southwestern St. Lucie County, regions that have grown beyond the district's current service boundaries. Mosquito control services currently cover about half of the county's 600 square miles. If voters approve the expansion, affected property owners in those areas would pay about $28 more per year in taxes to fund fogging, spraying and mosquito surveillance.

Both measures will appear on the November ballot and address separate needs as St. Lucie County continues to grow. County officials are encouraging voters to review their sample ballots ahead of time to see which questions apply to their specific address before heading to the polls.

hero.headline: Matt Gaetz, Joel Greenberg Named in New Federal Sex Trafficking Lawsuit
hero.body:
Former Florida Republican U.S. Congressman Matt Gaetz is among the defendants named in a new federal civil lawsuit filed on behalf of two women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2. The complaint also names former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg and several other defendants.

The lawsuit alleges that from 2017 through January 2019, Gaetz and Greenberg "coordinated recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts." West Palm Beach attorney Spencer Kuvin, who represents the plaintiffs, said the complaint was written in detail by design.

"We wanted the courts to understand the full breadth of this operation," Kuvin said. He said attorneys for the plaintiffs believe communications referenced in the complaint, particularly text messages, support the allegations. "The text messages we have we believe are incredibly damaging to Mr. Greenberg," Kuvin said.

Gaetz left Congress in 2024 and has previously denied wrongdoing connected to allegations investigated by the House Ethics Committee. Greenberg, the former Seminole County tax collector, is currently serving federal prison time following his conviction in a separate criminal case. The allegations in the civil complaint are claims made by the plaintiffs and have not been proven in court.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound Shooting Victim Dies, No Arrest Made in Banner Lake Case
hero.body:
A person shot during a Wednesday night shooting in Hobe Sound has died, the Martin County Sheriff's Office confirmed Thursday, marking a grim turn in a case that still has no arrest despite two people being questioned by investigators. The shooting occurred in the Banner Lake neighborhood, and deputies have not released information identifying a suspect or a motive as the investigation continues.

The sheriff's office opened its investigation Wednesday night after the shooting took place on Southeast Citrus Way, just off Florida Avenue. Residents in the area reported hearing three gunshots at around 8 p.m. The victim was airlifted to St. Mary's Hospital with injuries described by deputies as life-threatening at the time.

During the course of the investigation, one person was detained and a second individual was questioned by authorities. However, as of Thursday morning, neither person remained in custody and no charges had been filed. The sheriff's office later confirmed that the victim succumbed to injuries sustained in the shooting, elevating the case from a non-fatal shooting to a death investigation.

The case remains active, and no further details about a possible suspect, motive, or the relationship between the victim and those questioned have been made public. The shooting is one of several violent incidents reported recently across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County region, though it stands on its own as an open case with the Martin County Sheriff's Office continuing to work to determine what led to the gunfire on Southeast Citrus Way.

hero.headline: Former Officer Otto Lenke Sentenced to Death for Fort Pierce Bike Shop Murder
hero.body:
A judge has sentenced Otto Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, to death for the 2021 murder of Richard Benson, a Fort Pierce bike shop owner. Benson's family watched the sentencing via Zoom from out of state and was not present in the courtroom.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White, who prosecuted the case, said jealousy drove the killing. Benson had started dating a woman Lenke previously dated. During the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed jurors security video from inside the bike shop that they said captured Lenke not just killing Benson but torturing him beforehand. "He tormented him and basically made Richard's life a living hell, those last two minutes of his life by pouring that accelerant on him and lighting him on fire," White said.

White said Lenke used more than 20 years of law enforcement experience to plan and carry out the attack, believing his background would help him escape detection. "The defendant used his 20-plus years of experience in law enforcement to plan this attack, to carry out this attack," White said. He called the crime one of the most heinous in the circuit's history, noting it was captured on camera and carefully planned. "The jury got it right," White said. "This was probably one of the most heinous crimes in the history of our circuit. It was all caught on camera. It was well planned out."

The case is not finished. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to review all death sentences, and Lenke is expected to appeal his conviction. White said he believes the sentence delivers the outcome Benson's family sought. "I think this is something they wanted for Rich. This was justice," White said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Neighbors Push for Lighting on Boulevard After Fatal Crash
cards.teaser: Residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard say the under-construction corridor needs street lights now, after a fatal crash left them worried about pedestrians and drivers in the dark.
cards.body:
Residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for street lighting and other interim safety measures following a fatal crash on the roadway, which is in the middle of a Florida Department of Transportation widening project. Neighbor Howard Shapiro said the road lacks lighting, particularly in the early morning and at night, posing a risk to the children who walk along it to nearby schools.

"I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there," Shapiro said. He said the sidewalk FDOT is installing as part of the project will help, but that street lights need to be added as well. "They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's gonna be helpful. But street lights need to follow," he said.

FDOT is overseeing construction on a segment of Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Alcantara Boulevard and Parr Drive. The agency began work on the project in 2025 and, according to its website, crews are widening the road from two lanes to four while adding new sidewalks and lighting. Scott Samples, with the City of Port St. Lucie, said the finished project will improve both safety and traffic flow along the corridor. "We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway," Samples said.

When asked whether city staff could put in place any temporary safety measures to address residents' concerns while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility, not the city's. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can." FDOT has not said whether it will add any safety measures to the corridor following last week's fatal crash.

hero.headline: Martin County Commission Votes to Negotiate Deal to Restore MARTY Bus Service
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to authorize the county administrator to negotiate a new contract with MTM Transit to restore MARTY public bus service, which abruptly shut down last Thursday. The proposed deal, allowed under the county's emergency procurement rules, would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million.

The shutdown left several bus drivers without jobs, including Bill Lawrence, who worked for Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been operating MARTY. That company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as its reason for discontinuing service without warning. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days searching for a way to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county reviewed several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that has previously run the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. Commissioners also authorized county administration to begin terminating the county's contract with Martin County Transit LLC.

Getting the laid-off drivers back on the job is a top priority as negotiations move forward, Gorton said. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. During the one-year emergency contract, county officials plan to develop a standard multi-year agreement through the county's normal competitive bidding process. Officials said they hope to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow MARTY buses to resume operating as early as next week.

hero.headline: AG Vows Broader Corruption Crackdown After Fort Pierce Mimms Conviction
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is promising a broader crackdown on public corruption following the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms. A jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct but acquitted him of bid tampering in a case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels in Fort Pierce and a nonprofit connected to Mimms' niece, who served on the organization's board.

Prosecutors said Mimms used his position to benefit the nonprofit, which received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization for a community center that was never built. Prosecutors said Mimms later concealed his involvement in steering the award. Uthmeier said the evidence showed that "shenanigans took place" to ensure the nonprofit received the grant and that Mimms ultimately covered up his role. "He will be punished for abusing his office," Uthmeier said.

Uthmeier pointed to the conviction as an example of the state's broader effort to hold public officials accountable and said his office's Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway. He described the Mimms case as the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to announce. "We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take," Uthmeier said.

Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. "No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable," Keefe said. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Mimms is scheduled to be sentenced in December.

cards.headline: Otto Lenke Sentenced to Death for Fort Pierce Murder of Richard Benson
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce judge formally sentenced Otto Lenke to death for the 2021 murder of motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson. Lenke's sentence will now undergo an automatic review by the Florida Supreme Court.
cards.body:
Otto Lenke was formally sentenced to death Wednesday for the 2021 murder of Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, a killing that drew out through years of court proceedings before reaching this conclusion. Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn handed down the sentence, telling Lenke directly that the court's independent evaluation of the case led to the conclusion that death was the appropriate and just sentence for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson. Lenke sat motionless in the courtroom as the judge read the ruling.

Lenke, 67, was convicted in May 2026 of first-degree murder and arson in Benson's death. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank's Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators said the motive stemmed from a personal relationship: Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke, and prosecutors argued at trial that jealousy drove Lenke to kill him because he could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past.

Prosecutors said Lenke carefully planned the murder, using a car that day that belonged to his daughter so it would not be associated with him, and later cut up the gun used in the shooting and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, did not testify in his own defense during the trial.

Assistant prosecutors Brandon White and Justin Cormier said they were relieved by the judge's decision. White said Lenke would spend the rest of his life in solitary confinement until his death and that Benson's family had finally gotten justice after years of waiting. Cormier said prosecutors respected the judge's ruling and were glad justice could be served. Skip Thompson, a friend who worked with Benson at his motorcycle shop and attended every day of the trial, said he was glad Lenke received the death penalty but was concerned the case could return to court multiple times through the appeals process. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to automatically review every death sentence, meaning Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That review process could take years.

cards.headline: After Fatal Crash, Port St. Lucie Neighbors Push for Lighting on Port St. Lucie Boulevard
cards.teaser: Following a deadly crash, residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard say the road still needs street lights, even as a state widening project adds sidewalks and lanes.
cards.body:
Residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for street lighting after a fatal crash on the roadway last week. Neighbors say the stretch lacks adequate lighting at night and in the early morning hours, creating a hazard for pedestrians, drivers and schoolchildren who walk the area.

Howard Shapiro, who lives nearby, said he avoids walking in the area after dark because there are no lights. "I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there," Shapiro said. He said a new sidewalk under construction will help, but lighting needs to follow. "They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's gonna be helpful. But street lights need to follow," he said.

The Florida Department of Transportation is overseeing a project on a segment of Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Alcantara Boulevard and Parr Drive. Construction began in 2025, and according to FDOT, crews are widening the road from two lanes to four while adding new sidewalks and lighting. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said the completed project will improve safety. "We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway," Samples said.

When asked whether the city could provide temporary safety measures while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can."

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Council Approves Site Plan for Costco in Southern Grove
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a site plan for a new Costco store in the Southern Grove district, moving forward a $6 million land deal struck earlier this year.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a site plan application Monday for a new Costco store in the Southern Grove district, advancing a project tied to a $6 million land sale agreed to earlier this year. The approval brings the long-planned store closer to completion.

The new Costco will sit east of Southwest Village Parkway and south of the newly constructed Marshall Parkway. City leaders agreed earlier this year to sell the land to Costco for $6 million.

The store will be built next to a Costco distribution center that is currently under construction in the same area. The two projects together mark a significant expansion of Costco's presence in Southern Grove, a growing commercial corridor in Port St. Lucie.

With the site plan now approved, the project moves into its next phase of development. No opening date has been announced for the new store.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Woman Pleads Guilty to Exploiting Elderly Boca Raton Client
cards.teaser: Rachel Albert diverted nearly $20,000 from an elderly client through fraudulent checks and unauthorized credit card purchases. She was sentenced to jail time, probation and ordered to pay restitution.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman pleaded guilty Wednesday to exploiting an elderly client in Boca Raton, after prosecutors said she diverted nearly $20,000 from the victim through fraudulent checks and unauthorized credit card purchases. Rachel R. Albert, 57, entered the plea in a Palm Beach County courtroom to a charge of exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult, according to court documents.

Albert was sentenced to 364 days in the Palm Beach County jail and credited with 33 days already served. She will also serve three years of probation. The court ordered her to pay restitution to the victim and cover court costs.

According to a Boca Raton Police Department arrest report, Albert had access between November 2023 and October 2024 to the checkbook belonging to the victim and the victim's daughter. She wrote fraudulent checks totaling $15,330 and deposited them into her own bank account. Albert also had access to the victim's credit card for necessary purchases, but made unauthorized personal purchases totaling $2,711.35 on the card.

As part of her sentence, Albert is barred from contacting the victim, the victim's family or their property. She is also prohibited from working as a home health aide or in any capacity caring for a disabled adult or elderly person as defined under state law, including through a third party. The state attorney's office declined to pursue two additional counts of fraudulent use of personal identification information against Albert.

hero.headline: Former Melbourne Officer Sentenced to Death in Fort Pierce Mechanic's Murder
hero.body:
A former Melbourne police officer has been sentenced to death for killing a Fort Pierce motorcycle mechanic in 2021. Otto Lenke was found guilty in May of shooting and killing Richard Benson inside Benson's bike shop, Fast Frank's, which sits just down the street from Fort Pierce Police Department headquarters.

Prosecutors showed jurors surveillance video during the May trial proving that Lenke shot Benson, then poured denatured alcohol over his body and set him on fire while he was still alive. Prosecutors said the motive stemmed from Benson dating a woman Lenke had once been romantically involved with.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said justice was served and that he is pleased this part of the legal process is finished.

hero.headline: Martin County Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service Through MTM Transit Deal
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator begin negotiating a new contract with MTM Transit, aiming to restore MARTY public bus service that abruptly shut down last Thursday. The proposed deal, structured under the county's emergency procurement rules, would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million.

The service collapsed last week when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously running MARTY, suddenly stopped operations. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance expenses, as the reason for discontinuing service. The shutdown left riders without bus access and put several drivers out of work with no warning.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners Tuesday that county staff spent the past several days scrambling to find a replacement operator. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. After reviewing several proposals, county officials settled on MTM Transit, a company that has previously operated the county's bus system, as their preferred choice. Gorton said the one-year agreement would give the county time to develop a standard multi-year contract through its normal competitive bidding process. Commissioners also authorized administration to move forward with terminating the county's contract with Martin County Transit LLC.

Bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs in the shutdown is a top priority in the negotiations, according to Gorton. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Bill Lawrence, a former MARTY driver who was among those suddenly let go last Thursday, said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said. County officials say they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow bus service to resume as early as next week.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Ex-City Manager Mimms Convicted as AG Vows Corruption Crackdown
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms of official misconduct, and Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is pointing to the case as the opening move in a broader statewide crackdown on public corruption. Mimms was acquitted of bid tampering in the same trial. He is scheduled to be sentenced in December. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison.

The case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels in Fort Pierce and a nonprofit connected to Mimms' niece, who served on the organization's board. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to benefit the nonprofit and later concealed his involvement in the arrangement. The nonprofit received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization intended to fund a community center that was never built.

Uthmeier said evidence presented at trial showed "shenanigans took place" to ensure the nonprofit received the grant, and that Mimms ultimately covered up his role in the matter. "He will be punished for abusing his office," Uthmeier said. The attorney general declined to say what sentence he believes Mimms should receive, leaving that decision to the court in December.

Uthmeier cast the conviction as part of a larger state effort to root out corruption among public officials. "We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take," he said. He said his office's Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway and called the Mimms case the first of many public corruption prosecutions the state expects to announce. Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. "No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable," Keefe said.

cards.headline: Otto Lenke Sentenced to Death for Fort Pierce Murder of Richard Benson
cards.teaser: Otto Lenke, 66, has been sentenced to death for the 2021 killing and burning of Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson. The case had already drawn attention after a fellow inmate attacked Lenke inside the St. Lucie County Jail.
cards.body:
Otto Lenke, convicted of murdering Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Tuesday. The 66-year-old was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 in connection with Benson's 2021 death.

Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank's Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The killing happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators said the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke.

During the murder trial, prosecutors argued the killing was fueled by jealousy, saying Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. Prosecutors said Lenke carefully planned the murder, using a car belonging to his daughter that day so investigators would not connect it to him. He later cut up the gun used in the killing and disposed of it in pieces, according to prosecutors. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter.

The case drew local attention even before Tuesday's sentencing. While Lenke was awaiting retrial in the killing, fellow inmate Robert Castro, 30, was accused of attacking him inside a St. Lucie County Jail dorm on July 6, knocking off his glasses and cutting his nose, according to an arrest affidavit. Lenke's death sentence closes out the prosecution of Benson's killing.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Investigate Death of Man Found in Lincoln Park Lake
cards.teaser: A man in his 30s was pulled dead from a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are still working to notify his next of kin while they investigate how he ended up in the water.
cards.body:
A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. A citizen flagged down an officer just after 9 a.m. after spotting a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, according to Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago. Officers arrived and found the man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him from the lake, but he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police have identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin before releasing his name. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are trying to determine how he entered the water and what he was doing beforehand.

Santiago said there were no apparent signs of trauma on the man's body, though it appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the Lincoln Park area, speaking with potential witnesses and searching for surveillance footage that could help explain how the man ended up in the lake. Investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have carried the body to where it was found.

It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs played a role in the man's death, Santiago said. Police are waiting on the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Airport Schedule Change Renews Focus On Treasure Coast Travel Options
hero.body:
A schedule change to a Breeze Airways flight at Vero Beach Regional Airport is drawing new attention to how limited transportation options make travel difficult for Treasure Coast residents. The airline's route between the New York area and Vero Beach, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning, a shift that travelers say has disrupted their routines.

Peter Masella, who spoke about getting around the region, said, "In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around." He pointed to the absence of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying residents often must travel to other cities to find additional transportation options.

The Breeze Airways schedule change has created real complications for some flyers. A New York City physician said, "I'm a physician working in New York City, and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients' schedules two days in a row." Another traveler from Westchester, New York described the new logistics as a burden, saying, "Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It's very inconvenient."

At the same time, Breeze Airways has been expanding its presence at Vero Beach Regional Airport. Last month the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, adding to the airport's commercial flight options. Airport Director Brandon Dambeck said such changes are a normal part of how carriers manage their networks. "All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success," Dambeck said, explaining that airlines regularly evaluate route performance, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes. Travelers say they welcome the additional destinations, but argue that flight times fitting their schedules matter just as much as the number of places they can fly.

hero.headline: AG Cites Fort Pierce Manager's Conviction as First Case of New Corruption Unit
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier pointed to the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms as the first major result from the state's newly created public corruption unit, announcing at a press conference Wednesday that more than 25 active public corruption investigations are underway across Florida. Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier warned that additional charges against public officials are coming in the weeks ahead.

A St. Lucie County jury last week found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, while acquitting him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024 Mimms used his position to help a nonprofit organization secure the land deal, even though his niece served on the nonprofit's board, and that he later concealed his involvement and failed to disclose the family connection. Uthmeier said the nonprofit went on to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for a planned development on the property, but the infrastructure project never materialized.

"The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up," Uthmeier said. He said his office will continue investigating where the grant money went. "We'll keep digging," Uthmeier said. "I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going."

Uthmeier said the Mimms case reflects exactly the kind of conduct the public corruption unit was built to pursue. "This is the first big announcement," he said. "You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust." FDLE Commissioner Larry Keefe said rooting out public corruption is now a top priority for the agency. "When the people of Florida lose their sense of trust in their institutions, it's death by a thousand cuts," Keefe said. Sentencing for Mimms is expected at a later date. "This will be the first of many, sadly," Uthmeier said. "I hope we don't have to do too many, but we'll do as many as necessary to ensure the public knows that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers, and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take."

hero.headline: Martin County Terminates Transit Contract, Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin emergency negotiations with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service, which shut down abruptly last week and left hundreds of riders without transportation and 28 drivers without jobs. Commissioners approved the emergency action under the county's emergency procurement rules, aiming for a one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's transit system.

"We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton. The proposed deal with MTM Transit would serve as a temporary fix while county leaders work out a longer-term plan for public transportation. Gorton said restoring service quickly is essential so former drivers can return to their jobs. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," he said.

The sudden shutdown left transit workers scrambling. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said he and his coworkers are eager to get back on the road. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. With paychecks and benefits on hold, Lawrence said the wait has been financially painful. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," he said.

Gorton said the county is pushing to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit as soon as possible. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," he said. County leaders are continuing negotiations with MTM Transit and hope to complete an emergency operating contract within days. If the agreement is approved, officials say MARTY bus service could resume as early as next week, giving riders across Martin County back their transportation option and giving former drivers like Lawrence a path back to work. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," Lawrence said.

hero.headline: High-Speed I-95 Chase Ends in Arrest of Suspected Fentanyl Supplier Tied to Overdose Death
hero.body:
A suspected drug trafficker linked to a fatal fentanyl overdose is in custody after investigators say he hit a law enforcement vehicle and led detectives on a high-speed chase along I-95 through St. Lucie and Martin counties. James Arthur Green, 43, was arrested following a weeks-long narcotics investigation that also uncovered his suspected role in supplying the fentanyl that killed a person.

According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division made multiple undercover drug purchases during the investigation, gathering evidence that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died of an overdose. On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone to arrange another controlled narcotics buy, placing an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs.

Later that day, detectives carried out a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly took part in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine. When detectives moved to arrest him, Green fled, allegedly striking a sheriff's office vehicle before speeding onto southbound I-95. Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of about 115 mph, and detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone from his vehicle during the chase.

The Florida Highway Patrol and the Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it crossed into Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks and performed a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end. Investigators recovered the one pound of methamphetamine and two ounces of fentanyl tied to the controlled purchase, along with an additional 22 grams of methamphetamine, two grams of crack cocaine and one gram of fentanyl.

Through the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigation, Green faces charges including trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of cocaine, four counts of trafficking methamphetamine, sale of cocaine and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. The Florida Highway Patrol separately charged him with two counts of aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer, trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of methamphetamine, two counts of fleeing and eluding, tampering with evidence, reckless driving, dangerous excessive speeding and resisting an officer without violence. The sheriff's office said Green was already out on bond in an unrelated Miami-Dade County case at the time of his arrest and is now being held without bond. The investigation into the fatal overdose remains active.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Approves Lease for Marriott at Regional Airport
hero.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement Tuesday to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the Vero Beach Regional Airport, ending three years of negotiations over the project. Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

The hotel will sit just outside the gates of the airport terminal along Aviation Boulevard. Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said the project will improve the experience for travelers passing through the airport. "We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years," Dembeck said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience." Dembeck said passengers will be able to stay at the hotel while waiting for flights and walk straight over to the terminal.

The hotel is intended to serve more than just airport passengers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the project could draw new business investment to the area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said another major driver behind the hotel is its proximity to the Jackie Robinson Training Complex down the street. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said. He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" where families can enjoy virtual baseball. "Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players," Maxey said.

hero.headline: Martin County to negotiate $3M deal with MTM Transit to restart MARTY buses
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new one-year contract worth approximately $3 million with MTM Transit, aiming to restore MARTY bus service after it abruptly shut down last Thursday. The agreement would be reached under the county's emergency procurement rules.

MARTY service stopped last Thursday when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously running the system, discontinued operations and cited rising costs, including fuel and maintenance. The shutdown left several drivers without jobs, including Bill Lawrence, a former MARTY bus driver who said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, which had previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. During the one-year emergency contract, county officials plan to work toward a standard multi-year agreement through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs in last week's shutdown is a priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating the county's previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow MARTY buses to resume operating as soon as next week.

"This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

cards.headline: Martin County Terminates Transit Contract, Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service
cards.teaser: Commissioners voted to end the county's contract with Martin County Transit and fast-track an emergency deal with MTM Transit after last week's sudden shutdown left riders stranded and 28 employees out of work.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin negotiating an emergency one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's transit system. The action follows last week's abrupt shutdown of MARTY bus service, which left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs. County officials say the shutdown disrupted transportation across the community for residents who depend on MARTY buses to reach work, medical appointments and other essential destinations.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the county is using emergency procurement rules to quickly put a one-year contract in place with MTM Transit. "We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," Gorton said. He said restoring service depends on getting a new vendor under contract so former drivers can return to their jobs. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," Gorton said.

The shutdown left 28 employees suddenly unemployed, according to Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," Acevedo said. Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said he and his colleagues are ready to get back to work. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. Lawrence said the financial strain on drivers has been severe since the shutdown began. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," he said.

Gorton said the county is aiming to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit this week and resume bus service as early as next week. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. County leaders are continuing negotiations with MTM Transit and hope to complete the emergency operating contract in the coming days. Lawrence said he remains optimistic that drivers will soon be back on the road serving the community. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls for Chief Jeff Lee's Resignation
cards.teaser: More than 74% of St. Lucie County firefighters voted no confidence in Fire Chief Jeff Lee, and board member James Clasby says it's time for him to go. Scrutiny is also growing over the reassignment of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, who received a 92% no-confidence vote.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. More than 74% of firefighters who took part in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby said the vote should push the board to act. "I think it's a wake-up call," Clasby said. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." Asked whether that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The union vote also found that about 92% of participating firefighters had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol. Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December. A reassignment notice shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief, a decision Clasby questioned given the no-confidence numbers against him. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," Clasby said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and said the move had been under discussion for some time prior to recent events. In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters.

The no-confidence vote stems from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though all three have maintained the activity was consensual. Union representative Ryan Sapp, who represents the three firefighters in their fight for reinstatement, said previous settlement offers are now off the table and that Lee told him he does not believe a change in leadership would resolve the confidence or morale issues. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate the three firefighters and is working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled, with that effort expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.

hero.headline: Martin County to Negotiate $3M Deal With MTM Transit to Restore MARTY Bus Service
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new one-year contract worth approximately $3 million with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's public bus system. The move aims to restore MARTY bus service and rehire drivers after Martin County Transit LLC abruptly shut down operations last Thursday, citing rising operating costs including fuel and maintenance.

Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence was among those who suddenly lost their jobs when service stopped last week. He said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs is one of the county's top priorities in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they are hopeful a deal with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume operating as soon as next week.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls on Chief Lee to Resign After No-Confidence Vote
hero.teaser: More than 74% of St. Lucie County firefighters who voted said they have no confidence in Fire Chief Jeff Lee, and a fire board member says he should step down. The board is set to weigh reinstating three fired firefighters at its Oct. 21 meeting.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby said the vote should push the board toward action, including Lee's resignation. "I think it's a wake-up call," Clasby said. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." Asked whether that action should include Lee stepping down, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The no-confidence vote stems from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation. All three have maintained the activity was consensual. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. Their terminations sparked pushback from firefighters and community members, which led to the union vote. Union representative Ryan Sapp, who is representing the three firefighters in their push for reinstatement, said previous settlement offers are now off the table. Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership, who told him a change in leadership would not resolve the confidence or morale issues.

The vote comes as the district is already undergoing leadership changes. Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement effective in December, and a reassignment notice shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief. Clasby questioned that move given the no-confidence results against Gonzalez. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," he said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and that the move had been under discussion for some time before the recent controversy. In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while also working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled. That work is expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting. Sapp said the last settlement offer, which would have reinstated the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension, was not accepted.

cards.headline: Martin County Cancels Transit Contract, Fast-Tracks Deal to Restore MARTY Bus Service
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin emergency negotiations with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service within a week, following a sudden shutdown last week that left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs.

Commissioners approved the move under the county's emergency procurement rules, clearing the way for a one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's transit system. "We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton. The agreement is meant to serve as a temporary fix while county leaders work on a longer-term plan for public transportation.

The abrupt shutdown disrupted service for residents who depend on MARTY buses to reach jobs, medical appointments and other essential destinations, and it left 28 transit employees suddenly out of work. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. Gorton said rehiring those drivers depends on quickly finalizing a new contract. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," he said.

Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said he and his colleagues are ready to return to work and are counting on the county to move fast. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. With paychecks and benefits on hold since the shutdown, he said the financial strain is mounting. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," Lawrence said. Despite the uncertainty, he remains optimistic about getting back behind the wheel. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.

County officials said they are pushing to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit this week and resume bus service as soon as next week. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. Negotiations with MTM Transit are continuing, and county leaders say they hope to complete the emergency contract within days, a step that would restore transportation for riders across Martin County and open a path for former drivers to return to their jobs.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Approves Costco, Rehab Hospital and Entertainment District in Southern Grove
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved site plans for a 163,000-square-foot Costco, a 42-bed rehabilitation hospital and the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District, all along the Southern Grove jobs corridor.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for the Southern Grove area, the city's developing jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie. The plans include a long-awaited Costco retail store, an acute care rehabilitation hospital and the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District.

The Costco store will span 163,000 square feet. Scott Samples, with the City of Port St. Lucie, said the project has been in the works for a long time. "This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time," Samples said. "This is getting closer to the finish line." Samples said Costco still must close on the land and move through construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the Costco store marks the beginning of a new phase of growth for the area. The store will join other companies already based in Southern Grove, including Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers. McCurry said the jobs already established in the corridor are now drawing new commercial development. "They see all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see," McCurry said. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."

The council also approved a 5.5-acre site plan for the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District, which is set to bring restaurants and retail to the area. McCurry said the corridor has historically lacked dining, retail and entertainment options relative to its growing population. "This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities," McCurry said. "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come." The third approved plan sets aside space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital with 42 beds in a building of more than 55,000 square feet, offering both inpatient and outpatient services. McCurry said the hospital represents an expansion of health care access for the growing area. He said the three projects reflect a master plan city leaders set for Southern Grove two decades ago. "The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen," McCurry said.

hero.headline: Misplaced Cellphone Sparks False Weapon Rumor at Vero Beach High School
hero.body:
A misplaced cellphone in the cafeteria at Vero Beach High School triggered a false weapon rumor on Monday morning, though school officials confirmed there was no credible threat to students or staff. According to the School District of Indian River County, a student had left a cellphone in the cafeteria and hurried back to retrieve it. The confusion that followed caused inaccurate information to circulate among students, and that information eventually morphed into a rumor that a weapon was present at the school.

District officials stated clearly that the reported threat was not credible at any point. Vero Beach High School Principal Serra Finnegan sent families an update clarifying what had actually happened, according to the district. The explanation was meant to stop the spread of the rumor and reassure parents that the situation did not involve any actual danger.

The district also thanked the Indian River County Sheriff's Office for its partnership in responding to the situation. Officials encouraged families to help spread accurate information instead of repeating unverified rumors, noting how quickly such stories can travel among students on campus and across social media.

No weapon was ever found, and no credible threat was identified throughout the incident. The combined response from the school district and the sheriff's office was intended to calm concerns and make clear to the school community that the rumor did not reflect any real threat at Vero Beach High School.

hero.headline: Martin County Moves to Hire MTM Transit for $3M Emergency MARTY Bus Deal
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a one-year emergency contract worth roughly $3 million with MTM Transit, a move aimed at restoring MARTY public bus service after its abrupt shutdown last week. The decision comes days after Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been running MARTY, stopped service suddenly last Thursday, citing rising operating costs including fuel and maintenance.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days searching for a replacement operator. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county reviewed several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the proposed deal would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the normal competitive bidding process.

Commissioners also authorized county administration to begin terminating the county's existing contract with Martin County Transit LLC. Gorton said getting the former drivers back on the job is a top priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said.

Former MARTY driver Bill Lawrence, who lost his job when service halted last Thursday, said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said. County officials said they hope to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume running as early as next week.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls for Chief's Resignation After No-Confidence Vote
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters earlier this year. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said they had no confidence in district attorney Kim Sabol.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby called the results a wake-up call. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action," Clasby said. Asked whether that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The no-confidence vote stems from an investigation into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation. All three have said the activity was consensual. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. Boudrias said the firefighters involved "are all still friends." Union representative Ryan Sapp, who is representing the three firefighters in their push for reinstatement, said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote. "His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said. Sapp said a previous settlement offer to reinstate the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension was not accepted.

The leadership shakeup comes as Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December, and Gonzalez is being reassigned from assistant chief to battalion chief, according to a reassignment notice. Clasby questioned that move given the no-confidence vote against Gonzalez. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," he said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and that the move had been under discussion "for some time prior to recent events." In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin and is working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled, with that work expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting. Sapp said rebuilding trust in leadership could prove difficult given the vote's results, but added, "this is a great department. We have great men and women that work here. In light of all this bad publicity we've had, I promise you these members, these employees that I have, they genuinely enjoy serving this community and do the absolute best they can do."

hero.headline: Martin County Terminates MARTY Bus Contractor, Moves to Rehire Drivers
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin emergency negotiations with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service after last week's abrupt shutdown left hundreds of riders without transportation and 28 drivers out of work.

The county is pursuing a one-year emergency operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran Martin County's transit system. Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the county is acting under its emergency procurement rules to move quickly. "We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," Gorton said. He said getting a signed contract in place is essential to bringing drivers back to work. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," Gorton said.

The sudden shutdown disrupted transportation for residents who depend on MARTY buses to reach jobs, medical appointments and other essential destinations, according to county officials. It also left drivers scrambling. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. Former MARTY driver Bill Lawrence said he and his colleagues are ready to return to the road. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. He said the financial strain of being out of work without pay or benefits has been severe. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," Lawrence said.

County officials are working on an aggressive timeline to finalize the MTM Transit agreement and get buses running again. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. If the agreement is approved, officials say service could resume as early as next week, giving riders across Martin County their transportation option back and giving former drivers a path to return to their jobs. Lawrence said he's focused on getting back behind the wheel. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls on Chief Lee to Resign After No-Confidence Vote
cards.teaser: More than 74% of St. Lucie County firefighters voted no confidence in Fire Chief Jeff Lee, prompting a fire board commissioner to call for his resignation ahead of an Oct. 21 meeting on reinstating three fired firefighters.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters earlier this year. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby said the results should push the board to act. "I think it's a wake-up call," Clasby said. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." Asked whether that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The no-confidence vote stems from a third-party investigation into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. Investigators concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation. All three have said the activity was consensual. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. Their terminations drew pushback from firefighters and community members, which led to the union's no-confidence vote.

Union representative Ryan Sapp, who is representing the three firefighters in their push for reinstatement, said previous settlement offers are now off the table, including one that would have reinstated the three with a three-shift suspension. Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote. "His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said.

The vote comes as the district is already undergoing leadership changes. Sabol has submitted her retirement notice, effective in December, and a reassignment notice shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief. Clasby questioned that move given the no-confidence results against Gonzalez. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," he said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and that the move had been under discussion for some time before the recent controversy. In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while also working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled, with that work expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.
