cards.headline: Vero Beach Council Approves Lease for Marriott Hotel Near Airport
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council signed off on a lease agreement to build a four-story, 116-room Marriott near Vero Beach Regional Airport, a project tied to airport growth and the nearby Jackie Robinson Training Complex.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach City Council on Tuesday approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the area around Vero Beach Regional Airport. The hotel would sit just outside the terminal gates along Aviation Boulevard.

Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said the project has been in negotiations for three years. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience," Dembeck said. He said passengers will be able to stay at the hotel next door while waiting for flights and then walk straight over to the terminal.

The hotel is intended to serve more than just airport travelers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said it could help draw more businesses to Vero Beach and the surrounding area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said the hotel will also meet lodging demand from the nearby Jackie Robinson Training Complex. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said. He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" where kids can play virtual baseball before heading across the street to the diamond to play with Major League Baseball players. Developers said construction is expected to break ground next year, with completion targeted for the end of 2028.

He said passengers will be able to stay at the hotel next door, wait for their flight, and then walk straight over to the terminal.

The hotel is intended to serve more than just airport travelers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the project could help draw new businesses to Vero Beach and the surrounding area. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options," Cartland said. Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said the hotel will also meet lodging needs for families visiting the nearby Jackie Robinson Training Complex. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said.

Maxey said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" where children can play virtual baseball before heading across the street to the training complex diamond to play with major league players. Developers said construction is expected to break ground next year, with the hotel completed by the end of 2028.

hero.headline: UF/IFAS Extension Sets Fall Plant Sale Saturday in Fort Pierce
hero.teaser: The UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County Fall Plant Sale brings Florida-Friendly and native plants, workshops and garden tours to its Fort Pierce office Saturday, with a Friday accessibility event for those with mobility challenges.
hero.body:
The UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County Fall Plant Sale returns Saturday, Oct. 17, offering Florida-Friendly plants, including many native species, along with gardening advice for shoppers. The sale runs from 10 a.m. at the Extension office, 8400 Picos Road in Fort Pierce.

Quart-size plants are priced at $4, one-gallon plants at $7 and three-gallon plants at $12, all including tax. Shoppers can also take part in workshops and garden tours offered throughout sale hours, including a composting workshop scheduled from 10:30 to 11 a.m. An Ask an Expert session will also be available during the sale.

Ahead of the main event, the Extension office will host Mobility Day on Friday for people with accessibility challenges, running until noon. The event gives those with mobility issues a chance to shop and explore the sale offerings before the larger Saturday crowd arrives.

Proceeds from the sale and any donations collected will support educational programming through the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension in St. Lucie County. Additional details about the sale, including plant selection and scheduling, are available through the St. Lucie County event calendar.

The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

hero.headline: Martin County Commissioners OK Deal to Restore MARTY Bus Service

The vote came days after Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been operating MARTY, halted service and cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as the reason.

For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday's decision brought a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs when service stopped last week. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

"We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that has previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred option. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was among the drivers impacted when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously operating MARTY, abruptly stopped services last Thursday. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials say they are hopeful negotiations with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, potentially allowing buses to begin operating again next week. hero.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement Tuesday to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the Vero Beach Regional Airport, capping three years of negotiations over the project. The hotel will sit just outside the terminal gates along Aviation Boulevard.

Interim airport director Brian Dembeck said the project is designed to improve conditions for travelers passing through the airport. "We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years," Dembeck said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience." Dembeck said the hotel's location will let passengers stay nearby and walk straight to the terminal when it's time to fly. "They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."

The hotel's backers say its impact will reach beyond the airport. Brian Cartland, vice president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the new lodging option could help draw businesses to Vero Beach and the surrounding area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said the hotel is also meant to serve the Jackie Robinson Training Complex down the street. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said. He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" for young guests. "Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the major league baseball players," Maxey said. Developers expect to break ground on the project next year, with completion targeted for the end of 2028.

hero.headline: Martin County Advances Data Center Moratorium, But New Project Would Be Exempt
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to move forward with a one-year moratorium on new data center development as officials decide how to regulate the facilities going forward. The vote came one day after the county received its first-ever application for a data center in unincorporated Martin County, a hyper-scale facility of more than 950,000 square feet proposed on a lot off Kanner Highway west of I-95. Because that application was submitted before the moratorium was introduced, the project would not be subject to the new restrictions if they take effect.

Tuesday's vote marked the first of two required hearings on the moratorium. Commissioners are scheduled to take up the measure again on Oct. 27, when another vote will be needed before any pause on new data center projects could take effect. Commissioner Edward Ciampi said the moratorium gives the county room to gather input before moving forward. "An opportunity to say, 'pause,' let's hear from people, let's have the opportunity for experts to come and speak to us on both sides," Ciampi said. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county should take as much time as necessary before allowing more data centers to be built. "If it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, whatever it takes, whatever it takes, we should be doing this," Vargas said.

Residents who spoke at the meeting raised concerns about wildlife, water use and noise tied to large-scale data center development. Sergei Kelley told commissioners the facilities threaten rural land and the animals that depend on it. "For me it's wildlife so these areas are in largely rural or large plots of land and so you take that area and develop it and these facilities are massive, millions and millions of square feet, no animals can live there anymore, or the hum is going to affect the animals," Kelley said. Martin County resident Scott Butler pointed to the amount of water the facilities require. "The fear of the use of all this water we have," Butler said, adding residents need a clearer picture of "what these data centers are going to use."

Other residents urged commissioners to slow down before approving any new industrial development. One resident told commissioners that "once land is converted into industrial use the consequences can remain long after." Another said the county needs "serious studies completed in order to go forward with something of this consideration." The hyper-scale proposal off Kanner Highway is moving forward under current county rules even as commissioners weigh whether to restrict future projects. The Oct. 27 vote will determine whether the one-year moratorium takes effect for data center applications submitted after Monday.
